description: Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along the local second tangential direction (X2, the optical-element vertical direction) in the right-handed local optical-element frame (X1, X2, z).
documentation:
Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along the local second tangential ($X_2$, optical-element vertical) direction is the signed radius of the front-surface normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$ and $\hat{z}$ in the right-handed local optical-element frame $(\hat{X}_1,\hat{X}_2,\hat{z})$. The coordinates $x_1$ and $x_2$ lie in the local tangent plane at the surface vertex, and $z$ is the local front-surface-normal sag coordinate. This is a radius of curvature, not a reciprocal curvature.

At the surface vertex, after subtracting planar tilt so that $\partial z/\partial x_2=0$ there, the signed radius is defined by the second derivative of the sag in the $X_2$ normal section:

$$
\frac{1}{R_2} = \left.\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x_2^2}\right|_{x_2=0}
$$

where $z(x_2)$ is the front-surface sag along $\hat{z}$, $x_2$ is displacement along $\hat{X}_2$, and $R_2$ is this signed radius; $z$, $x_2$, and $R_2$ are in meters. For small sag this definition implies $z(x_2)-z(0)\simeq x_2^2/(2R_2)$ near the vertex, and a flat section is the limiting case $1/R_2=0$.

For spherical surface models the first- and second-local-tangential radii of the front surface are equal. For cylindrical, toroidal, or separably curved surface models they may differ, so this quantity is distinct from the orthogonal first-local-tangential front-surface quantity x_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element and from the rear-surface quantity [vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element); [vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:second_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element) uses the same second-local-tangential front-surface radius convention.

Sign convention: Positive when the center of curvature of the front surface in the normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$ and $\hat{z}$ lies on the $+\hat{z}$ side of the local tangent plane.

description: Radial e-folding decay length of the ion heat flux in the scrape-off layer, defined by its outward logarithmic decrease.
documentation:
The ion heat decay length in the scrape-off layer (SOL) is the radial distance over which the ion heat-flux profile falls to $1/e$ of its separatrix value, characterizing the spatial scale of ion heat exhaust across the open-field-line region.

The decay length is defined by the inverse magnitude of the outward logarithmic radial gradient of the ion heat flux $q_i$:

$$
\lambda_{q,i} = \left| \frac{\partial \ln q_i}{\partial r} \right|^{-1}
$$

where $r$ is radial distance measured outward from the separatrix and $q_i$ is the ion contribution to the heat flux. This species-resolved quantity is the ion-channel specialization of [heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer); the corresponding electron channel is [electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer). It excludes the electron heat contribution and any unspecified total heat-flux combination.

description: Signed first local-tangential coordinate of each optical fiber center in the bundle-local (X1, X2) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed position of an individual optical-fiber center along the first local-tangential axis of its fiber bundle. It describes the fiber-bundle geometry in the local $(X_1, X_2)$ coordinate frame, not a machine-coordinate position.

For a fiber center, the coordinate is defined by

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r}_f - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $x_1$ is the first local-tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_f$ is the position vector of the individual fiber center, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the fiber-bundle local frame, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the oriented unit vector along its first local-tangential axis.

The quantity applies to individual fibers belonging to the fiber bundle. Each fiber center has its own coordinate; no summation, averaging, or replacement by the bundle geometric center is implied. It is distinct from the bundle's machine-frame [vertical coordinate], which uses the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The local-coordinate meaning is shared with [first local-tangential coordinate of a reflector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflector), but the intrinsic owning object here is the fiber bundle and the coordinate refers to fiber centers rather than reflector-outline vertices.

Sign convention: Positive when the fiber-center displacement from the local-frame origin has a component in the direction of the oriented first local-tangential axis.

description: IPB98(y,2) empirical-scaling reference for global energy confinement time, providing the denominator for the H98 confinement enhancement factor.
documentation:
The IPB98(y,2) energy confinement time is the global energy-confinement timescale predicted by the IPB98(y,2) empirical scaling law. It is an energy-channel performance benchmark rather than a species-resolved or local transport time.

The underlying global energy confinement time is defined by

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the global energy confinement time, $W$ is the total thermal energy stored in the plasma, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power leaving the plasma. The quantity documented here is the IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction of this timescale, not the directly evaluated confinement time for a particular plasma state.

The value applies to the complete plasma energy content and its global loss balance; it is not a local profile quantity, a particle confinement time, or a confinement time assigned to an individual species. It is a single empirical reference value for the energy channel.

The [energy confinement enhancement factor](name:energy_confinement_enhancement_factor) compares the actual global energy confinement time with this reference through $H_{98} = \tau_E / \tau_{E,98}$, where $H_{98}$ is the dimensionless confinement enhancement factor and $\tau_{E,98}$ is this IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction.

concepts.definition: The content of a confined quantity divided by the net rate at which it is lost.

description: Predicted equivalent blackbody temperature of extraordinary-mode electron cyclotron emission evaluated at a frequency-selective ECE channel.
documentation:
The extraordinary-mode radiative temperature is the blackbody-equivalent temperature assigned to the predicted electron cyclotron emission in the extraordinary polarization at an ECE channel. It represents radiation intensity, not the kinetic temperature of the emitting electrons.

The defining radiance equivalence is

$$
I_{\nu,X} = B_\nu\left(T_{\mathrm{rad},X}\right)
$$

where $I_{\nu,X}$ is the predicted extraordinary-mode spectral radiance, $\nu$ is the channel's selected emission frequency, $X$ identifies the extraordinary polarization, $B_\nu$ is the blackbody spectral-radiance function, and $T_{\mathrm{rad},X}$ is the corresponding radiative temperature.

This quantity is resolved for the extraordinary polarization and evaluated at the frequency associated with one ECE channel; it is not a sum over channels, polarizations, or emission modes, and it excludes the ordinary-mode contribution. The [radiative ordinary-mode temperature at an ECE channel](name:radiative_ordinary_mode_temperature_at_ece_channel) is the corresponding ordinary-polarization quantity, while [radiative temperature at an ECE channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel) denotes the channel-level radiation temperature without this extraordinary-mode restriction. Differences between the predicted extraordinary-mode value and a measured channel radiation temperature can indicate mode coupling or optical-depth effects.

dd_sources.documentation: Predicted radiation temperature of the e(X)traordinary mode

description: Instantaneous equivalent-electron hydrogen source rate delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection systems; each hydrogen atom contributes one equivalent-electron count.
documentation:
The hydrogen source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral hydrogen atoms are admitted to the plasma vessel by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. Because hydrogen has atomic number one, each atom contributes one equivalent-electron count.

The defining relation is:

$$
\dot{S}_{\mathrm{H}} = Z_{\mathrm{H}}\dot{N}_{\mathrm{H}} = \dot{N}_{\mathrm{H}}, \qquad Z_{\mathrm{H}} = 1
$$

where $\dot{S}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the neutral hydrogen-atom delivery rate in atoms per second, and $Z_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the hydrogen atomic number. This is the hydrogen component of the total [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection). Its time integral gives the accumulated hydrogen inventory [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection].

Sign convention: Positive when hydrogen gas is being delivered into the vessel, increasing the equivalent-electron inventory.

description: Duration of a single frequency sweep during which a probing electromagnetic wave is launched.
documentation:
Launched wave duration is the time interval of one complete swept-frequency launch of a probing electromagnetic wave. It is defined by the start and end times of the same launched-wave sweep, independent of how any received signal is analyzed.

For a sweep beginning at $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and ending at $t_{\mathrm{end}}$, the launched wave duration is:

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}} = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}}$ is the launched wave duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the sweep start and end times, all measured in seconds.

The corresponding launched frequency during this interval is described by launched_wave_frequency. This quantity specifies only the duration of the complete sweep; it does not define the detailed frequency waveform, dwell time at individual frequencies, received-wave interval, or signal-analysis interval.

description: Major-radius coordinate of an optical element’s geometric center or local-geometry origin, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius location of an optical element’s geometric reference point: its center for circular geometry or the origin defining the local geometry of a planar element.

For the reference point, the major radius is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. Equivalently, $R$ is the radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies only to the optical element’s designated center or local-geometry origin and represents a single-point coordinate, not an average over the element or the radial size or curvature of any optical surface. It is therefore distinct from a radius describing the element’s shape.

This quantity is an optical-element specialization of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), which defines the same major-radius concept for a general geometric point or reference position.

description: Parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection is the signed, field-aligned component of the effective convection velocity representing transport of momentum carried by neutrals in a resolved internal state. The parallel direction is along the local magnetic field.
documentation:
Parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection is the scalar component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of an effective convection velocity for transport of momentum carried by a neutral population in one resolved internal state. It is a transport velocity for momentum, not the neutral bulk-flow velocity itself.

The scalar projection is defined by

$$
v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}}$ is this parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding [neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection), and $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/\lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

The scope is a single resolved neutral internal state, so no summation or averaging over internal states is implied. This quantity is the field-aligned component only; it excludes perpendicular components, particle-density convection velocities, energy convection velocities, diffusivities, and source terms. In a convective momentum-transport closure, it is the effective velocity factor associated with the transported neutral internal-state momentum.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of the effective convection velocity is in the direction of the local magnetic field.

description: Dimensionless ratio of thermal radiation emitted by a surface to blackbody radiation at the same surface temperature, with the stated spectral and angular averaging.
documentation:
Surface emissivity is the effectiveness of a material surface in emitting thermal electromagnetic radiation relative to an ideal blackbody at the same temperature. It is a material property of the emitting surface and is distinct from the emitted energy flux described by [energy flux due to surface emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

The effective emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{M_{\mathrm{emit}}(T_s)}{M_{\mathrm{bb}}(T_s)}
$$

where $M_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the surface thermal radiative exitance, $M_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the blackbody exitance, and $T_s$ is the surface temperature. The ratio applies to the specified spectral band and angular averaging; it is not a wavelength- and direction-resolved emissivity. Incident radiation and geometric surface area, such as [optical-element area], are excluded.

description: Wetted area of the divertor is the sum, over the included divertor target surfaces, of the target-surface footprint area where deposited heat flux is at least one e-folding below that target's peak deposited heat flux.
documentation:
Wetted area of the divertor is the aggregate area of the heat-flux footprint on the included divertor target surfaces. For each target surface, the wetted region is the subset of the plasma-facing target surface where deposited heat flux is at least one e-folding below the peak deposited heat flux on that target.

The aggregate area is the sum of the per-target wetted areas:

$$
A_{\mathrm{wet,div}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} A_{\mathrm{wet},i}
$$

where $\mathcal{T}$ is the set of included divertor target surfaces and $A_{\mathrm{wet},i}$ is the [wetted area of divertor target](name:wetted_area_of_divertor_target) for target $i$.

The included target set consists of the plasma-facing divertor target surfaces of the divertor assembly being described; non-target divertor structures and areas below the heat-flux threshold are excluded. This quantity is a non-negative scalar area, not a signed projected area.

description: Dimensionless statistical weight assigning each Monte Carlo marker the number of real particles it represents, expressed as a real-particle count divided by the simulated marker count.
documentation:
This quantity is the statistical weight of one Monte Carlo particle marker: the number of real physical particles represented by that marker. It converts a discrete marker ensemble into the corresponding physical particle population.

$$
w = \frac{N_{\mathrm{real}}}{N_{\mathrm{sim}}}
$$

where $w$ is the marker weight, $N_{\mathrm{real}}$ is the represented real-particle count, and $N_{\mathrm{sim}}$ is the simulated-particle count associated with the marker. The weight is dimensionless and may be used to form macroscopic distribution moments by weighting marker contributions. It is the ratio-valued derivative of particle_simulated_count, while particle_count denotes the corresponding particle-count quantity rather than the marker weight itself.

description: Local volumetric rate of energy release from all included nuclear-fusion reaction channels, including energy carried by charged particles and neutrons.
documentation:
Fusion power density is the local energy-release rate generated by nuclear-fusion reactions per unit volume. It may represent a specific reaction channel or the channel-summed quantity, with unqualified fusion power density understood as the sum over included channels.

The defining reaction-rate sum is

$$
P_{\mathrm{fus}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{n_{a,r}(\mathbf{x})\,n_{b,r}(\mathbf{x})}{1+\delta_{a_rb_r}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_r\,E_r
$$

where $r$ indexes fusion channels, $n_{a,r}$ and $n_{b,r}$ are reactant number densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_r$ is the reaction-rate coefficient in m$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_r$ is the energy released per reaction in joules, and $\delta_{a_rb_r}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise. The deuterium–deuterium and deuterium–tritium instances are represented by [deuterium-deuterium fusion power density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion). This energy-release quantity includes neutron and charged-particle product energy and is distinct from [fusion neutron emissivity].

description: Minimum geometric clearance between the plasma separatrix and the nearest limiter or wall element, evaluated at the closest-wall point.
documentation:
The gap is the shortest geometric separation between the plasma separatrix, or last closed flux surface, and the nearest wall or limiter element. It quantifies the boundary clearance at the wall location where this separation is smallest.

$$
g_{\mathrm{cw}} = \min_{\mathbf{x}_s \in \mathcal{S},\,\mathbf{x}_w \in \mathcal{W} \cup \mathcal{L}} \left\|\mathbf{x}_s - \mathbf{x}_w\right\|
$$

Here, $g_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the closest-wall gap, $\mathcal{S}$ is the plasma separatrix, $\mathcal{W}$ is the wall surface, $\mathcal{L}$ is the limiter surface, $\mathbf{x}_s$ and $\mathbf{x}_w$ are points on those surfaces, and $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean distance.

The quantity is an aggregate minimum over the full separatrix and all relevant wall or limiter elements, rather than a separation at an arbitrary boundary location. It excludes the position coordinate of the gap reference point; that coordinate is represented separately by the [major-radius coordinate of the plasma-boundary gap reference point](name:radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

description: Toroidal electromotive force evaluated on the last closed flux surface that drives the conventionally signed ohmic plasma current.
documentation:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the toroidal electromotive force associated with the inductive electric field around the last closed magnetic-flux surface. It is the net voltage available to drive the ohmic component of the confined plasma current.

For a closed toroidal contour $C$ on the last closed flux surface, the loop voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{loop}} = \oint_C \mathbf{E} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the loop voltage, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector, $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is the directed line element, and $C$ is oriented in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. The quantity is a contour-integrated scalar evaluated at the plasma boundary, not a local electric-field component or an external-coil terminal voltage.

This boundary quantity represents the total loop voltage driving plasma current, including the inductive contribution associated with changing poloidal magnetic flux. It excludes no plasma-current-driving contribution merely because it is externally generated; the narrower [external loop voltage](name:external_loop_voltage) denotes only the externally generated contribution and is therefore not equivalent to the total boundary loop voltage.

The loop voltage is related to the ohmic plasma-current drive through the toroidal component of the electric field and the plasma conductivity. The right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame uses $R$ for major radius, $\phi$ for toroidal angle, and $Z$ for vertical height.

Sign convention: Positive when the electromotive force drives conventional plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

description: Signed component along the z axis of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror's translation direction or rotation axis at its home position, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
Signed component along the z axis of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror's translation direction or rotation axis at its home position is the scalar projection of that mirror direction vector onto the z-axis basis direction in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The $\hat{z}$ basis direction is vertical.

For mirror direction unit vector $\mathbf{u}$, the component is defined by:

$$
u_z = \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert = 1
$$

where $u_z$ is the z-axis component of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror direction unit vector, $\mathbf{u}$ is the unit vector defining that mirror's translation direction or rotation axis at its home position, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the positive z-axis basis vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, and $\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert$ is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbf{u}$.

The quantity applies to an individual electron-cyclotron launcher mirror at its home position. It is a single Cartesian component of the movement direction or rotation axis, not an aggregate over launchers or mirrors and not an average over a range of mirror motion.

It is not a mirror position, displacement, the [vertical coordinate] of a point, or the [angle of the electron-cyclotron launcher mirror]. The corresponding [x-axis component](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [y-axis component](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) complete the same home-position unit vector; with $u_x$ and $u_y$ denoting those linked components, the components satisfy $u_x^2 + u_y^2 + u_z^2 = 1$.

description: Imaginary part of the radial flux-coordinate component of the complex first-order perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction in the confined plasma, for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis. It is not the cylindrical major-radius component.
documentation:
Imaginary part of the radial perturbed plasma magnetic field is the imaginary component of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the confined plasma. It applies to one toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis and to the radial coordinate component in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

The complex radial component is decomposed into real and imaginary parts as:

$$
\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) = \delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) + i\,\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta)
$$

where $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$ is the radial flux-coordinate component of the complex perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}$ is the corresponding [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ is this quantity, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\rho$ is the radial flux coordinate, and $\theta$ is the poloidal flux coordinate.

The scope is the confined-plasma region for the specified toroidal mode; it excludes the perturbed magnetic field in the vacuum region, any sum over toroidal mode numbers, and any real-valued instantaneous perturbation obtained after applying a toroidal and temporal phase factor. The radial direction here is the coordinate direction associated with increasing $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; it is distinct from the major-radius $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is a local eigenfunction component, not a flux-surface average, volume integral, or magnitude.

Together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), this quantity forms the complex radial component $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$. Together with the [poloidal](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) imaginary components, it forms the imaginary vector part of the perturbed plasma magnetic-field eigenfunction. The overall complex phase of a linear eigenfunction is arbitrary, so a phase rotation mixes the real and imaginary parts while leaving the represented complex eigenfunction unchanged.

Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary radial component points toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ for the adopted complex eigenfunction phase.

description: Signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique passive conductor loop-element cross-section, measured counterclockwise from the outward radial direction in the poloidal plane.
documentation:
The alpha angle is the signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique, trapezoidal or parallelogram-shaped cross-section of one passive conductor loop element. It specifies the orientation of that element’s cross-sectional geometry in the poloidal plane.

The angle is defined from the directed first-axis vector:

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}},\,\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha inclination angle, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the directed first axis of the cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward radial unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the upward vertical unit vector, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the radial component to the vertical component. These directions are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies independently to each passive loop element and to its own oblique cross-section; it is not an aggregate angle for a complete passive loop or a collection of elements. It describes the first cross-sectional axis only, not the transverse dimensions of the element and not the overall loop reference-axis inclination represented by the [tilt angle of the passive loop](name:tilt_angle_of_passive_loop). The alpha angle supplies orientation information for interpreting the element’s other cross-sectional geometry, but does not determine those dimensions.

Sign convention: Positive when the first axis rotates counterclockwise from the outward radial direction toward the positive vertical direction in the poloidal plane.

description: Local volumetric rate of nuclear energy deposition in limiter-tile material from neutron interactions and associated absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation.
documentation:
Nuclear power density of a limiter tile is the local volumetric energy deposition rate within the material of one limiter tile caused by neutron interactions and associated gamma-radiation absorption. It is the nuclear contribution to the broader [power density of a limiter tile], not the total local energy source.

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{tile}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the nuclear power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the material volume of the limiter tile, and $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the corresponding [nuclear power of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_limiter_tile).

The quantity includes energy deposited volumetrically by neutron scattering and capture and by absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation. Surface heat loads, externally applied heating, and nonnuclear energy-transfer mechanisms are excluded.

description: Real part of the complex first-order plasma pressure perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
documentation:
The real part of the complex pressure perturbation eigenfunction $\tilde{p}$ gives the in-phase component of the linearized first-order pressure variation associated with a given toroidal MHD mode, distributed over the poloidal cross-section.

The full pressure field decomposes as:

$$
p = p_0 + \text{Re}\!\left[\tilde{p}(R,Z)\, e^{i(n_\phi \phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $p_0$ is the equilibrium pressure profile, $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex MHD eigenfrequency. The quantity $\text{Re}(\tilde{p})$ is the real component of the parent eigenfunction perturbed_plasma_pressure evaluated on the poloidal plane.

Together with the [perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part), it fully specifies the complex amplitude and phase of $\tilde{p}$; the amplitude is $|\tilde{p}| = \sqrt{\text{Re}(\tilde{p})^2 + \text{Im}(\tilde{p})^2}$. Analogous real-part eigenfunctions for other linearized MHD perturbation quantities include [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

This quantity is produced by linear MHD stability solvers as part of the eigenvalue problem on the poloidal grid. Because the eigenfunction phase is fixed by the solver normalization convention, the absolute sign of $\text{Re}(\tilde{p})$ is convention-dependent; only relative magnitudes and phase angles among the perturbed quantities in the same eigenfunction carry physical content.

description: Signed terminal-potential difference across a resistive shunt, providing the voltage used with its resistance to determine current in an associated structure segment.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed electrical potential difference between the two terminals of a shunt resistor. It applies to the shunt element associated with a divertor or vessel structure segment, rather than to an individual terminal potential or a voltage across another circuit element.

The defining terminal difference is

$$
V_{\mathrm{shunt}} = V_{\mathrm{first}} - V_{\mathrm{second}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{shunt}}$ is the shunt terminal voltage, $V_{\mathrm{first}}$ is the electric potential of the first terminal, and $V_{\mathrm{second}}$ is the electric potential of the second terminal.

The quantity is a direct terminal difference, with no spatial averaging or charge-state aggregation. For an ohmic shunt, the associated structure-segment current $I_{\mathrm{shunt}}$ is related to this voltage and the [resistance of the shunt](name:resistance_of_shunt), $R_{\mathrm{shunt}}$, by $I_{\mathrm{shunt}} = V_{\mathrm{shunt}}/R_{\mathrm{shunt}}$. It does not itself represent the current or the shunt resistance.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric potential of the first shunt terminal exceeds that of the second shunt terminal.

This quantity gives the major-radius coordinate of a point on the geometric outline of an antenna strap. It identifies the point's perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is pointwise and unaggregated over the antenna-strap outline: each value applies to one outline point. It does not represent the strap's reference-point coordinate, center coordinate, radial extent, or outer-radius bound.

The complementary [toroidal angle of the antenna strap](name:toroidal_angle_of_antenna_strap) specifies the angular location of the same outline point. The [radial coordinate of the antenna strap](name:radial_coordinate_of_antenna_strap) instead locates a specified strap geometry reference point and is therefore not interchangeable with this outline coordinate.

description: Geometric equilibrium coefficient with inverse-square major-radius scaling, spanning direct reciprocal-square factors and flux-coordinate metric ratios in toroidal plasma geometry.
documentation:
This quantity is a geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium whose scale contains the reciprocal square of the [major radius]. It includes both direct inverse-square radius factors and geometric factors formed from a flux-coordinate gradient divided by the squared major radius.

Its common form is

$$
G = \frac{g}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is the geometric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius, and $g$ is a dimensionless geometric factor. For [inverse_of_square_of_major_radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius), $g=1$; for [ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius), $g$ is the squared magnitude of the gradient of the toroidal flux coordinate.

The quantity is a metric factor for flux-coordinate equilibrium and transport formulations, not the major radius or its square itself. Its specific numerator is determined by the concrete member of this geometric-coefficient family.

description: Vector-potential perturbation associated with a change in the plasma magnetic field relative to a reference state, retaining radial, poloidal, and toroidal components.
documentation:
The perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential is the vector-valued departure of the plasma magnetic vector potential from its reference state. Its curl determines the associated perturbed magnetic field, subject to the chosen vector-potential gage.

The perturbation is defined by

$$
\delta \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\delta \mathbf{A}$ is the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the plasma magnetic vector potential, and $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is its reference-state value. The associated magnetic-field perturbation satisfies $\delta \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{A}$, where $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic field and $\nabla$ is the spatial differential operator.

This quantity denotes the complete perturbation vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It includes the radial, poloidal, and toroidal components without summing their signed projections. The [radial perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential), [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential), and [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential) are component-specific instances of this vector quantity.

The perturbation excludes the reference-state contribution and is distinct from the full [plasma magnetic vector potential](name:plasma_magnetic_vector_potential), which includes both reference and perturbed parts. Because a vector potential is gage-dependent, only its curl determines the corresponding magnetic-field perturbation uniquely.

Sign convention: Positive when a resolved component of $\delta \mathbf{A}$ points along its defined positive radial, poloidal, or toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
label_note: delta A = A - A_ref with curl relation; links resolve; minor: lists a poloidal component while naming the cylindrical frame, and 'gage'

description: Net toroidal plasma current generated non-inductively by electron-cyclotron wave absorption and resonant wave–particle interactions, summed over all wave sources.
documentation:
This quantity is the net toroidal plasma current attributable to electron-cyclotron wave-driven current generation. It excludes inductive current and current produced by other non-inductive mechanisms.

The total driven current is the toroidal projection of the driven current density integrated over a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{EC}} = \int_A j_{\phi,\mathrm{EC}}(R,Z)\,dA
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{EC}}$ is the electron-cyclotron-driven current-density component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $A$ is the plasma cross-sectional area in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $dA$ is its differential area. The quantity is a current contribution, not the absorbed electron-cyclotron wave power; its broader wave-driven-current counterpart is [current due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Sign convention: Positive when the driven current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

label_note: cross-section integral of the EC-driven toroidal current density; I per registry; sign follows increasing phi; link resolves

description: Relative phase angle of a reflected radio-frequency power-wave phasor at an antenna element in an ion-cyclotron heating launcher, measured relative to the forward power-wave phasor of that same element.
documentation:
This quantity is the relative phase of a complex reflected radio-frequency power-wave phasor at a selected antenna strap or module with respect to the complex forward radio-frequency power-wave phasor of the same strap or module. It specifies the element-local reflection phase of an ion-cyclotron heating launcher rather than an absolute phase or an inter-element phase.

For element $i$, the reflected phase is defined by

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{ref},i} = \arg\!\left(b_i^{\mathrm{ref}} (a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}})^*\right) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\phi_{\mathrm{ref},i}$ is this reflected phase, $b_i^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the complex reflected power-wave phasor at element $i$, $a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the complex forward power-wave phasor at the same element, $(a_i^{\mathrm{fwd}})^*$ is its complex conjugate, and $\arg$ extracts the phase angle. The phase is defined modulo $2\pi$.

The scope is a single selected launcher strap or module and the pair of forward and reflected traveling power waves at the same element reference plane. The forward wave propagates toward the antenna element, and the reflected wave propagates away from the antenna element toward the feeding network. The first launcher element is not the phase reference for this quantity, and the quantity is not averaged or summed over launcher elements.

This quantity is a reflected-wave member of the broader [phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna] family. It is distinct from the [wave phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), which describes inter-element phasing, and together with the [reflected power of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) it specifies the phase-and-magnitude state of the reflected power wave without including the magnitude itself.

Sign convention: Positive when the reflected-wave phasor at the selected element leads the forward-wave phasor at the same element in phase under the adopted temporal phasor convention.

description: Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region.
documentation:
The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase reference of that complex eigenfunction.

$$
A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential.

Sign convention: Positive when the real radial projection points toward increasing major radius $R$.

description: Vector Fick's-law transport coefficient relating the diffusive momentum flux to the local momentum-density gradient, abstracting over plasma species, neutral populations, charge states, and directional projections in a magnetized plasma.
documentation:
Momentum diffusivity is the proportionality coefficient between the diffusive momentum flux and the negative local gradient of momentum density, following a Fick's-law closure for the fluid momentum balance. Physically, it encapsulates contributions from collisional viscosity, turbulent mixing, charge-exchange friction, and diamagnetic drifts. As a vector quantity, its radial, poloidal, toroidal, parallel, and vertical components capture the strongly anisotropic transport characteristic of magnetized plasma, where diffusivity along magnetic field lines greatly exceeds cross-field values.

The diffusive momentum flux density component along direction $\hat{e}_i$ is

$$
\Gamma_{m,i} = -D_{m,i} \frac{\partial (m n v_i)}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $D_{m,i}$ is the momentum diffusivity component, $m$ is particle mass, $n$ is number density, and $v_i$ is the fluid velocity component along $\hat{e}_i$, making $m n v_i$ the local momentum density.

This parent name abstracts over species-resolved and process-attributed children including plasma_momentum_diffusivity for the total plasma and analogous neutral-population variants; the [radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:flux_surface_normal_plasma_momentum_diffusivity) is the cross-field specialization and [parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity) is the field-aligned form. Values are inferred from fluid transport simulations by computing the diffusive momentum flux relative to the local momentum-density gradient, or estimated analytically from neoclassical and turbulence theory.
label_note: link label radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient points at flux_surface_normal_plasma_momentum_diffusivity; also calls a diffusivity a vector and attributes diamagnetic drifts to it

description: Length of the minor, beta-inclined side of a parallelogram-shaped cross-section in a passive conductor element.
documentation:
The beta-inclined side length is the geometric length of a parallelogram-shaped cross-section of a passive conductor element.

For the endpoints of the beta side, the length is defined by

$$
\ell_{\beta} = \left\|\mathbf{r}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{r}_{\beta,1}\right\|
$$

where $\ell_{\beta}$ is the beta-side length, $\mathbf{r}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its two endpoints, and the norm is the Euclidean distance between those endpoints.

This quantity applies to one passive-loop conductor element and to its minor, beta-inclined side only; it is not an aggregate over multiple elements, the alpha-inclined major side, or the cross-sectional thickness. The beta-side convention identifies this dimension as the minor counterpart of the alpha-side dimension.

It is the minor-side component of the broader [length of a passive loop element](name:length_of_passive_loop_element), which covers either inclined side. The corresponding major-side quantity is the [major length of a passive loop element](name:major_length_of_passive_loop_element); the two side lengths describe distinct directions of the same oblique cross-section.

description: Projection magnitude of the refractive-index vector onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field, equal to the perpendicular wave-vector magnitude normalized by the vacuum wave number.
documentation:
The perpendicular refractive index $N_\perp$ is the magnitude of the component of the refractive-index vector projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field direction. It is the field-normal part of the dimensionless wave-propagation vector used to describe electromagnetic waves in a magnetized plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
N_\perp = \left|\mathbf{N} - (\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b})\hat{b}\right|, \qquad \mathbf{N}=\frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0=\frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{N}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number, $\omega$ is angular frequency, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field.

This scalar is the nonnegative magnitude of the perpendicular projection, not a signed projection along a chosen transverse basis direction. Together with the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index) $N_\parallel=\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b}$, it satisfies $N_\perp^2+N_\parallel^2=|\mathbf{N}|^2$; the corresponding unnormalized quantity is the [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude].

Perpendicular refractive index

description: Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
documentation:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the hot, charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density), distinct from the cold recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not summed across different isotopes and does not represent the cold component itself.

Within this model, the hot and cold fractions are complementary and sum to unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) gives the corresponding recycled component, with the energy threshold separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

dd_sources.documentation: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))

description: Linear 20–80% decay time of the total toroidal current carried by runaway electrons during a disruption, measuring current loss between 80% and 20% of its pre-disruption value.
documentation:
This quantity is the linear 20–80% decay time of the total toroidal current carried by runaway electrons during a disruption. It characterizes current loss between specified fractions of the pre-disruption current rather than an exponential decay constant.

$$
\tau_{20\text{–}80} = \frac{t(0.2)-t(0.8)}{0.6}
$$

where $\tau_{20\text{–}80}$ is the decay time and $t(X)$ is the time at which the runaway-electron current reaches the fraction $X$ of its pre-disruption value. The ordering assumes a decreasing current, so the 20% crossing follows the 80% crossing.

This quantity applies to the total runaway-electron current, not to runaway-electron density, energy, or a local current. The same linear convention is used for [linear electron decay time at magnetic axis due to disruption](name:linear_electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption), but that quantity describes electron temperature rather than runaway current.

Value

description: Length of the minor oblique parallelogram side of a plasma-filament element, inclined at angle beta to the vertical height axis.
documentation:
The minor oblique parallelogram-side length of a plasma-filament element is the Euclidean length of the side inclined at angle beta to the vertical height direction. It characterizes one side of the element's oblique cross-sectional geometry.

The side length is defined by the separation of its two endpoints:

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle $\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

This quantity specializes [length of the plasma filament] by selecting its minor, beta-inclined side. The paired major-length quantity selects the complementary oblique side of the same element.

description: Neutral momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed flux density of linear momentum carried by neutral particles and attributed to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift.
documentation:
Neutral momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed flux density of linear momentum carried by neutral particles and attributed to the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic contribution. It is the neutral-species specialization of [momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

With $i$ denoting the transported momentum component and $j$ denoting the flux direction, the underlying diamagnetic contribution is

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_{n,ij} = \rho_n u_{n,i} v^{\mathrm{dia}}_{n,j}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_{n,ij}$ is the neutral momentum-flux contribution, $\rho_n$ is neutral mass density, $u_{n,i}$ is the neutral velocity component carrying momentum, and $v^{\mathrm{dia}}_{n,j}$ is the velocity contribution associated with diamagnetic drift.

This quantity includes only the diamagnetic contribution and excludes neutral momentum flux attributed to other transport mechanisms. It is not resolved by internal neutral state, unlike [neutral state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:neutral_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and the name imposes no particular momentum component or flux direction.

Sign convention: Positive when neutral momentum is transported in the positive direction of the oriented flux surface.

dd_sources.documentation: Diamagnetic component, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.

description: Dimensionless toroidal plasma-momentum flux contribution driven by the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential in gyrokinetic turbulence, generalized across parallel and perpendicular velocity-space channels.
documentation:
This quantity is the normalized contribution to toroidal plasma-momentum transport produced by fluctuations of the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential in gyrokinetic turbulence. It represents transport across an oriented surface, not local momentum density or the total momentum contained in a volume.

The normalization is defined by

$$
\Pi_{\delta A_\parallel}^{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\Pi_{\delta A_\parallel}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\Pi_{\delta A_\parallel}^{\mathrm{norm}}$ is the normalized quantity, $\Pi_{\delta A_\parallel}$ is the toroidal momentum-flux contribution driven by the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference momentum-flux scale. The subscript $\delta A_\parallel$ identifies the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential.

Toroidal momentum refers to the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This parent is agnostic to velocity-space projection and covers both the parallel and perpendicular channel contributions without selecting either channel or requiring that the channels be summed.

The quantity excludes momentum-flux contributions attributed to other fluctuation mechanisms and is distinct from local momentum density, total momentum in a volume, and the channel-resolved [parallel momentum-flux contribution](name:parallel_momentum_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential) or [perpendicular momentum-flux contribution](name:perpendicular_momentum_flux_normalized_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential). It is also distinct from the normalized contribution driven by a perturbed parallel magnetic field.

This quantity is the normalized, driver-specific specialization of [momentum flux due to the perturbed parallel vector potential](name:momentum_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential). The normalization changes the reference scale while preserving the signed character of the underlying momentum-flux contribution.

description: Net electric current carried by a conducting cryostat element in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed net electric current carried by a conducting cryostat element along the toroidal direction. It represents current in the passive cryostat structure, including induced eddy current, rather than current carried by the plasma or another component.

$$
I_\phi = \int_{S_\perp} J_\phi\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $I_\phi$ is the net toroidal current in A, $J_\phi = \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal component of the local electric current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, and $S_\perp$ is the cryostat element cross-section normal to the toroidal direction. The unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is distinct from [toroidal current of vacuum vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel), which is confined to the vacuum vessel, and from [toroidal halo current](name:toroidal_halo_current), which is carried by halo plasma. It is a component of the broader current represented by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).

Sign convention: Positive when the electric current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

description: Volume enclosed by the plasma boundary, representing the total confined-plasma region inside the last closed magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric volume of the confined plasma enclosed by the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. It represents the full enclosed region rather than a local flux-surface shell or material volume.

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the spatial domain inside the plasma boundary, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element at position $\mathbf{x}$.

The integration domain is the entire confined-plasma region bounded by the last closed magnetic flux surface, and the result is the total volume aggregated over that domain. It excludes regions outside the plasma boundary and volumes belonging to material structures or other non-confined regions.

This quantity is the terminal enclosed value of [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) when the flux surface coincides with the plasma boundary. It provides the integration domain for volume-averaged quantities such as [volume-averaged ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature).

description: Squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying the whole-boundary corner deviation of the last closed flux surface from the reference ellipse set by the boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. Positive values make the corner regions boxier, approaching the circumscribing rectangle; negative values make them more diamond-like.
documentation:
Squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying the deviation of the corner regions of the last closed flux surface from the reference ellipse whose semi-axes are set by the boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. It is the whole-boundary summary of the quadrant-level squareness values, characterizing whether the poloidal cross-section corners bulge outward toward the circumscribing rectangle or are pinched inward relative to the elliptical reference contour.

In a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, each quadrant of the boundary is bounded by its radial extremum (innermost or outermost major-radius point) and its vertical extremum (topmost or bottommost point), and a reference ellipse is constructed through these two extrema; the semi-axes of this ellipse are fixed by the boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. Along the diagonal from the ellipse center $O$ toward the corner $F$ of the rectangle circumscribing the quadrant, the quadrant squareness is

$$
\zeta = \frac{\overline{OD} - \overline{OE}}{\overline{OF} - \overline{OE}}
$$

where $D$ is the intersection of the diagonal with the plasma boundary, $E$ its intersection with the reference ellipse, and $\overline{OD}$, $\overline{OE}$, $\overline{OF}$ are distances from the ellipse center. With this construction $\zeta = 0$ when the boundary follows the elliptical arc, $\zeta = 1$ when it passes through the rectangle corner, and $\zeta < 0$ when the corner is indented inside the ellipse (diamond- or bean-like).

This whole-boundary quantity summarizes the four quadrant-resolved members [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and decomposes into [inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) on the high-field side (smaller major radius $R$) and [outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) on the low-field side (larger $R$). Use the quadrant- or side-resolved members when the boundary corners are shaped asymmetrically; this quantity carries no information about up-down or in-out asymmetry of the corner shaping.

description: Global plasma stored energy obtained from the volume integral of total kinetic pressure, including thermal and fast-particle pressure contributions.
documentation:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions rather than representing only one pressure population.

The defining relation is

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{MHD}}$ is the MHD plasma stored energy, $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total kinetic pressure determined by the equilibrium reconstruction, $V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the complete plasma volume, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only, and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$ defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure integral.

dd_sources.documentation: Plasma energy content = 3/2 * int(p,dV) with p being the total pressure (thermal + fast particles) [J]. Time-dependent; Scalar
Plasma energy content = 3/2 * integral over the plasma volume of the total kinetic pressure (pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code)

description: Effective transport coefficient describing diffusive redistribution of momentum density within a selected ion state along a specified transport direction.
documentation:
Effective ion-state momentum diffusivity is the transport coefficient for the diffusive redistribution of momentum carried by a selected ion state. It represents the combined effective action of the diffusive transport processes included in the momentum closure, without implying a particular microscopic mechanism.

For transport direction $a$, the diffusive momentum flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{M,s}^{(a)} = -D_{M,s}^{(a)}\frac{\partial M_s}{\partial x_a}
$$

where $\Gamma_{M,s}^{(a)}$ is the diffusive flux of the selected momentum-density component, $D_{M,s}^{(a)}$ is the effective ion-state momentum diffusivity, $M_s$ is the momentum density of ion state $s$, and $x_a$ is the coordinate in transport direction $a$.

The quantity applies to momentum transport resolved for one ion state and for a specified transport direction; it is not an aggregate over ion states. It describes the diffusive contribution only and excludes the distinct advective contribution represented by an effective momentum-convection velocity, such as [radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity).

This quantity is the direction-resolved effective form of [ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_state_momentum_diffusivity). The accepted poloidal_effective_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity is a concrete poloidal specialization of the same definition; changing the direction changes the directional coefficient, not the underlying diffusive transport concept.
label_note: direction-resolved Fick coefficient for one ion state; links resolve

description: Visible-camera brightness is band-integrated photon radiance along a specified viewing direction over the wavelengths admitted by a visible passband. It gives the photon rate per projected collecting area and accepted solid angle, with the spectral dependence integrated over that band.
documentation:
Visible-camera brightness is the photon radiance of a radiation field along a specified viewing direction after integration over a visible wavelength interval or passband. It is normalized to projected collecting area, observation time, and accepted solid angle, and counts photons rather than radiant energy.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by integrating the spectral photon radiance over the visible passband:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)\, d\lambda
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ is the visible-camera brightness, $L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, and $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$ is the wavelength interval defining the visible passband.

The quantity is non-negative because spectral photon radiance is non-negative over the passband. It is distinct from [spectral radiance], which retains wavelength dependence, and from [radiance at spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which refers to an individual spectral line or narrow line interval; it also differs from energy radiance because photons are counted without weighting by photon energy.

dd_sources.documentation: Radiance image. First dimension : line index (horizontal axis). Second dimension: column index (vertical axis).

label_note: B_vis where the registry brightness symbol is L_gamma; unresolved [spectral radiance]

description: Vorticity is the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field, measuring the signed local angular rotation of fluid elements. It is the parent quantity for radial, toroidal, vertical, and field-aligned projections of that curl.
documentation:
Vorticity is the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field and represents the local rotational content of the single-fluid plasma flow. For solid-body rotation it is twice the angular-velocity vector of a fluid element.

The vorticity field $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is defined by the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field:

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the vorticity field, $\mathbf{v}$ is the [plasma bulk velocity], and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator with right-handed orientation.

The scope is the local magnetohydrodynamic plasma bulk-flow field at a point in the plasma. The bare name carries no surface, volume, time, species, or charge-state aggregation. It is not vorticity magnitude, flow shear, strain rate, divergence, or magnetic-field-line twist.

The unqualified quantity is the parent for scalar directional projections of the same curl. [Radial vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), [toroidal vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity), and [vertical vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity) are projections onto $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, respectively; [parallel vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) is the projection along the local magnetic-field direction. The bare name does not designate a poloidal projection.

Sign convention: Positive when $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ has a positive projection on the stated scalar direction: $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or the local magnetic-field direction for a field-aligned projection.

description: Signed coefficient multiplying the ion toroidal momentum to represent its implicit source or sink in the momentum transport equation.
documentation:
This quantity is the proportional coefficient for the implicit contribution to the toroidal momentum source of the represented ion population. It describes momentum addition or removal that depends on the primary toroidal momentum itself.

The implicit toroidal momentum-source contribution is defined by

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{imp}} = \alpha_{\phi,\mathrm{imp}} M_{\phi}
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit toroidal momentum-source contribution, $\alpha_{\phi,\mathrm{imp}}$ is this source-rate coefficient, and $M_{\phi}$ is the primary toroidal momentum quantity of the represented ion population.

The quantity applies to the toroidal component of one represented ion population and is not a total obtained by summing over all ion populations. It excludes the explicit additive source contribution, which does not multiply the primary toroidal momentum.

The coefficient is the toroidal directional specialization of the [implicit ion momentum source rate](name:implicit_ion_momentum_source_rate); the linked parent describes the same implicit proportional source without selecting a particular momentum direction. A positive coefficient contributes momentum gain when multiplied by positive toroidal momentum, while a negative coefficient represents a damping or loss contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the associated implicit source contribution is a gain of toroidal ion momentum; negative when it is a loss.

description: Molecular neutral species flow at an outlet is the pressure-volume throughput of one molecular neutral species removed across a pumping outlet. It is defined by the outlet partial pressure of that species and the corresponding effective pumping speed, not by total neutral pressure.
documentation:
Molecular neutral species flow at an outlet is the pressure-volume throughput of one molecular neutral species removed across a pumping outlet. It is species-specific and uses the outlet partial pressure of that molecular neutral species rather than the [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure).

The outlet throughput is defined by the product of the outlet species partial pressure and the effective pumping speed for that species:

$$
Q_{s,\mathrm{out}} = p_{s,\mathrm{out}} S_{s,\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $Q_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is this molecular neutral species flow at the outlet, $p_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the outlet partial pressure of molecular neutral species $s$, and $S_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the effective pumping speed for species $s$ at the outlet.

This quantity is an outlet removal throughput, distinct from a gas source into the vessel such as [gas injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection). It is the molecular, species-resolved outlet form of [neutral species flow](name:molecular_neutral_species_flow_at_outlet) and a species-specific specialization of [gas flow].

Sign convention: Positive when the molecular neutral species is removed through the outlet in the pumping direction away from the vessel.

description: Cumulative thermal energy transferred from a calorimetry component to its coolant since pulse start, determined from the coolant enthalpy gain.
documentation:
This quantity is the cumulative thermal energy extracted from a calorimetry component and carried away by its associated coolant between pulse start and the evaluation time.

The accumulated energy is defined by the time integral of the coolant enthalpy gain:

$$
E_{\mathrm{abs}}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{c}}(t')\left[h_{\mathrm{out}}(t') - h_{\mathrm{in}}(t')\right] \, dt'
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)$ is the coolant-absorbed energy at evaluation time $t$, $t_0$ is pulse start, $t'$ is the integration time, $\dot{m}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant mass flow rate associated with the component, and $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the coolant specific enthalpies at the component outlet and inlet, respectively.

The quantity applies to the coolant associated with the calorimetry component and represents the total accumulated enthalpy transfer over the full interval from $t_0$ to $t$, rather than an instantaneous power or a local heat flux. It excludes thermal energy retained within the component.

Differentiation with respect to $t$ gives the corresponding coolant-absorbed power. The same cumulative coolant-transfer concept evaluated specifically for a plasma-facing component is [coolant-absorbed energy accumulated of a plasma-facing component](name:coolant_absorbed_energy_accumulated_of_plasma_facing_component); this quantity retains the broader calorimetry-component locus.

description: Plasma-associated magnetic vector potential whose curl gives the corresponding magnetic induction, including perturbations relative to a reference state in a gage-dependent vector representation.
documentation:
The plasma magnetic vector potential is the gage-dependent vector field associated with the magnetic field in the plasma. It retains the complete vector quantity rather than selecting a radial, poloidal, toroidal, vertical, or field-parallel component.

The defining relation connecting the vector potential to its associated magnetic induction is:

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm pl} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_{\rm pl}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}_{\rm pl}$ is the plasma-associated magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm pl}$ is the corresponding plasma-associated magnetic induction, and $\nabla \times$ is the spatial curl operator. Only the curl is directly field-defining; $\mathbf{A}_{\rm pl}$ itself depends on the chosen gage.

This parent denotes the full unprojected plasma-associated vector potential across equilibrium and perturbed states. It retains its radial, poloidal, toroidal, vertical, and field-parallel components as a vector, without component averaging, Fourier selection, or magnitude formation. The concrete [perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential) represents the change in this quantity relative to a reference state.

The plasma-associated quantity is distinct from the external-source-only [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential). Together with the broader [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential), it provides the plasma-associated contribution to the magnetic-field description; the vacuum quantity instead excludes plasma-current contributions.

description: Normalized shearing rate due to E×B drift is the flux-surface-radius derivative of the toroidal E×B drift velocity, normalized by the gyro-Bohm reference rate set by the reference sound speed over the reference minor radius.
documentation:
Normalized shearing rate due to E×B drift is the dimensionless measure of how rapidly the toroidal component of the E×B drift velocity varies across neighboring flux surfaces, expressed relative to the gyro-Bohm reference rate. It is the gyro-Bohm-normalized counterpart of shearing_rate_due_to_e_cross_b_drift.

With a flux-surface minor-radius coordinate $r = a_\mathrm{ref}\,\rho$, it is defined as

$$
\hat{\gamma}_{E\times B} = \frac{a_\mathrm{ref}}{c_\mathrm{ref}}\,\frac{\partial u_{\phi,E\times B}}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\!\left(\frac{u_{\phi,E\times B}}{c_\mathrm{ref}}\right)
$$

where $u_{\phi,E\times B}$ is the toroidal component of the E×B drift velocity in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame in m s$^{-1}$, $c_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference sound speed in m s$^{-1}$, $a_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference minor radius in m, and $\rho$ is the normalized flux-surface minor-radius coordinate increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

The shear is taken of the toroidal drift velocity $u_{\phi,E\times B}$ itself, not of the associated angular rotation frequency. The angular quantity [toroidal_rotation_frequency_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_rotation_frequency_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) is the same drift divided by the local major radius $R$; because $R$ varies across a flux surface, the radial derivative of that angular frequency differs from this velocity-based shear. The derivative is with respect to the flux-surface coordinate $\rho$, not along the major-radius coordinate $R$; a uniform toroidal E×B drift gives zero shearing rate, since only variation between neighboring flux surfaces contributes.

Sign convention: Positive when $u_{\phi,E\times B}$, taken positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, increases with increasing normalized flux-surface minor-radius coordinate $\rho$.

description: Poloidal magnetic flux at a pellet-path point is the value of the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux function evaluated at the position of a pellet along its injection trajectory. For an axisymmetric equilibrium it depends only on the major-radius and vertical coordinates of that trajectory point.
documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a pellet-path point is the value of the equilibrium [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function sampled at the location of a pellet along its injection trajectory. It labels the magnetic flux surface threading that trajectory point and shares the sign and normalization of the underlying equilibrium flux function.

The quantity is the equilibrium poloidal flux function evaluated at the pellet position:

$$
\psi_p = \psi\!\left(R_p, Z_p\right)
$$

where $\psi(R, Z)$ is the axisymmetric equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux function in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height, and $(R_p, Z_p)$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the pellet-path point. Because the equilibrium is axisymmetric, $\psi$ is independent of the toroidal angle $\phi$, so the toroidal location of the trajectory point does not enter this value.

This is one scalar flux value associated with a single point on the pellet trajectory; sampled at successive points or instants along the path it traces the sequence of flux-surface labels crossed by the pellet. It differs from [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface), which is the flux value attached to a specified magnetic flux surface independent of any trajectory. It is not the toroidal magnetic flux, the pellet trajectory geometry, or a derivative of the flux label with respect to a flux coordinate.

Sign convention: Positive when the vertical magnetic field on the horizontal disk that defines the equilibrium poloidal flux points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
