description: Signed normal projection of the external-coil vacuum magnetic field with its toroidally averaged component removed, evaluated on a generic control surface.
documentation:
Normal non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the signed component of the toroidally varying external-coil vacuum magnetic field normal to a generic control surface. It is a scalar projection evaluated at points on that surface, rather than the full magnetic-field vector.

The defining projection is

$$
B_n(R,\phi,Z)=\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}(R,\phi,Z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}(R,\phi,Z)
$$

where $B_n$ is the normal magnetic-field component, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the oriented unit normal to the control surface. The coordinates $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are major radius, toroidal angle, and vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the external-coil vacuum contribution at each selected point of a generic control surface, which is not assumed to be a magnetic flux surface. Its aggregation convention is the inherited removal of the toroidal-angle average from the vacuum field; no surface or area average is implied.

It excludes the toroidally symmetric vacuum field and magnetic-field contributions generated by plasma currents. It also excludes tangential components and is distinct from cylindrical projections such as the [vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field); the normal direction is defined by the control surface rather than by the cylindrical basis.

The scalar $B_n$ is the surface-normal component of the vector [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field). Reversing the assigned orientation of the control-surface normal reverses $B_n$, while the parent vector itself is unchanged.

Sign convention: Positive when the non-axisymmetric magnetic field points in the direction of the chosen positive unit normal to the control surface.

description: Total neutron emission rate produced by deuterium–tritium, deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion reactions in the plasma.
documentation:
This quantity is the aggregate number of neutrons emitted per unit time by fusion reactions in the plasma.

The total rate is the sum of the neutron-emission rates from the included fusion channels:

$$
S_n = R_{n,\mathrm{DT}} + R_{n,\mathrm{DD}} + R_{n,\mathrm{TT}}
$$

where $S_n$ is the total neutron emission rate, and $R_{n,\mathrm{DT}}$, $R_{n,\mathrm{DD}}$, and $R_{n,\mathrm{TT}}$ are the neutron-emission rates from deuterium–tritium, deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion reactions, respectively.

The quantity includes all three stated fusion reaction channels and their combined neutron production; it is not restricted to a single reaction channel, neutron energy group, or local spatial region. It represents an aggregate emission rate rather than a neutron flux per unit area.

The [deuterium–tritium neutron flux](name:deuterium_tritium_flux) describes the deuterium–tritium channel contribution, which is included in this total together with the deuterium–deuterium and tritium–tritium contributions.

description: Linear 20–80% decay time of the volume-averaged thermal electron temperature during a disruption, based on its pre-disruptive value.
documentation:
This quantity is the characteristic disruption decay time of the volume-averaged thermal electron temperature, determined by a linear 20–80% construction. It describes the reduction of the bulk electron thermal state over the plasma volume, rather than a local temperature or an exponential e-folding time.

The defining relation is

$$
\tau_{e,V}^{20\text{--}80} = \frac{t(0.2)-t(0.8)}{0.6}
$$

where $\tau_{e,V}^{20\text{--}80}$ is the decay time, $t(f)$ is the time at which the volume-averaged temperature $T_{e,V}(t)$ reaches the fraction $f$ of its pre-disruptive value, and $f$ is a dimensionless temperature fraction. The reference $T_{e,V,0}$ is the pre-disruptive volume-averaged thermal electron temperature, so $t(0.8)$ marks the 80% level and $t(0.2)$ marks the 20% level. For a decreasing temperature, $t(0.2)>t(0.8)$.

The quantity applies to the thermal electron population and uses a volume average over the plasma rather than a pointwise or magnetic-axis value. It is specific to the temperature loss occurring during a disruption and excludes decay times obtained from an exponential e-folding fit or from another electron-temperature reduction interval.

The same linear 20–80% construction applied at the magnetic axis is [linear electron decay time at the magnetic axis due to disruption](name:linear_electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption); [electron decay time at the magnetic axis due to disruption](name:electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption) instead represents an exponential e-folding timescale for a local temperature decrease.

description: Wave curvature of an electron-cyclotron beam is the signed inverse radius of curvature of its phase front along one selected principal transverse direction of the phase ellipse.
documentation:
Wave curvature of an electron-cyclotron beam is the signed curvature of the beam phase front resolved along one selected principal transverse direction of the phase ellipse. It is a scalar Gaussian-optics phase-front parameter for a single principal direction.

The selected scalar curvature is defined by the reciprocal of the corresponding signed curvature radius of the phase front:

$$
\kappa_i = \frac{1}{R_i}
$$

where $\kappa_i$ is the wave curvature of the electron-cyclotron beam resolved along selected principal transverse direction $i$, $R_i$ is the signed radius of curvature of the beam phase front along that direction, and $i$ identifies one of the two principal axes of the phase ellipse.

The quantity applies to an electron-cyclotron beam represented by a local Gaussian phase ellipse. It is defined only after one principal transverse direction $i$ has been selected; the selector may be the first or second principal phase-ellipse axis, or an explicitly defined beam-local horizontal or vertical axis when that naming convention is used. No averaging, summation, or magnitude over the two principal directions is implied.

The two scalar values obtained by selecting the two principal phase-ellipse axes are the principal curvatures of the local phase-front curvature tensor. This quantity is distinct from beam-envelope size, absolute wave phase, and beam propagation-angle quantities such as the [toroidal angle of the electron-cyclotron beam](name:toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), which specify other aspects of the same beam rather than phase-front bending.

Sign convention: Positive when the beam phase front is divergent in the selected principal transverse direction as distance increases along the beam-propagation direction.

description: Signed vertical component of the gage-dependent magnetic vector potential, resolved along increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical component $A_Z$ is the signed projection of the gage-dependent [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$ onto the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It retains the component aligned with increasing vertical height while preserving the gage dependence of $\mathbf{A}$.

The defining projection is:

$$
A_Z = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $A_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential), and $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector toward increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is a pointwise cylindrical component of the full vector field in the physical region under consideration; no species, charge-state, flux-surface, or volume aggregation is implied. It is distinct from the vertical position coordinate $Z$, from the magnitude of $\mathbf{A}$, from the [parallel projection](name:parallel_magnetic_vector_potential), and from the [poloidal projection](name:poloidal_magnetic_vector_potential).

Together with the [radial component](name:radial_magnetic_vector_potential) and [toroidal component], $A_Z$ forms the cylindrical decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$. The curl of the complete vector potential gives the magnetic induction, so spatial variation of $A_Z$ contributes through that curl relation, but $A_Z$ alone does not define a magnetic-induction component. The [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) denotes the external-source contribution only and is not implied by this unqualified component.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic vector potential has a component in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, the direction of increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Pressure associated with an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna module, representing mechanical normal loading or contained-gas pressure at hardware components.
documentation:
Pressure associated with an ion-cyclotron-heating antenna module represents the compressive normal stress or contained-gas pressure acting at its hardware components.

At a surface, pressure is defined as the normal force distributed over the loaded area:

$$
p = \frac{F_n}{A}
$$

where $p$ is pressure, $F_n$ is the force normal to the surface, and $A$ is the area over which that force acts. For contained gas, the same scalar represents the isotropic normal stress exerted by the gas.

The scope is the antenna module and its associated hardware components, including local mechanical or gas-pressure conditions at individual sensing locations. The quantity is not a plasma pressure, a pressure amplitude, a pressure variation, or an aggregate sum or average over the module.

Pressure is a mechanical or fluid-state property and is independent of electrical properties such as the antenna's [resistance](name:resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [strap current].

description: Full non-negative vertical extent of an iron-core segment’s rectangular cross-section, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The height of an iron-core segment is the full separation between its upper and lower boundaries in the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes the segment’s rectangular cross-section and is distinct from its radial width and transverse thickness.

$$
H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $H$ is the segment height and $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries, respectively. The height is non-negative and is measured independently of the segment’s position or orientation in the toroidal direction. It is the vertical counterpart to [width of iron core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and differs from [thickness of iron core segment](name:thickness_of_iron_core_segment), which measures the transverse face-to-face dimension.

description: Absolute static pressure of the coolant or working fluid at a plant-system component port, referenced to perfect vacuum rather than atmospheric or another gage reference.
documentation:
The quantity is the local thermodynamic pressure of the coolant or working fluid at a component-port interface, with perfect vacuum as the zero-pressure reference. Static pressure is the isotropic mechanical stress of the fluid and excludes kinetic-energy contributions associated with bulk flow.

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-p_{\mathrm{abs}}\mathbf{I}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the isotropic fluid Cauchy stress, $p_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the absolute static pressure, and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor.

The value represents local pressure at the port, not stagnation pressure, pressure drop, or pressure difference. At a cooling-circuit inlet, it is related to [cooling-circuit inlet pressure], while [coolant flow through a plant component port] describes mass transport rather than mechanical pressure.

description: Real-valued poloidal component of the perturbed plasma magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a specified toroidal mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
documentation:
This quantity is the real-valued poloidal component of the perturbed plasma magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction associated with one toroidal mode of a linear MHD perturbation.

$$
A_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{real}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{pol}}\right)
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{real}}$ is the real poloidal component, $\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the complex poloidal component of the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, and $\operatorname{Re}$ is the real-part operator.

The quantity applies to the confined plasma contribution for a specified toroidal mode and retains only the poloidal component and real part of the complex eigenfunction. It is not the full perturbed vector potential, its imaginary component, a magnitude, or a component of the perturbed magnetic field.

The parent [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential) contains the corresponding complex poloidal component before real-part extraction. The real and imaginary components together represent the complex eigenfunction amplitude; the perturbed magnetic field is obtained from the curl of the full perturbed vector potential rather than from this component alone.

Sign convention: Positive when the real component points along the positive poloidal basis direction used to define $\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{pol}}$.

description: Signed ratio of the minor to major semiaxes of the electric-field polarization ellipse of a polarimeter probing beam in its incident state, before plasma entry. It gives only the ellipticity component of the initial polarization vector, not the ellipse orientation.
documentation:
Signed ratio of the minor to major semiaxes of the electric-field polarization ellipse of a polarimeter probing beam in its incident state, before plasma entry, is the initial polarization ellipticity of that beam. It is the ellipticity component of the beam's initial polarization vector and specifies the shape and handedness of the incident polarization ellipse, not its orientation.

For an incident electric-field polarization ellipse with major semiaxis amplitude $a_0$ and minor semiaxis amplitude $b_0$, the initial ellipticity $\epsilon_0$ is defined by:

$$
\epsilon_0 = \sigma_0 \frac{b_0}{a_0}
$$

where $\epsilon_0$ is the initial polarization ellipticity, $a_0$ is the major semiaxis amplitude, $b_0$ is the minor semiaxis amplitude with $0 \le b_0 \le a_0$, and $\sigma_0$ is the handedness sign of the incident polarization state.

This quantity applies to a single polarimeter probing beam along a specified line of sight in its pre-plasma state. It is not averaged or summed over multiple lines of sight, and it does not describe the full polarization vector, beam intensity, wavelength, path geometry, path-integrated ellipticity, or any post-plasma polarization state.

It provides the reference value for Cotton-Mouton ellipticity changes induced during traversal of magnetized plasma. It is the incident-state counterpart of [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam), which denotes the polarization ellipticity after plasma traversal; it is distinct from the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle), which describes rotation of the polarization-ellipse orientation rather than the semiaxis ratio.

Sign convention: Positive when, in the right-handed beam-local basis $(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{k})$ with $\hat{k}$ along beam propagation, $\hat{e}_1$ along the major semiaxis, and $\hat{e}_2 = \hat{k} \times \hat{e}_1$, the electric-field vector rotates from $+\hat{e}_1$ toward $+\hat{e}_2$ as time increases.

description: Net conventional electric current circulating toroidally in a passive conducting structure, induced electromagnetically rather than driven by an external power supply.
documentation:
The quantity is the net conventional electric current circulating in a passive conducting structure. It represents an induced current caused by changing magnetic flux linked with the structure, including contributions from the plasma, active coils, and neighboring conducting structures, rather than an intentionally supplied drive current.

For an oriented cross-section $S$ of the structure, the net current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{passive}} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric-current density and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented area element normal to the toroidal current path.

This is a structure-level net current. [Current of a passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop) is the corresponding quantity for one identified passive loop, while [toroidal current of the vacuum vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel) is the vessel-specific case.

Sign convention: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Vertical Cartesian coordinate of the geometric center of a divertor target surface, identifying its location along the facility's vertical axis.
documentation:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a divertor target surface. It identifies the center point rather than the target's vertical extent or surface outline.

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, the coordinate is defined by

$$
z_{\mathrm{target}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the position vector of the target surface center relative to the frame origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The $z$ direction corresponds to $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [x coordinate of the divertor target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [y coordinate of the divertor target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target), this quantity locates the target surface center. It is distinct from the [vertical length of the divertor target](name:vertical_length_of_divertor_target) and the [vertical outline of the divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), which describe extent and boundary geometry rather than the center position.

description: Signed direction cosine of a strain gage’s second measurement direction along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the x projection of the unit vector defining a strain gage’s second measurement direction. It describes orientation, not the gage’s spatial location or its first measurement direction.

The direction cosine is defined by:

$$
d_{2x} = \hat{\mathbf d}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf x}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf d}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. Together with the [y direction cosine of the second measurement direction] and [z direction cosine of the second measurement direction], it specifies that direction. It is distinct from the [x coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage rather than defining its orientation.

Sign convention: Positive when the second measurement direction has a component along increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

description: Total neutron production rate from thermonuclear neutron-producing deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction branches among Maxwellian bulk ions, excluding beam-target and beam-beam fast-ion contributions.
documentation:
The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of neutrons produced per unit time by the neutron-producing thermal deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction branches between bulk ions with locally Maxwellian velocity distributions. It is the channel-summed member of [neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), equal to the sum of [deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], [deuterium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], and [tritium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion].

The channel-summed thermal neutron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{c \in \{DD,DT,TT\}} \nu_{n,c}\,\frac{n_{a_c} n_{b_c}}{1+\delta_{a_c b_c}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_c(T_{a_c},T_{b_c})\,dV
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total source rate, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $c$ labels a neutron-producing thermal fusion branch, $\nu_{n,c}$ is the neutron multiplicity of branch $c$, $a_c$ and $b_c$ are its reactant ion species, $n_{a_c}$ and $n_{b_c}$ are their local bulk number densities, $\delta_{a_c b_c}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_c$ is the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity, $T_{a_c}$ and $T_{b_c}$ are the local reactant temperatures, and $dV$ is a volume element. The denominator prevents double counting of identical reactant pairs.

Only reactions among locally Maxwellian bulk ions are included; beam-target, beam-beam, fusion-product, and other nonthermal fast-ion contributions are excluded. For deuterium-deuterium fusion, only the D(d,n)$^3\mathrm{He}$ neutron branch contributes; the D(d,p)T proton branch is not counted. For deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium neutron branches $\nu_{n,c}=1$, while for tritium-tritium fusion $\nu_{n,c}=2$.

description: Vertical coordinate of the center of an arc-of-circle element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Vertical coordinate of an arc-of-circle center is the $Z$ coordinate of the point that is the center of the circle whose circumference contains the arc defining a curved conductor element. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an arc-of-circle center with position vector $\mathbf{x}_c$, the coordinate is

$$
Z_c = \mathbf{x}_c \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the arc-of-circle center, $\mathbf{x}_c$ is the position vector of that center relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies only to the center of the supporting circle for an arc-of-circle element. It is not the vertical coordinate of an arbitrary point on the conductor, nor the [vertical coordinate of a coil conductor element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor_element) when that name denotes the element location itself rather than the center of the circle defining an arc.

Together with the [radial coordinate of the arc-of-circle center](name:radial_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center) and the [toroidal angle of the arc-of-circle center], it specifies the same circle center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the arc-of-circle center is displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the origin of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Radial outline of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate of each filament-outline point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
documentation:
Radial outline of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of each point on the plasma-filament outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. It gives the radial location of the outline locus and is the filament-outline specialization of the generic [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For an outline point with Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in a right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, with the $z$ axis coincident with the toroidal symmetry axis, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is a coordinate of each outline point, not a signed radial vector projection, flux-surface-normal displacement, filament width, or aggregate radius. It should not be confused with the [outer radius of a plasma filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), which denotes an outer radial extent rather than the coordinate of an individual outline point.

description: Full radial extent of a rectangular passive conducting structure element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The radial width is the full major-radius extent of a rectangular passive conducting structure element, measured between its inner and outer radial boundaries.

$$
W = R_{\mathrm{outer}} - R_{\mathrm{inner}}
$$

where $W$ is the radial width, and $R_{\mathrm{outer}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{inner}}$ are the major-radius coordinates in meters of the outer and inner boundaries in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is non-negative and describes radial extent only; it is distinct from the full vertical extent given by [height of passive structure](name:height_of_passive_structure) and from the element length given by [length of passive structure].

description: Geometric area of the actual filter-window surface that intercepts or transmits incoming radiation, including surface curvature rather than only its projected aperture.
documentation:
The filter-window surface area is the geometric area of the actual material surface associated with a radiation filter and participating in interception or transmission of incoming radiation. It is the window-specific component of the parent [filter area].

The area is defined by integrating the surface-area element over the filter-window surface:

$$
A_w = \int_{S_w} dS
$$

where $A_w$ is the filter-window area, $S_w$ is the actual window surface, and $dS$ is an infinitesimal surface-area element.

This quantity includes curvature of the material surface and excludes a planar projected aperture area or areas belonging to other filter components.

description: Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is perpendicular to the segment's radial width along R and vertical height along Z.
documentation:
Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The thickness is the face-to-face separation of paired points on the two opposite toroidal-facing faces along the local toroidal unit vector:

$$
t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_+ - \mathbf{x}_-) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \right|
$$

where $t$ is the segment thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_-$ and $\mathbf{x}_+$ are position vectors in m of paired points on the two opposite faces lying on the same line parallel to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the local toroidal unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [width of the iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), the radial extent along $R$, and the [height of the iron-core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), the vertical extent along $Z$, the thickness completes the mutually orthogonal triplet of extents describing the segment as a rectangular block whose cross section lies in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane and is extruded along $\phi$. It excludes any diagonal, chordwise, or arc-length measure across the segment.

description: Length of the alpha-inclined parallelogram side in the oblique cross-sectional geometry of an ion-cyclotron-range antenna strap.
documentation:
Major length of antenna strap is the length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle alpha in the oblique trapezoidal cross-sectional geometry of an ion-cyclotron-range antenna strap. It is a geometric side dimension of the conductor section.

This quantity is distinct from the reference base dimension [length of antenna strap] and from the beta-inclined side dimension [minor length of antenna strap](name:minor_length_of_antenna_strap). The inclination is defined by the signed [alpha angle of antenna strap](name:alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap); no slant-height or trigonometric conversion is implied without the specified cross-sectional construction.

Sign convention: Positive when measured along the alpha-inclined side from its directed base-edge endpoint to the opposite endpoint.

description: Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal projection.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle, $\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples. The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is defined by [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by [poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

description: Thermodynamic temperature of the working coolant at a generic inlet or outlet port of a power-conversion component.
documentation:
Coolant temperature is the thermodynamic temperature describing the thermal state of the working fluid at a connection port of a power-conversion component.

The quantity applies to coolant at a generic plant-component port, which may be an inlet or an outlet. It denotes the local fluid state at that port; no summation, spatial averaging, or integration is implied. It excludes the temperature of the component structure or any other material.

Unlike [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet), this quantity does not restrict the port to an outlet. It is a thermal-state quantity, whereas [coolant transit time of plant component port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) describes the elapsed transport time between component ports rather than the coolant temperature.

description: Toroidal component of the helium-4 ion fluid velocity evaluated at the H-mode pressure pedestal top, resolved along the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Toroidal component of the helium-4 ion fluid velocity evaluated at the H-mode pressure pedestal top, resolved along the direction of increasing toroidal angle, is the signed bulk-flow component of helium-4 ions along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The pedestal top is the core-side shoulder of the H-mode pressure pedestal. As a species-level intensive quantity, it is the density-weighted mean over all helium-4 ionization charge states in the ion population.

The charge-state-aggregated toroidal component at the pedestal top is defined by

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{ped}}^{{}^4\mathrm{He}} =
\frac{\sum_q n_q^{{}^4\mathrm{He}} \left(\mathbf{v}_q^{{}^4\mathrm{He}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\right)}
{\sum_q n_q^{{}^4\mathrm{He}}}
$$

where $q$ labels helium-4 ionization charge states, $n_q^{{}^4\mathrm{He}}$ is the local number density of charge state $q$, $\mathbf{v}_q^{{}^4\mathrm{He}}$ is its fluid velocity, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$; all quantities are evaluated at the pedestal-top location.

This quantity is local to the pedestal top and is not an average over the full pedestal or scrape-off layer. It is a species-level helium-4 velocity, so it differs from charge-state-resolved helium-4 velocities by the density-weighted charge-state aggregation and from other isotope velocities only by the selected ion species.

Sign convention: Positive when the helium-4 ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

description: Dimensionless neoclassical measure of electron pitch-angle scattering relative to trapped-electron bounce motion, including inverse-aspect-ratio scaling.
documentation:
This quantity is the trapped-electron neoclassical collisionality parameter, measuring electron pitch-angle scattering relative to the characteristic bounce motion of trapped particles. It distinguishes the geometry-scaled regime from the parent [electron collisionality].

The parameter is defined by

$$
\nu_e^* = \frac{\nu_e q R}{\epsilon^{3/2} v_{te}}
$$

where $\nu_e$ is the electron pitch-angle-scattering frequency, $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ is the major radius, $\epsilon$ is the inverse aspect ratio, and $v_{te}$ is the electron thermal speed. The denominator represents the trapped-electron bounce-frequency scaling, including the inverse-aspect-ratio dependence.

This quantity is a geometry-normalized collisionality measure, not a collision frequency or a transport coefficient. Its localized pedestal-top counterpart is [normalized electron collisionality at the pedestal top].

description: Reference magnetic-field vector of the equilibrium magnetic induction evaluated at the reference point, retaining field strength and direction before selecting a component such as the toroidal reference magnetic field.
documentation:
The reference magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\rm ref}$ is the equilibrium [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) evaluated at the reference point used to define a local field reference. It represents the vector field at that locus, retaining both field strength and direction rather than selecting a cylindrical component or scalar magnitude.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the reference field may be resolved as

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm ref}=B_{R,{\rm ref}}\hat{R}+B_{\phi,{\rm ref}}\hat{\phi}+B_{Z,{\rm ref}}\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\rm ref}$ is the reference magnetic field, $B_{R,{\rm ref}}$ is its signed radial component, $B_{\phi,{\rm ref}}$ is the [toroidal reference magnetic field](name:toroidal_reference_magnetic_field), $B_{Z,{\rm ref}}$ is its signed vertical component, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ are the basis vectors for increasing major radius, toroidal angle, and vertical height.

This quantity is defined at the reference point for the equilibrium field; it is not the spatially unrestricted local [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field). It has no species population, and its aggregation convention is a point value at the reference locus, not a spatial average or finite-volume reduction.

The parent quantity is distinct from component-resolved reference fields: the [toroidal reference magnetic field](name:toroidal_reference_magnetic_field) is its projection along $\hat{\phi}$ at the reference point, not a separate vector field. It is also distinct from the unrestricted [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), which does not by name impose the reference locus.

Sign convention: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{B}_{\rm ref}$ points along the corresponding positive basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where the positive directions are increasing major radius $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and increasing vertical height $Z$.

description: Instantaneous ethane-gas injection rate into the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent electrons per second, with 18 equivalent electrons assigned to each neutral C2H6 molecule.
documentation:
This quantity is the instantaneous rate at which neutral ethane molecules are delivered to the plasma vessel, converted to an equivalent-electron rate. It counts the electrons associated with neutral molecular composition, not free electrons produced by ionization.

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)=18\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_2H_6}}(t)
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron injection rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_2H_6}}$ is the neutral ethane molecular injection rate in molecules per second, and $t$ is time in seconds. The factor $18=2\times6+6\times1$ is the total atomic-number electron count of one C2H6 molecule.

This is an instantaneous rate rather than a cumulative inventory; its time integral gives the accumulated equivalent-electron count represented by [accumulated ethane count](name:accumulated_ethane_count). It excludes other molecular species, including the distinct [ethylene source rate](name:ethylene_source_rate).

description: Commanded bias potential difference applied between a neutron-detector module's bias terminal and electrical return, not its raw output signal.
documentation:
The commanded bias voltage is the electrical potential difference specified for energizing a neutron-detector module between its bias terminal and return or reference terminal. It is a setpoint, distinct from the instantaneous detector waveform represented by [voltage of neutron detector].

$$
V_{\mathrm{bias,set}} = \phi_{\mathrm{bias}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{bias,set}}$ is the commanded bias voltage, and $\phi_{\mathrm{bias}}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the electrical potentials of the bias and return/reference terminals, respectively, expressed in volts.

The quantity specifies the intended applied potential and excludes the measured supply output, detector signal amplitude, pulse waveform, and derived neutron count rate. Its setpoint meaning distinguishes it from the detector bias voltage represented by [voltage of mass spectrometer](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) and the spectrometer supply command [requested voltage of spectrometer](name:requested_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel).

Sign convention: Positive when the bias terminal is at higher electrical potential than the return or reference terminal.

description: Vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field probe, expressed as its signed Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the signed height coordinate of the probe center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It locates the probe center along the vertical direction and does not define the orientation of the probe's sensitive axis or the magnetic-field component measured by the probe.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate, the probe-center coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the poloidal magnetic-field probe center, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the position vector of that geometric center relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field probe as a physical object. For a probe with finite extent, it refers to the center position rather than to the probe size, winding distribution, support structure, or any spatial average of the measured magnetic field.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), it specifies the probe-center position in the $(R,Z)$ poloidal cross-section at a given toroidal angle. The same signed-coordinate concept is used for other magnetic diagnostic objects, such as the [vertical coordinate of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), the [vertical coordinate of a flux loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop), and the [vertical coordinate of a Rogowski coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), but those names apply to different objects.

Sign convention: Positive when the probe-center position lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

description: Instantaneous propane (C3H8) injection rate into the plasma vessel, converted from molecules to equivalent electrons using 26 electrons per neutral molecule.
documentation:
This quantity is the instantaneous source rate of propane gas entering the plasma vessel, expressed using the equivalent-electron convention. Each neutral C3H8 molecule contributes the total electron count of its constituent atoms.

The equivalent-electron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t)=26\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t)
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t)$ is the equivalent-electron source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t)$ is the propane molecular injection rate in molecules per second, $t$ is time, and 26 is the dimensionless electron count per neutral molecule: three carbon atoms contribute 18 electrons and eight hydrogen atoms contribute 8 electrons. This is an instantaneous rate, distinct from the accumulated [propane count], which is the time-integrated equivalent-electron inventory.

description: Co-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the co-passing orbit class. Positive values indicate net addition; negative values indicate net removal.
documentation:
Co-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the co-passing orbit class. Co-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is in the plasma-current direction.

The net source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \left\langle s_{n,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{co,th}} - s_{n,\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{co,th}} \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the co-passing thermal particle source rate, $s_{n,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{co,th}}$ is the local rate of thermal-particle addition, $s_{n,\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{co,th}}$ is the local rate of thermal-particle removal, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over a magnetic flux surface, and $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label of that surface.

The quantity applies only to the thermal population on co-passing, untrapped passing orbits and is aggregated by flux-surface averaging. Positive values represent a net source to this orbit class, while negative values represent a net sink. It excludes trapped and counter-passing orbit populations and describes particle-number transfer rather than energy or momentum transfer.

This is one orbit-class contribution to the broader [thermal particle source rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate), which aggregates source and sink contributions over the thermal orbit populations. The [counter-passing thermal particle source rate](name:counter_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) is the corresponding orbit-class contribution for particles circulating opposite to the plasma-current direction.

description: Magnetic shear evaluated at the plasma boundary, equal to the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, flux-surface averaged over the separatrix.
documentation:
Magnetic shear at the plasma boundary is the flux-surface average of [magnetic shear] over the outermost closed flux surface — the separatrix bounding the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label ($\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 1$ at the separatrix), the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{bdy}} = \left\langle \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $\langle \cdot \rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the separatrix.

This boundary evaluation is distinct from interior counterparts such as magnetic_shear_at_pedestal_top and [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), which are evaluated on flux surfaces interior to the last closed flux surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is positive as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases outward at the separatrix.

description: Effective resistance of the plasma column, defined by irreversible ohmic power divided by the square of the total plasma current.
documentation:
The effective plasma-column resistance is the circuit-level coefficient relating irreversible electrical dissipation in the plasma to the total plasma current. It is distinct from local electrical resistivity and from inductive contributions to the plasma voltage.

$$
R_{\rm pl} = \frac{P_{\rm ohm}}{I_{\rm p}^{2}}
$$

where $R_{\rm pl}$ is the effective resistance, $P_{\rm ohm}$ is the [power due to ohmic dissipation](name:total_power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) in W, and $I_{\rm p}$ is the total conventional plasma current in A. The quantity is non-negative for irreversible ohmic dissipation. It represents only the resistive part of the plasma circuit response; inductive electromotive-force contributions are included in the [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary), not in this resistance.

description: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient measuring how the lower outboard (low-field-side) corner of the plasma boundary departs from the reference ellipse defined by boundary minor radius, lower elongation, and lower triangularity.
documentation:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is one of four corner-specific shape parameters in the Luce (2013) plasma boundary parameterization, describing how much the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary deviates from the reference ellipse defined by the boundary minor radius $a$, lower elongation $\kappa_l$, and lower triangularity $\delta_l$. The lower outer quadrant is the low-field-side, large-$R$ corner below the magnetic-axis height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

Within the Luce corner parameterization, the coefficient is related to the lower-outer superellipse exponent $n_{lo}$ by

$$
\zeta_{lo} = 1 - \frac{2}{n_{lo}}
$$

where $n_{lo}$ controls the local corner curvature of the lower-outboard boundary segment. The reference ellipse corresponds to $n_{lo}=2$.

Positive values indicate that the lower-outboard boundary corner lies outside the reference ellipse at the corresponding corner location, giving a more rectangular boundary; $\zeta_{lo}=0$ indicates the reference ellipse; negative values indicate that the corner lies inside the reference ellipse, giving inward concavity relative to that ellipse. This coefficient excludes the upper-outboard and high-field-side corner contributions represented by [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary); [outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) combines the outboard corner behavior, and [squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) is the global single-coefficient summary.

description: Full vertical extent of an ICRH antenna strap conductor cross-section, measured parallel to the Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The antenna-strap height is the full vertical extent of the rectangular conductor cross-section, measured parallel to the $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a geometric cross-section dimension, not the antenna elevation or its distance from the plasma.

$$
H = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $H$ is the strap height and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries. The dimension is non-negative and complements the [toroidal width of the antenna strap] and [thickness of the antenna strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap), which describe the other conductor extents. For an annular cross-section, the radial boundaries are specified by the [inner radius of the antenna strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap) and [outer radius of the antenna strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap).

description: Second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element is the non-negative principal radius of curvature of the element's front surface along the second local tangential (X2) axis in the right-handed local optical-element frame (X1, X2, local z). It applies to cylindrical or toroidal surface forms with a defined second tangential curvature.
documentation:
Second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element is the non-negative principal radius of curvature of the optical element's front surface along the second local tangential axis $X_2$ in the right-handed local optical-element frame $(X_1, X_2, z_\mathrm{loc})$. In this frame, $X_1$ and $X_2$ are the first and second local surface-tangent axes and $z_\mathrm{loc}$ is the local surface-normal axis.

The radius is the reciprocal of the magnitude of the corresponding signed principal curvature:

$$
R_2 = \frac{1}{|\kappa_2|}
$$

where $R_2$ is the second local tangential front-surface radius of the optical element and $\kappa_2$ is the signed principal curvature of that front surface along $X_2$.

This quantity is defined for a single front surface of a single optical element when that surface form has a specified principal curvature in the second local tangential direction, including cylindrical and toroidal surfaces. It is not aggregated over multiple optical elements or over multiple surfaces, and it excludes the first local tangential front-surface radius, any back-surface radius, aperture size, and position coordinates.

The second local tangential direction is object-local and must not be reinterpreted as a laboratory vertical direction unless the optical element's local frame is independently aligned that way. Together with the [first local tangential front-surface radius], when that counterpart is defined, this radius specifies the two principal curvature radii of the front surface; a flat second tangential direction corresponds to an unbounded radius, not to a negative value.

description: Full clear-opening extent of a rectangular diagnostic aperture along its object-local first tangential axis, used to define the aperture geometry for étendue calculations.
documentation:
This quantity is the full clear opening of a diagnostic aperture measured along its object-local first tangential direction. It describes the physical aperture boundary rather than a plasma property or an aperture-area average.

The width is defined by the separation of the two opposing boundaries along the first local tangential coordinate:

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\rm max} - x_{1,\rm min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first-local-tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\rm max}$ and $x_{1,\rm min}$ are the maximum and minimum signed coordinates of the clear opening along the first local tangential axis. The aperture-local basis is $(\hat e_1,\hat e_2,\hat e_3)$, with $\hat e_1$ denoting that first local tangential direction.

The quantity applies only to a rectangular diagnostic-aperture geometry and uses the complete opening between its opposing boundaries; it is not a radius, diameter, area, or an average over multiple apertures. The orthogonal opening dimension is represented by [second local tangential width of aperture](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_aperture). For circular apertures, the corresponding transverse dimensions are described by [diameter of diagnostic aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture) or [radius of diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture).

This quantity identifies the vertical location of the X-point and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) and the [vertical coordinate of the strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point).

description: Major-radius coordinate of each point on the vacuum-vessel cross-sectional outline, measured from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on the vacuum-vessel cross-sectional outline, measured from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

The major-radius coordinate is defined from the corresponding Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ basis, and $R$ is the resulting distance from that axis.

The quantity applies to points defining the vacuum-vessel cross-sectional outline. For an annular vessel-layer representation, it applies to the inner-contour outline; it otherwise denotes the corresponding vessel-outline points without adding a separate radial or wall-thickness meaning. It is not the distance from the magnetic axis or a signed projection normal to a magnetic flux surface.

Together with the [vertical coordinate of the outline](name:vertical_outline), it locates each outline point in the cylindrical $(R, Z)$ cross-sectional plane; the two coordinates describe the outline geometry, while $\phi$ identifies the toroidal position when applicable.

description: Halo current in the halo plasma region during a disruption is the electric current vector carried by the halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and the first wall. Its poloidal and toroidal components are obtained by integrating the halo current density over oriented cross sections of the halo region.
documentation:
Halo current in the halo plasma region during a disruption is the electric current vector carried by the halo plasma flowing on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and the first wall. It resolves into a poloidal component and a toroidal component, each obtained by integrating the halo current density over an oriented cross section of the halo region.

The component currents are surface integrals of the halo current density, and the current vector is their sum along the corresponding unit directions:

$$
\mathbf{I}_\mathrm{h} = I_{\mathrm{h},\theta}\,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta + I_{\mathrm{h},\phi}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \qquad I_{\mathrm{h},a} = \int_{S_a} \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a\,dS,\quad a\in\{\theta,\phi\}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}$ is the halo current density, $S_a$ is an oriented cross section of the halo region with positive normal $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is tangent to increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is the angular coordinate in the meridional plane of that $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame about the chosen magnetic-axis reference and is distinct from the toroidal angle $\phi$.

The scalar coefficient $I_{\mathrm{h},\theta}$ is [poloidal_halo_current](name:poloidal_halo_current) and $I_{\mathrm{h},\phi}$ is [toroidal_halo_current](name:toroidal_halo_current). This integrated current vector is distinct from halo_current_density, the local field $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}$ prior to integration over $S_a$, and it counts only current carried by the halo plasma itself, excluding current confined to passive conducting structures after path closure outside the halo region.

Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal component is directed along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ and the toroidal component is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to a specified conducting boundary. It is nonnegative and does not denote the loop center's major-radius position.
documentation:
Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to a specified conducting boundary of that annulus. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected boundary point:

$$
r = \sqrt{(R_b - R_c)^2 + (Z_b - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the center position of the annular cross-section and $(R_b,Z_b)$ is the selected boundary position in the same fixed-$phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This parent quantity abstracts over [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). It satisfies $r \ge 0$ and is a size of the conductor cross-section, not a signed component along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ and not the major-radius coordinate of the loop center. For a circular annulus, [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is related by $A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and thickness_of_passive_loop is $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$.

description: Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the last closed plasma-boundary contour, defining its horizontal cross-sectional size.
documentation:
The minor radius is the effective horizontal semi-axis of the last closed plasma-boundary contour and characterizes the radial extent of the plasma cross-section.

The minor radius $a$ is defined by

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $a$ is the minor radius, $R_{\max}$ is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the boundary contour, and $R_{\min}$ is the minimum major-radius coordinate on that contour.

This quantity applies to the complete last closed plasma-boundary contour and is determined from its global major-radius extrema. It is a nonnegative geometric size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate such as the [radial coordinate at the outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane) and not a flux-surface average.

The [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) uses this minor radius as the horizontal reference semi-axis when forming the boundary's vertical-to-horizontal shape ratio.

description: The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is its projection in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is the projection of that major-axis direction onto the $y$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The major-axis direction is the orientation of the principal semiaxis of the cone's elliptic cross-section.

The component is defined by

$$
e_{\mathrm{maj},y} = \hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ is the y component of the shatter-cone major-axis unit vector, $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ is the unit vector along the major axis of the elliptic shatter cone, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

This quantity applies to the geometry of an elliptic shatter cone and to the major semiaxis orientation of its elliptic cross-section; its aggregation convention is none, because it is a single vector component rather than a sum or mean. It is distinct from the unsigned major-axis length, from the [y component of the shatter-cone direction unit vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which describes the cone direction rather than the major-axis orientation, and from the [y component of the minor-axis unit vector](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which refers to the orthogonal minor semiaxis.

Together with the [x component](name:x_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) and [z component](name:z_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), this quantity forms the Cartesian representation of $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$; the linked x and z components and $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ satisfy $(e_{\mathrm{maj},x})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},y})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},z})^2 = 1$, where $e_{\mathrm{maj},x}$ and $e_{\mathrm{maj},z}$ are the linked x and z components. The major-axis and minor-axis unit vectors jointly orient the elliptic cone and satisfy $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}} = 0$, where $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}}$ is the minor-axis unit vector with [x](name:x_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), [y](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), and [z](name:z_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) components.

Sign convention: Positive when $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ has a component in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

description: Additional externally introduced resistance in a poloidal-field coil circuit, varying with time and added to the winding resistance to form the effective coil resistance.
documentation:
This quantity is the additional lumped ohmic resistance introduced externally in the circuit of an individual poloidal-field coil. It represents resistance from added circuit elements such as dynamically switchable resistors, rather than the coil winding itself.

At a given time, the effective coil resistance is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R_{\mathrm{winding}} + R_{\mathrm{ext}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the total effective resistance of the coil circuit, $R_{\mathrm{winding}}$ is the static winding resistance represented by [resistance of a poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $R_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is this additional external resistance.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field coil and is a scalar lumped circuit property that may vary as the externally added resistance changes. It excludes the static winding resistance itself and does not denote an unrelated power-supply or Thevenin resistance. Its additive relationship to [resistance of a poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) distinguishes it from the baseline winding resistance; together they determine the coil circuit's effective ohmic opposition and resistive voltage drop.

dd_sources.documentation: Additional resistance due to e.g. dynamically switchable resistors. The coil effective resistance is obtained by adding this dynamic quantity to the static resistance of the coil.

description: Transverse extent of the intact cylindrical pellet before injection and shattering, defined as the full width of its circular cross-section perpendicular to the pellet axis.
documentation:
Transverse extent of the intact cylindrical pellet before injection and shattering is the full width of its circular cross-section measured perpendicular to the pellet axis. It defines the pellet cross-sectional geometry before fragmentation, ablation, or interaction with the plasma.

For an ideal right circular cylindrical pellet, the diameter and axial length determine the pellet volume by

$$
V_\mathrm{pellet} = \frac{\pi}{4} d_\mathrm{pellet}^2 L_\mathrm{pellet}
$$

where $V_\mathrm{pellet}$ is the pellet volume, $d_\mathrm{pellet}$ is the pellet diameter, and $L_\mathrm{pellet}$ is the [length of pellet](name:length_of_pellet).

This quantity excludes the axial extent of the pellet, which is the [length of pellet](name:length_of_pellet), and excludes characteristic sizes of shattered fragments, ablated material, or the post-shattering material cloud.

description: Effective capacitance of an impedance-matching element in an ion-cyclotron heating antenna, relating stored charge to the RF voltage used for circuit tuning.
documentation:
This quantity is the non-negative lumped capacitance associated with an impedance-matching element in an ion-cyclotron heating antenna module. It represents the element's ability to store electric charge and participate in tuning the radio-frequency transmission circuit.

For an ideal lumped capacitive element, the capacitance is defined by

$$
C = \frac{Q}{V}
$$

where $C$ is the capacitance, $Q$ is the charge stored on the element, and $V$ is the electric potential difference across the element.

The quantity applies to the specified matching element of the antenna and does not represent the capacitance of an unrelated circuit component or the entire transmission system. It is a circuit parameter rather than a power, current, or operating-frequency quantity.

Together with the [resistance of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), it characterizes the antenna's effective RF impedance; the [frequency of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) identifies the RF operating frequency at which the matching condition is evaluated.

description: Implicit coefficient of the electron particle source term, multiplying local electron density to represent its stiff source or sink contribution.
documentation:
This quantity is the implicit electron particle source coefficient for the electron density balance. It represents the density-proportional part of the electron particle source or sink, rather than the complete source term.

$$
s_{e,\mathrm{implicit}}(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_{e,\mathrm{implicit}}(\mathbf{x})\,n_e(\mathbf{x})
$$

Here $s_{e,\mathrm{implicit}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the implicit electron particle source rate density at position $\mathbf{x}$, $\alpha_{e,\mathrm{implicit}}(\mathbf{x})$ is this rate coefficient, and $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron number density.

The quantity applies specifically to the electron particle channel and represents the coefficient multiplying electron density; it is not a summed ion coefficient, an energy-source coefficient, or a volume-integrated source. The full [electron particle source rate](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_electron_particle_source_rate) also includes source contributions not represented by this implicit density-proportional part. Its role is analogous to the coefficient in the [implicit electron energy source rate](name:implicit_electron_energy_source_rate), but the multiplied primary quantity is electron density rather than electron energy.

Sign convention: Positive when the implicit electron particle contribution increases the electron population.

description: Inner radius of an antenna strap is the perpendicular distance from the strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical boundary of its annular cross-section.
documentation:
Inner radius of an antenna strap is the perpendicular distance from the strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical boundary of its annular cross-section. It identifies the inner boundary of the conductor material and is the smaller of the two annular boundary radii.

Use [radius of antenna strap](name:radius_of_antenna_strap) for the boundary-radius concept without selecting a surface, and [outer radius of antenna strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap) for the larger boundary radius. If $r_\mathrm{in}$ and $r_\mathrm{out}$ denote the inner and outer radii, respectively, then $0 \le r_\mathrm{in} \le r_\mathrm{out}$. This quantity is distinct from the [height of antenna strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap), [toroidal width of antenna strap], and [thickness of antenna strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap).

description: Geometric volume occupied by the material of an individual shattered pellet fragment, distinguishing fragment size from the intact pellet and surrounding propellant.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric volume enclosed by the material boundary of one shattered pellet fragment. It describes the fragment’s physical size rather than the volume of the complete pellet, injector, or surrounding propellant.

The volume is defined from the fragment’s material domain:

$$
V_f = \int_{\mathcal{D}_f} d^3\mathbf{r}
$$

where $V_f$ is the volume of the individual fragment, $\mathcal{D}_f$ is the three-dimensional region occupied by its material, and $d^3\mathbf{r}$ is the volume element integrated over that region.

The scope is one individual fragment within the shattered-pellet population. This is an extensive geometric quantity for that fragment and is not an aggregate over multiple fragments; it excludes surrounding gas and does not represent the volume of the intact pellet, injector, or complete fragment cloud.

The associated [toroidal coordinate of the pellet fragment](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_pellet_fragment) locates the same fragment around the machine symmetry axis, while this quantity characterizes its geometric size.

description: Source rate due to injection is the instantaneous rate of electron-equivalent particles supplied by active injection, formed by nuclear-charge weighting of the injected species. It represents the injection-only material source and excludes particle production or loss after injection.
documentation:
Source rate due to injection is the instantaneous rate of electron-equivalent particles supplied by active injection. It is an additive material source for the plasma particle inventory, formed by weighting each injected particle by the total nuclear charge associated with that injected particle.

The electron-equivalent aggregate is defined by

$$
S_\mathrm{inj}(t) = \sum_j Z_j \frac{dN_{j,\mathrm{inj}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{inj}$ is this source rate, $N_{j,\mathrm{inj}}$ is the cumulative count of injected particles of species $j$, $Z_j$ is the total nuclear charge number carried by one injected particle of species $j$, and $t$ is time.

The sum is over active injection only and excludes changes to free-particle populations caused after injection by ionization, recombination, charge exchange, recycling, pumping, or plasma reactions. For an elemental species not resolved by charge state, the contribution is charge-state-summed before the nuclear-charge weighting is applied; species-resolved injected source rates such as [deuterium source rate due to injection](name:deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection) are unweighted summands until this weighting relation is applied. The electron-equivalent convention makes [electron source rate due to injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) the nearest electron-population counterpart, while [electron source rate] is broader because it is not restricted to active injection. A [gas source rate at wall](name:total_particle_source_rate_at_wall_due_to_gas_injection) is wall-referenced rather than a species-weighted aggregate; a [total particle source rate] includes additional source mechanisms when defined with a compatible counting convention.

description: Argon prefill count is the total amount of neutral argon (Ar) introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with 18 per atom.
documentation:
Argon prefill count is the total amount of neutral argon (Ar) introduced during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each neutral argon atom contributes 18 equivalent electrons.

The equivalent-electron count is obtained by accumulating injected argon atoms over the prefill interval and weighting them by the argon atomic number:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ar,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{Ar}} N_{\mathrm{Ar,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{Ar}} \int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ar}}(t)\,dt = 18\int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ar}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ar,prefill}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{Ar,prefill}}$ is the accumulated neutral-argon atom count, $Z_{\mathrm{Ar}}=18$ is the argon atomic number, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon atom injection rate, $t_0$ is the prefill start time, and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time.

This quantity includes only argon introduced before breakdown and excludes wall recycling, neutral-beam or pellet fueling, later gas injection, and retained or ionized inventory. It is the argon-specific component of [prefill count](name:prefill_count) and follows the isotope-resolved convention used for [tritium prefill count].

description: Geometric length of either inclined side of the oblique cross-section of a passive loop element, including its major and minor sides.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric side length of an oblique or parallelogram cross-section belonging to a passive loop element. It describes the side itself rather than an electrical or material property.

For side endpoints with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, the length $\ell$ is defined by

$$
\ell = \|\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1\|
$$

where $\ell$ is the side length, and $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are the endpoint position vectors.

The scope includes both side orientations of the passive loop element's oblique cross-section: the major-side instance [major length of a passive loop element](name:major_length_of_passive_loop_element) and the minor-side instance [minor length of a passive loop element](name:minor_length_of_passive_loop_element). It excludes the cross-section thickness measured perpendicular to the element's central segment, represented separately by [thickness of a passive loop element](name:thickness_of_passive_loop_element). The length is nonnegative and is independent of which side orientation is selected.
label_note: opens 'This quantity is' against 'Length {locus}'; ell where the registry gives L

description: Dimensionless Coulomb logarithm at the H-mode pressure pedestal top, expressing the range of impact parameters contributing to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering.
documentation:
The Coulomb logarithm at the H-mode pressure pedestal top is the local dimensionless factor that represents the effective range of impact parameters contributing to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering. It is the pedestal-top specialization of the [coulomb logarithm](name:coulomb_logarithm).

$$
\ln\Lambda = \ln\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right), \qquad b_{\max} \sim \lambda_D
$$

where $\Lambda$ is the impact-parameter ratio, $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum effective impact parameters, respectively, and $\lambda_D$ is the Debye screening length; these three quantities are lengths. Debye shielding limits the long-range contribution, while the short-range limit is set by the applicable classical or quantum scattering scale.

This quantity is evaluated locally at the pressure pedestal top and is not a collision frequency, collisionality, or spatially averaged Coulomb logarithm.

dd_sources.documentation: Value
Value

description: Signed vertical coordinate of each point on the centerline representing the middle of an annular cryostat vessel layer, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical coordinate identifies the height of a point on the cryostat centerline, where the centerline represents the middle of the annular vessel layer. It applies specifically to the annular cryostat unit's centerline rather than to the inner or outer layer boundary.

For a centerline point, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the position vector of the centerline point, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is pointwise for each centerline point and is not an average over the centerline or an aggregate over cryostat units. It excludes contour points describing the annular layer boundaries; those are represented by the [vertical outline of the cryostat], which describes a different geometric locus.

Sign convention: Positive when the centerline point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.
