description: Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a designated reference location, serving as the major-radius coordinate where the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this reference quantity, the designated location is the radius at which the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified, making it the reference specialization of major_radius.

At the designated reference location, the major radius is defined geometrically by:

$$
R_0 = \sqrt{X_0^2 + Y_0^2}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $X_0$ and $Y_0$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the reference location perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. The Cartesian basis is right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$; the corresponding cylindrical frame is right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). It is not a pointwise plasma-radius field, a flux-surface average, or a region integral, and it has no species or plasma-population scope.

Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference radius. It is also distinct from a [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) assigned to an arbitrary geometric point or measurement location.

The reference radius and the vacuum toroidal magnetic field form the reference pair $R_0$ and $B_0$, where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic field specified at the reference radius. Their product $R_0B_0$ supplies the geometric-field scale used in normalized toroidal-flux and current-density definitions.

description: Dimensionless fraction of the cold recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
documentation:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the cold, low-energy recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density), distinct from the hot charge-exchange-born component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the cold neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not summed across different isotopes and does not represent the hot component itself.

Within this model, the cold and hot fractions are complementary and sum to unity. The [hot neutral fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the corresponding charge-exchange-born component, with the energy threshold separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

dd_sources.documentation: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))

description: Signed angular offset that fixes the phase origin of a linear MHD eigenmode relative to its zero-phase complex representation.
documentation:
A reference phase is a signed angular offset that establishes the phase origin of a complex linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation or eigenmode. For a vector of phase components, each component applies to the corresponding angular dependence of the mode.

For one phase component, the offset rotates the zero-phase eigenfunction according to

$$
\delta\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{x}) = \Re\left\{\hat{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})e^{i\phi_{\rm ref}}\right\}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{X}$ is the real perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{X}}$ is its zero-phase complex eigenfunction, $\phi_{\rm ref}$ is the reference phase, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\Re$ denotes the real part. The quantity is the phase offset itself, not the mode amplitude, mode number, or oscillation frequency. Poloidal and toroidal components share this definition; the [toroidal linear MHD mode reference phase](name:toroidal_linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase) is a concrete toroidal instance, while [MHD mode reference phase](name:mhd_mode_reference_phase) denotes the broader angular reference.

Sign convention: Positive when the complex phase is advanced in the positive angular direction of the selected mode representation relative to its zero-phase reference; for a toroidal component, this is increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.
label_note: phi_ref where the registry phase symbol is varphi

description: Volume enclosed by the first-wall surface, representing the interior region inside the innermost plasma-facing boundary rather than the wall material itself.
documentation:
The first-wall volume is the total interior volume enclosed by the innermost plasma-facing surface of the vacuum vessel. It includes the space available to the confined plasma, edge and scrape-off-layer regions, and neutral gas, but excludes the material volume of the wall.

For an axisymmetric first-wall contour in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the volume is defined by

$$
V_{\rm FW}=2\pi\iint_A R\,dR\,dZ
$$

where $A$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the first-wall contour, $R$ is major radius in meters, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. For non-axisymmetric geometry, the complete three-dimensional enclosed region, including bounded ports and recesses, defines the volume.

This enclosed volume is distinct from [volume enclosed by the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which is limited by the last closed flux surface, and from [area of the first wall](name:area_of_first_wall), which measures the wall's material surface rather than an enclosed region.

dd_sources.documentation: Volume available to gas or plasma enclosed by the first wall contour

description: Dimensionless ratio of an electromagnetic wave’s phase-gradient vector to its vacuum wavenumber, retaining propagation direction and signed components.
documentation:
The refractive-index vector describes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to propagation in vacuum. It preserves the direction of the wave phase gradient while expressing its magnitude relative to the vacuum reference.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the [wave vector], $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

Directional representations include the projection parallel to the local magnetic field, represented by [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), and the magnitude of the perpendicular projection, represented by [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index). The same normalized phase-propagation concept applies to propagation through an [optical element].
label_note: unresolved [wave vector] and [optical element]

description: Signed radial component of the gage-dependent magnetic vector potential, resolved along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The radial component of the magnetic vector potential is the signed projection of the electromagnetic vector potential onto the radial direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector-potential field, $\mathbf{B}$ is its associated magnetic-field vector, and $\nabla \times$ is the spatial curl operator. The radial component is the projection $A_R = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{R}$, where $A_R$ is the radial vector-potential component and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius. The potential is gage-dependent: replacing $\mathbf{A}$ by $\mathbf{A} + \nabla\chi$, where $\chi$ is a scalar gage function and $\nabla\chi$ is its gradient, leaves $\mathbf{B}$ unchanged.

This quantity applies locally to the magnetic vector potential and has no species or region restriction. It is a single directional component, not the full [vector potential](name:vector_potential), a sum or average over directions or positions, or the poloidal component represented by the [poloidal vector potential](name:poloidal_vector_potential). The radial projection is distinguished from the vertical component by its alignment with increasing $R$ rather than increasing $Z$.

Sign convention: Positive when the gage-fixed component points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ basis, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

description: Vertical Z-coordinate of the reference point of a lower-hybrid antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical coordinate locates the reference point of a lower-hybrid antenna along the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation is:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{ant}} = Z(P_{\mathrm{ant}})
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ant}}$ is the antenna reference point and $Z(P_{\mathrm{ant}})$ is its vertical coordinate. This quantity refers to the antenna reference point; the [vertical coordinate of a lower-hybrid antenna row](name:vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row) refers instead to a row reference point.

Sign convention: Positive when the antenna reference point lies in the direction of increasing $Z$.

description: X-axis component of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror’s translation or rotation axis at its home position.
documentation:
This quantity is the Cartesian x projection of the unit vector that defines an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror’s translation direction or rotation axis at its home position.

Let $\hat{d}$ denote this direction unit vector and $\hat{x}$ the x-axis unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis. The component is defined by

$$
d_x = \hat{d} \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $d_x$ is the signed x-axis component and the unit-vector condition is $|\hat{d}|=1$.

The component is dimensionless and is bounded by $-1 \leq d_x \leq 1$. Together with the [y-axis direction component](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [z-axis direction component](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), it specifies the mirror-axis orientation.

description: Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic-field real part is the in-phase φ component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for one specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. In this frame, R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
documentation:
Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic-field real part is the real component of the toroidal projection of the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the plasma region for one specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The toroidal projection is the component along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The physical toroidal perturbation associated with the complex eigenfunction is represented by

$$
\delta B_\phi(R,\phi,Z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)\exp\!\left(i(n\phi-\omega t)\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta B_\phi$ is the physical first-order toroidal magnetic-field perturbation, $\delta\tilde{B}_\phi$ is the complex toroidal eigenfunction amplitude, $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency, and $t$ is time. This quantity is $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)]$.

Together with [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), this quantity specifies the complex toroidal perturbation component [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) for the selected harmonic. It is distinct from the radial and poloidal real-part components [radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) and [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), from the equilibrium toroidal magnetic field, and from the vacuum-region counterpart [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part). A global complex phase rotation of the eigenfunction changes the split between real and imaginary parts while leaving the reconstructed physical perturbation unchanged when the same Fourier convention is used.

Sign convention: Positive when $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi]$ is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

description: Dimensionless mode-number vector labeling the radial branch and poloidal and toroidal periodicities of a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation.
documentation:
This quantity is the collection of discrete mode labels that identifies a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation across its radial, poloidal, and toroidal structure. It is a mode-index vector, not a spatial wavevector or a physical displacement vector.

$$
\mathbf{N} = (n_r, m, n_\phi)
$$

where $n_r$ is the non-negative radial branch index, $m$ is the integer poloidal Fourier harmonic, and $n_\phi$ is the integer toroidal Fourier harmonic. The components correspond to the [radial mode number](name:radial_mode_number), [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number), and [toroidal MHD mode number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number).

The radial index labels branch structure by radial nodes, while the angular indices label periodicity around the poloidal and toroidal coordinates. Coupled poloidal harmonics may belong to one eigenmode, so this quantity identifies the mode labels without requiring a single separable spatial harmonic.
label_note: mode-index vector (n_r, m, n_phi) with resolving links to each component

description: Vertical vorticity is the Z-component of the curl of plasma bulk velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measuring local rotation about the vertical axis.
documentation:
Vertical vorticity is the component of the plasma vorticity vector along the vertical direction. It measures the signed local rotation of the bulk plasma flow in the horizontal plane and is one directional projection of [vorticity](name:vorticity).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining relation is:

$$
\omega_Z = \boldsymbol{\omega}\cdot\hat{Z} = (\nabla\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the local bulk plasma velocity in m/s, $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the vorticity vector in s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector. Here $R$ is major radius in m, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in m.

The related [toroidal vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity) projects the same vorticity vector onto $\hat{\phi}$ instead. The major-radius-scaled quantity [vertical vorticity divided by major radius](name:ratio_of_vertical_vorticity_to_major_radius) is distinct because it includes an additional inverse-length factor.

Sign convention: Positive when the bulk velocity field rotates in the right-hand sense about the positive vertical direction $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

description: Instantaneous rate of neutral molecular nitrogen admitted to the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent-electron particles with fourteen counts assigned to each molecule.
documentation:
This quantity is the equivalent-electron source rate carried by neutral molecular nitrogen admitted to the plasma vessel. It represents delivered molecular inventory, not free-electron production, ionization rate, or nitrogen ions retained in the plasma.

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}} = 14\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{N_2}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{N_2}}$ is the injection rate of nitrogen molecules. The factor 14 assigns seven equivalent-electron counts to each of the two nitrogen atoms in a molecule.

This species-resolved rate is consistent with the aggregate [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection). Integrating it over a time interval gives the corresponding accumulated nitrogen inventory represented by [accumulated nitrogen count].

description: Net toroidal electric current sustained by non-inductive current-drive mechanisms, excluding the contribution from inductive electric-field drive.
documentation:
The quantity is the net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma as a result of non-inductive current-drive mechanisms. It excludes current produced by the transformer-induced electric field and includes the algebraic sum of the included non-inductive contributions. The plasma-specific realization is [plasma current due to non-inductive current drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive).

The current is defined by the flux of non-inductive current density through a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NI}} = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the corresponding electric-current density, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented area element of the poloidal cross-section. Contributions such as [current due to electron-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive) and [current due to ion-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_ion_cyclotron_current_drive) are instances of this quantity, whereas [plasma current due to ohmic induction] is excluded.

Sign convention: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

dd_sources.documentation: Total non-inductive parallel current
Total non-inductive current (toroidal component). Positive sign means anti-clockwise when viewed from above.

description: Signed equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux function evaluated at a diagnostic measurement location, identifying the nested magnetic surface intersecting that location.
documentation:
The signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is the equilibrium flux function evaluated at a physical measurement position. It labels the nested magnetic surface passing through that position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal magnetic-flux function is defined by

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at cylindrical coordinates $(R,Z)$, $B_Z(R',Z)$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, $R$ and $R'$ are major-radius coordinates, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\pi$ is the circle constant. The toroidal angle $\phi$ completes the right-handed cylindrical frame; axisymmetry makes $\psi$ independent of $\phi$.

This quantity applies to the equilibrium magnetic field at one physical measurement position and has no species or population restriction. It is a point evaluation, not a sum, average, or integral over multiple measurement positions. It is not a normalized flux coordinate and does not represent a perturbation or fluctuation of the equilibrium flux.

The same flux-function definition is used for [poloidal magnetic flux at a beam-tracing point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_beam_tracing_point), but that quantity differs in evaluation locus. A normalized surface label at the same type of location is [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at a measurement position], which is derived by applying axis and boundary references to the signed flux value.

Sign convention: Positive when the net vertical magnetic flux through the defining horizontal disk is directed in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Poloidal flux

description: Vector diffusion coefficient for bulk neutral-particle momentum, governing anisotropic diffusive redistribution driven by neutral-neutral viscosity and charge-exchange collisions in edge and divertor plasma.
documentation:
Neutral momentum diffusivity is the direction-dependent transport coefficient that relates the diffusive neutral-fluid momentum flux in each spatial direction to the local gradient of neutral momentum density, forming the neutral-particle analog of plasma_momentum_diffusivity. As a vector quantity it encompasses distinct directional components — including parallel_neutral_momentum_diffusivity, poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity, [toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), and [vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity) — reflecting the anisotropy imposed by the magnetic geometry and the varying collisional regimes of edge and divertor regions.

The component $\chi_{n,\mathrm{mom}}$ along a direction $\hat{e}$ enters the neutral fluid momentum balance through the diffusive flux:

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{mom}} = -\chi_{n,\mathrm{mom}} \, \nabla_{\hat{e}}(m_n n_n u_n)
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_n$ is the neutral number density, and $u_n$ is the neutral fluid velocity component along $\hat{e}$.

The dominant physical mechanisms contributing to neutral momentum diffusivity are neutral-neutral viscous collisions and charge-exchange interactions with background ions; the latter can transfer substantial momentum between the neutral and ion populations and are especially significant in dense regions where charge-exchange mean-free paths are short. This coefficient is computed within fluid-neutral transport models that solve the neutral momentum equation self-consistently alongside the plasma fluid equations.
label_note: subscript n for neutral where the registry symbol is 0; also calls the diffusivity a vector

description: Collected conventional electrical current carried by the ion population assigned to one mass-resolved channel.
documentation:
The collected ion current is the conventional electrical current delivered to a detector by ions assigned to one selected atomic-mass or mass-to-charge channel. It represents the channel-specific ion population rather than the complete detector signal across all mass channels.

The defining charge-collection relation is

$$
I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \frac{dQ_{\mathrm{ion}}}{dt} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{C}} q_k\frac{dN_k}{dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the collected ion current, $Q_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the charge delivered by collected ions, $t$ is time, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of ion populations assigned to the selected channel, $q_k$ is the charge carried by an ion in population $k$, and $N_k$ is the cumulative number of ions from population $k$ collected by the detector.

The aggregation is over all ion arrivals assigned to the selected channel and species, including any charge states represented by that channel; it is not an aggregate over the full mass spectrum or over unrelated channels. The quantity excludes neutral-gas pressure and the detector-bias potential represented by the [voltage of a mass-spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Unlike [ion current density](name:ion_current_density), which is a local vector charge flux per area, this quantity is the total collected current associated with one channel. Its channel-specific value can therefore contribute to determining the corresponding species abundance, while remaining distinct from a current density.

Sign convention: Positive when positive ion charge is collected by the detector channel.

description: Signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by the outermost flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption.
documentation:
The toroidal magnetic flux function evaluated on the outermost flux surface bounding the halo-current region during a disruption is the net toroidal magnetic-field flux through the enclosed poloidal cross-section. It is distinct from the [toroidal halo current](name:toroidal_halo_current), which describes current rather than magnetic flux.

The flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{A}_h)=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dA=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}B_{\phi}\,dA
$$

where $\mathcal{A}_h$ is the poloidal area enclosed by the halo boundary, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $B_{\phi}$ is its toroidal component, and $dA$ is the poloidal area element. The boundary value is the halo-region counterpart of [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Area-normalized vector source term due to diamagnetic drift is the pressure-gradient-driven contribution to a transport momentum balance. It represents directional transfer of linear momentum associated with diamagnetic drift, not the total source from all mechanisms.
documentation:
Area-normalized vector source term due to diamagnetic drift is the part of a transport momentum-balance source vector produced by diamagnetic drift in a magnetized plasma. The diamagnetic-drift contribution is the pressure-gradient-driven part of the directional transfer of linear momentum, separated from other transport mechanisms.

When represented from a local source density over a balance region, the area-normalized source is defined by

$$
\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{1}{A}\int_V \mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{dia}}\,dV
$$

where $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the area-normalized vector source term due to diamagnetic drift, $\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the local vector source density due to diamagnetic drift, $V$ is the balance region, $dV$ is the volume element, $A$ is the surface area used for the normalization, and the subscript $\mathrm{dia}$ denotes the diamagnetic-drift contribution.

The scope is restricted to the diamagnetic-drift part of the source, meaning the contribution associated with pressure gradients in the charged plasma population and balance region specified by the more specific quantity. At this parent level no species, charge state, momentum projection, or vector component is selected; the aggregation convention is integration over the balance region followed by normalization by the associated surface area.

This quantity does not denote the total source from all mechanisms, a volume average, or a scalar particle, heat, or energy source. It also excludes source terms from other drift, collisional, neutral, wave, or externally applied mechanisms except insofar as they are part of the diamagnetic-drift contribution itself.

The [momentum source due to diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is the momentum-source specialization of this parent: it keeps the same diamagnetic-drift mechanism and area normalization while specifying the balanced transferred quantity as projected linear momentum.

Sign convention: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ transfers linear momentum in the positive direction of the basis vector onto which that component is projected.
label_note: area-normalised diamagnetic-drift source restricted to charged populations; link resolves

description: Diamagnetic momentum diffusivity is the Fickian coefficient relating the diamagnetic-drift contribution to diffusive momentum flux to the negative local momentum-density gradient across plasma and neutral populations.
documentation:
Diamagnetic momentum diffusivity is the proportionality coefficient between the diamagnetic-drift contribution to diffusive momentum flux and the negative local gradient of momentum density, following a Fickian closure for momentum transport.

The diamagnetic contribution to the diffusive momentum flux in direction $i$ is

$$
\Gamma_{m,i}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -D_{m,i}^{\mathrm{dia}} \frac{\partial (m n v_i)}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\Gamma_{m,i}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic-drift contribution to momentum flux in direction $i$, $D_{m,i}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the corresponding diamagnetic momentum diffusivity, $m$ is particle mass, $n$ is particle number density, $v_i$ is the momentum-carrier velocity component in direction $i$, and $x_i$ is the coordinate along that direction. The product $m n v_i$ is the local momentum-density component, and the superscript `dia` identifies the diamagnetic-drift contribution.

The quantity spans plasma and neutral populations, including aggregate populations, individual species, specified ionic charge states, and specified neutral internal states. It may be resolved in any spatial direction; this parent-level quantity imposes no particular directional projection or charge-state aggregation.

This is a mechanism-specific component of [momentum diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity), not the total coefficient containing collisional, turbulent, charge-exchange, or other transport mechanisms. The [ion charge-state diamagnetic momentum diffusivity](name:ion_charge_state_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity) and [neutral state diamagnetic momentum diffusivity](name:neutral_state_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity) are respective charge-state-resolved specializations, while the ion and neutral aggregate forms apply the same relation after the corresponding population aggregation.

dd_sources.documentation: Diamagnetic component, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
Diamagnetic component, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.

label_note: extends the diamagnetic-drift contribution to neutral populations, which carry no charge to drift

description: Geometric area of the neutron-sensitive detector surface, excluding passive housing, shielding, supports, electronics, projection effects, and solid-angle weighting.
documentation:
The quantity is the geometric area of the neutron-sensitive active surface of the detector. It includes the physical sensitive face, including contributions from segmented or curved surfaces, and excludes passive detector structures.

The area is defined by integration over the neutron-sensitive surface:

$$
A = \int_{S_{\rm active}} dS
$$

where $S_{\rm active}$ is the neutron-sensitive surface and $dS$ is an element of geometric surface area. This is the active-surface component represented by [area of neutron detector]; it is not an effective area weighted by detection efficiency, neutron incidence angle, projection, or solid angle.

description: Dimensionless mode-number vector labeling the discrete Fourier periodicities of a coherent wave perturbation.
documentation:
This quantity is the collection of discrete mode labels that identifies a coherent wave perturbation through its periodic phase dependence. It is a mode-index vector, not a spatial wavevector, physical displacement vector, or full linear-MHD eigenmode label.

For a coherent perturbation represented by a single Fourier phase in periodic coordinates, the wave mode-number vector is defined by

$$
\tilde{q}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, t) = \hat{q}\,\exp\!\left[i\left(\mathbf{N}_w \cdot \boldsymbol{\alpha} - \omega t\right)\right]
$$

where $\tilde{q}$ is the coherent wave perturbation of a field quantity, $\hat{q}$ is its complex amplitude, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is the set of periodic coordinates used to label the phase, $\mathbf{N}_w$ is the wave mode-number vector, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency.

This parent covers Fourier harmonic labels of coherent waves, such as the [toroidal wave mode number](name:toroidal_wave_mode_number) associated with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It does not by itself assert a radial branch index or a poloidal harmonic; those belong only to more specific quantities when explicitly defined, and distinguish it from the broader linear-MHD [mode number].

Sign convention: Positive when increasing the associated periodic coordinate at fixed time increases the Fourier phase in the representation above.
label_note: unresolved [mode number]

description: Normalized toroidal-flux surface label evaluated at the sawtooth mixing radius, marking the outer boundary of the plasma region homogenized during a sawtooth crash.
documentation:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal magnetic-flux label of the magnetic surface passing through the sawtooth mixing radius. It identifies the outer boundary of the plasma region homogenized during a sawtooth crash.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}}) = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}})$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the mixing radius, $r_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the sawtooth mixing radius, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the mixing surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the equilibrium boundary.

The scope is the single magnetic surface at the sawtooth mixing radius within the plasma region affected by the crash. This is a locus-specific evaluation of the broader [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), not a coordinate assigned to every magnetic surface, a volume average, or a flux-surface average. It is distinct from the corresponding coordinate at the [sawtooth inversion radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius), because the mixing radius and inversion radius represent different sawtooth characteristics.

description: Neutral gas pressure of a gage is the pressure indicated by a barometry gage for residual neutral gas in the vacuum vessel or surrounding vacuum system. It represents local vacuum conditions rather than a kinetic neutral-particle pressure moment.
documentation:
Neutral gas pressure of a gage is the local residual-neutral-gas pressure indicated by a barometry gage. The word gage identifies the instrument producing the indication and does not mean a pressure difference relative to atmosphere.

The quantity applies to neutral gas contributing to the gage response in the vacuum vessel or surrounding vacuum system. It aggregates the gage response without resolving thermal, fast, species, or internal-state components.

This instrument-indicated quantity is distinct from kinetic neutral-particle pressures such as [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure), [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure), [neutral internal-state pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure), and [total neutral internal-state pressure](name:total_neutral_internal_state_pressure). Those quantities denote pressure moments or state-resolved sums of neutral particle populations, whereas neutral gas pressure of a gage denotes the pressure represented by the barometry gage response and need not equal any one kinetic component.

description: Outward extent of the hard X-ray emissivity peak from its maximum to the outer half-maximum point toward the separatrix in normalized toroidal flux.
documentation:
This quantity is the outward half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak, measured from the emissivity maximum toward the separatrix in normalized toroidal flux. It characterizes the radial spread of hard X-ray emission associated with nonthermal electrons on the outer side of the peak.

$$
h_{\mathrm{outer}} = \rho_{\mathrm{half,out}} - \rho_{\mathrm{peak}}, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}(\rho_{\mathrm{half,out}}) = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}(\rho_{\mathrm{peak}})
$$

Here, $h_{\mathrm{outer}}$ is the outward half-width, $\rho_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate of the hard X-ray emissivity maximum, $\rho_{\mathrm{half,out}}$ is the outer coordinate where the emissivity reaches half its peak value, and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray emissivity as a function of normalized toroidal-flux coordinate $\rho$.

The quantity applies only to the outer side of the emissivity peak, with increasing $\rho$ directed toward the separatrix. It is a nonnegative extent and is distinct from the inward half-width, which measures the corresponding distance on the magnetic-axis side of the peak. Together, the two directional widths characterize the asymmetric spread of the peak; the [inner hard X-ray half-width at the emissivity peak](name:inner_hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak) provides the inward counterpart.

description: Signed terminal voltage of a correction coil, including the resistive voltage drop and the inductive voltage associated with changes in coil currents.
documentation:
Signed terminal voltage of a correction coil is the electric potential difference across the terminals of a correction-coil winding, evaluated with a specified terminal polarity. A correction coil is a winding used to correct or control magnetic-field errors or perturbations; this quantity does not assume a particular spatial symmetry or toroidal mode number.

For a lumped coupled-circuit representation, the terminal voltage of coil $k$ is

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{d I_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} M_{kj} \frac{d I_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage, $R_k$ is the [resistance of the correction coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil), $I_k$ and $I_j$ are coil currents, $L_k$ is the self-inductance of coil $k$, $M_{kj}$ is the signed mutual inductance coupling circuit $j$ to coil $k$, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is a circuit terminal voltage, not a magnetic-field amplitude or a measure of the imposed perturbation. It excludes voltage drops in external leads, feedthroughs, or power-supply elements unless the reference terminals are defined to include those elements.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric potential at the terminal where positive current enters the coil in the chosen winding orientation is greater than the electric potential at the terminal where it leaves.

Voltage on the coil terminals

description: Major-radius coordinate assigned to the selected flux surface, defined as the midpoint between its minimum and maximum cylindrical R values.
documentation:
The quantity is the representative major-radius location of the selected flux surface, rather than the radial coordinate of one particular point. It summarizes the surface’s inboard and outboard radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

It is defined as the midpoint of the minimum and maximum major-radius coordinates on the selected flux surface:

$$
R_{\rm fs} = \frac{R_{\min} + R_{\max}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\rm fs}$ is the representative radial coordinate of the flux surface, and $R_{\min}$ and $R_{\max}$ are respectively the minimum and maximum values of the cylindrical major-radius coordinate over that surface.

The definition applies to the complete selected flux surface and uses the extrema midpoint as its aggregation convention; it is not an area-weighted, volume-weighted, or flux-weighted average. It does not denote the radial coordinate of a particular point, such as the magnetic axis or a specified midplane location.

This quantity is the flux-surface specialization of the parent [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). It differs from the [normalized minor radius of a flux surface](name:normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface), which characterizes minor-radius position relative to a reference length rather than the surface’s major-radius location.

dd_sources.documentation: Major radius of the flux surface of interest, defined as (min(R)+max(R))/2

description: Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a point or defined location, serving as the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is the radial coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and is independent of toroidal angle.

Using a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ along the toroidal symmetry axis, it is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $X$ and $Y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the axis, and $R$ is the resulting distance. The cylindrical basis satisfies $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$; $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an extended or derived quantity, major radius may be evaluated pointwise, averaged over a flux surface, fixed at a reference location, or combined algebraically with another quantity. Thus [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius) is an average, whereas [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius) identifies a fixed normalization location; products, ratios, and differences of major radii are derived quantities rather than alternate definitions of $R$.
label_note: R = sqrt(X^2+Y^2) in the right-handed frame; opening fits '{qualifier} radius {locus}'; links resolve

description: Linear winding density of a Rogowski coil, specifying the number of turns in a single winding layer per unit coil length.
documentation:
The turns-per-length quantity specifies the linear winding density of a Rogowski coil. For a multilayer winding, it refers to one winding layer rather than the combined count of all layers.

The winding density is defined by

$$
n_t = \frac{N_\ell}{\ell}
$$

where $n_t$ is the Rogowski-coil turns density, $N_\ell$ is the number of complete winding turns in one layer over the selected winding length, and $\ell$ is that winding length.

This quantity applies to the physical winding of the Rogowski coil and is a linear density, not a discrete total turn count. It excludes the effective cross-sectional area, which is a separate geometric quantity described by the [area of the Rogowski coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), and it does not represent the signed winding current described by the [current of the Rogowski coil](name:current_of_rogowski_coil). The winding density and effective cross-sectional area together determine the coil's electromagnetic coupling and therefore its current-sensing sensitivity.

dd_sources.documentation: Number of turns per unit length. In case of multiple layers, turns are counted for a single layer

description: Effective ionic charge of the plasma immediately upstream of a divertor-target sheath, combining all positive ion species through charge moments.
documentation:
Effective charge at a divertor target is the local charge-squared-weighted ionic content of the plasma adjacent to the target, evaluated at the sheath entrance. It characterizes impurity content relative to the total positive charge density.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{\sum_i n_i Z_i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the local number density of positive-ion species $i$ and $Z_i$ is its positive integer charge state. The sums include all positive ion species and charge states represented in the local plasma. The quantity equals unity for a pure singly charged hydrogenic plasma and increases when higher-charge ions contribute.

This effective-charge interpretation is the charge-moment form of [charge at the divertor target], with the same target-local plasma scope; it is not a density or a charge-state-specific abundance.

description: Geometric rear-surface clearance between an ion-cyclotron heating antenna strap and the conducting wall or conductor behind it.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric standoff between the rear surface of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna strap and the conducting wall or other conductor located behind that surface.

The clearance is the shortest separation between the two relevant surfaces:

$$
d_{back} = \min_{\mathbf{r}_b \in S_b,\,\mathbf{r}_c \in S_c} \left\|\mathbf{r}_c - \mathbf{r}_b\right\|
$$

where $d_{\rm back}$ is the rear-surface clearance, $S_b$ is the strap back surface, $S_c$ is the facing conducting-wall or conductor surface, and $\mathbf{r}_b$ and $\mathbf{r}_c$ are position vectors on those surfaces.

The quantity applies only to the rear-facing separation of the antenna strap and does not denote the strap thickness, the distance to its inner or outer cylindrical boundaries, or either oblique cross-sectional length. The related [inner radius of the antenna strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), [outer radius of the antenna strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), [major length of the antenna strap](name:major_length_of_antenna_strap), and [minor length of the antenna strap](name:minor_length_of_antenna_strap) describe other strap dimensions rather than this conductor clearance.

This geometric clearance is an antenna-design parameter that influences the strap's loading resistance and radio-frequency coupling efficiency to the plasma; it is not itself an electrical resistance, coupling coefficient, or power quantity.

description: Net angular-momentum transfer rate per unit volume from neutral particles to the plasma, summed over all neutral internal states and retaining the complete torque-vector direction.
documentation:
Torque density for neutral particles is the net angular-momentum transfer rate to the plasma per unit volume produced by neutral–plasma momentum exchange, summed over all neutral internal states. It retains the complete torque-vector direction rather than selecting a toroidal component or a particular neutral state.

The defining relation is

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{n\to p} = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0} \frac{1}{\Delta V}\frac{d\boldsymbol{L}_{p\leftarrow n}}{dt}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{n\to p}$ is the torque-density vector transferred from neutrals to the plasma, $\boldsymbol{L}_{p\leftarrow n}$ is the corresponding angular momentum transferred to the plasma, $\Delta V$ is a volume element, and $t$ is time.

This is the neutral-exchange contribution to the broader [torque density](name:torque_density); it excludes source terms unrelated to neutral–plasma momentum exchange. The [toroidal neutral torque density](name:toroidal_neutral_torque_density) is its toroidal component.

Sign convention: Positive when each resolved component points along the corresponding positive unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ basis, with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.
label_note: subscript n for neutral where the registry symbol is 0

description: Incident angle at wall is the angle between the incoming neutral-particle velocity and the wall-surface normal directed into the material. It is the species-specific angular coordinate for physical sputtering by neutral projectiles; zero is normal incidence and grazing incidence approaches a right angle.
documentation:
Incident angle at wall is the geometrical angle between the velocity direction of an incident neutral particle at impact and the local wall-surface normal directed from the plasma-facing side into the wall material. It characterizes the incidence direction of a selected neutral-particle species on the wall.

The incidence angle $\alpha$ is defined by

$$
\alpha = \arccos\left(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}\right)
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}$ is the unit direction of the incoming neutral-particle velocity at the impact point and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}$ is the local wall-surface unit normal directed into the wall material.

The scope is a specified neutral incident species interacting with the wall. The allowed interval is $0 \le \alpha \le \pi/2$: $\alpha=0$ corresponds to normal incidence into the wall, and $\alpha=\pi/2$ corresponds to tangential grazing incidence. Directions for which the particle is leaving the wall-facing half-space are not incident angles.

This quantity is the angular argument for the physical sputtering dependence of that neutral species at the wall. It is not the physical sputtering coefficient, not an angle for emitted or sputtered particles, and not an average over neutral species or wall locations.

dd_sources.documentation: Array of incident angles of this incident species, on which the physical sputtering coefficient is tabulated

label_note: angle between incoming velocity and inward wall normal, 0 to pi/2, matches the sputtering-table source; alpha notation and qualifier template hold

description: Vorticity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed field-parallel scalar component of the curl of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift velocity. It identifies the diamagnetic contribution to plasma vorticity and excludes rotational contributions from other flow mechanisms.
documentation:
Vorticity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed field-parallel scalar component of the curl of the diamagnetic-drift contribution to plasma velocity. It represents local rotation of the pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drift about the local magnetic-field direction.

The scalar component is defined by projecting the curl of the diamagnetic-drift velocity onto the local magnetic-field direction:

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \left(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}\right)
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is vorticity due to diamagnetic drift, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift], and $\nabla \times$ denotes the spatial curl.

The scope is local plasma-fluid vorticity at a point in the plasma region where the diamagnetic-drift velocity is defined. The aggregation convention is unaveraged: no volume integral, flux-surface average, time average, or species/charge-state sum is included by this name.

It is not the magnitude of vorticity and must retain the sign of the field-parallel projection. It is not total vorticity; it excludes rotational contributions from electric-field drift, parallel flow, neutral flow, imposed rotation, or turbulence unless those contributions are part of the diamagnetic-drift velocity.

It is obtained from [bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift] by taking the curl and retaining the field-parallel component. In a decomposition of [parallel vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) by flow mechanism, this quantity is the diamagnetic-drift term; other drift or flow terms are separate contributions.

Sign convention: Positive when $\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ has a component in the direction of the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

description: Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed component.
documentation:
The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector rather than a signed component.

For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity is defined by

$$
B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total magnetic-field vector at that position.

The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces.

Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

description: Magnitude of the poloidal magnetic-field component evaluated at the pressure-pedestal-top location on the high-field side, characterizing the local magnetic geometry.
documentation:
The poloidal magnetic field at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top is the magnitude of the magnetic-field projection into the poloidal plane at that location.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, it is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{pol}} = \sqrt{B_R^2+B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude, $B_R$ is the radial component of the magnetic field, and $B_Z$ is its vertical component; $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This is a local value at the pressure-pedestal-top position on the high-field side. It excludes the toroidal magnetic-field component and is neither a flux-surface average nor a spatially aggregated field quantity.

The associated [poloidal magnetic flux at pedestal top](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal_top) identifies the magnetic-flux value at the same pedestal-top locus; it is a location-defining quantity rather than this field magnitude.

dd_sources.documentation: Value

label_note: subscript 'pol' where the registry poloidal symbol is upright p

description: Direction-resolved extent from an emissivity maximum to the corresponding half-maximum location, with components describing one-sided widths of the emitting region.
documentation:
This quantity is the direction-resolved half-width of an emissivity maximum. Each component gives the extent from the peak location to a corresponding location where the emissivity has decreased to one-half of its peak value.

Let $E(q)$ denote the emissivity as a function of coordinate $q$, let $q_{\rm pk}$ denote the coordinate of its maximum, and let $q_{1/2,k}$ denote the half-maximum coordinate in direction $k$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1/2}=\left(\Delta_{1/2,k}\right),\qquad \Delta_{1/2,k}=\left|q_{1/2,k}-q_{\rm pk}\right|,\qquad E(q_{1/2,k})=\frac{1}{2}E(q_{\rm pk})
$$

Here, $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1/2}$ is the vector of directional half-widths, $\Delta_{1/2,k}$ is one directional extent, $q$ is the coordinate used to locate the emissivity, $k$ identifies a direction or side, and $E$ is emissivity. The quantity applies to an emissivity peak and is dimensionless when the underlying coordinate is dimensionless; it does not represent the peak position, peak magnitude, or an integrated emissivity. When opposing half-maximum locations are available, their corresponding one-sided extents combine to give the full width across the peak. The [hard X-ray half-width at emissivity peak](name:hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak) is a concrete instance, while the [inner hard X-ray half-width at emissivity peak](name:inner_hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak) selects the inward component.
label_note: direction-resolved half-maximum extents; links to its hard-X-ray instances resolve

description: Effective Fickian transport coefficient relating particle flux to particle-number-density gradients, with directional or population-specific components represented by more specific quantities.
documentation:
Particle diffusivity is an effective Fickian coefficient describing the diffusive part of particle transport driven by a particle-number-density gradient. It may be resolved by transport direction or by the particle population being transported.

For each resolved direction $i$, the diffusive particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{p,i}\,\frac{\partial n_p}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive particle flux, $D_{p,i}$ is the corresponding diffusivity component, $n_p$ is the particle number density, and $x_i$ is the coordinate along the resolved transport direction. The minus sign defines down-gradient diffusive transport for a positive coefficient.

This parent quantity does not specify a particle population, charge-state aggregation, transport direction, or microscopic mechanism. Population- and direction-specific instances include [neutral particle diffusivity](name:neutral_particle_diffusivity) and [poloidal particle diffusivity].
label_note: unresolved [poloidal particle diffusivity]

description: Parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed scalar field-aligned component of conventional current density associated with an equilibrium constraint locus. It sums charge transport from all charged-particle populations unless a narrower component or population is specified.
documentation:
Parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed scalar field-aligned component of conventional current density associated with an equilibrium constraint position. The constraint position supplies the spatial locus or selected magnetic surface to which the value applies, while narrower quantities may add an averaging or population qualifier.

The field-aligned projection is defined by

$$
j_\parallel = \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $j_\parallel$ is this parallel current density, $\mathbf{j}$ is the [current density](name:current_density), $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude.

The supported scope is the conventional charge-current sum over all charged-particle populations at the specified constraint locus unless a narrower population is explicitly specified. This excludes the unprojected [current density](name:current_density), other vector components of current density, and current-density quantities not associated with a constraint position.

Narrower quantities specialize this parent by retaining the same field-aligned projection and constraint-position scope while adding further qualification. For example, the [flux-surface-averaged parallel current density at constraint position](name:flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density_at_constraint_position) is the flux-surface average of $j_\parallel$ over the selected closed magnetic surface; this parent itself does not impose that averaging convention.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current density has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field.
label_note: j dot b at the constraint locus; component template and parallel notation hold; links resolve

description: Temporal duration over which a spectrometer channel accumulates incident photons to form one spectral measurement.
documentation:
The integration duration is the elapsed time between the start and end of the photon-accumulation interval for a spectrometer channel. It defines the temporal window contributing to one spectral measurement and is distinct from the channel's spectral response, including its [effective spectral width](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

It is defined by

$$
\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t$ is the integration duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the times at which photon accumulation begins and ends. The accumulated signal is determined by the time integral of the [incident spectral flux] over this interval.

label_note: unresolved [incident spectral flux]

description: Signed angular offset that fixes the complex phase of a mode relative to its zero-phase reference.
documentation:
A mode reference phase is the angular offset applied to a complex perturbation or eigenfunction to establish its phase relative to a zero-phase reference. It specifies phase orientation without defining the mode number, amplitude, or geometric position angle.

For a complex mode amplitude, the reference phase is represented by

$$
\tilde{X} = |\tilde{X}| e^{i\phi_{\rm ref}}
$$

where $\tilde{X}$ is the complex perturbation amplitude, $|\tilde{X}|$ is its magnitude, and $\phi_{\rm ref}$ is the reference phase. The quantity generalizes the phase used by [linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase](name:linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase) and is the phase component of [mode_reference_phase](name:mode_reference_phase).

Sign convention: Positive when the complex mode phase is advanced in the defined angular direction from its zero-phase reference.
label_note: phi_ref where the registry phase symbol is varphi

description: Wavelength specifying either the short-wavelength or long-wavelength edge of a photon-detection response interval.
documentation:
A response-band boundary wavelength is the spectral location of one edge of an optical detector's photon-sensitivity interval. It identifies where the accepted response range begins or ends, rather than describing the response magnitude within that range.

The wavelength is related to the corresponding electromagnetic frequency by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{edge}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the boundary wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the electromagnetic frequency at that boundary.

This quantity applies to either endpoint of a photon-detection response interval: the lower endpoint is represented by [lower-bound wavelength of a visible camera](name:lower_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera), and the upper endpoint by [upper-bound wavelength of a visible camera](name:upper_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera). It is an endpoint value, not a spectral average, integrated response, or response-equivalent width.

The two boundary wavelengths delimit the admitted spectral interval; the lower-wavelength boundary precedes the upper-wavelength boundary. This distinguishes each boundary from [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which characterizes the extent of a response rather than one endpoint, and from the general wavelength quantity, which need not be associated with a response-band boundary.
label_note: opens 'A response-band boundary wavelength is' against 'Wavelength {locus}', and narrows the camera wavelength to a band edge

description: Local plasma electrical-conductivity tensor mapping the electric-field vector to the conductive current-density vector, including anisotropic diagonal and off-diagonal coupling.
documentation:
Plasma electrical conductivity is the local rank-two material response that relates the plasma electric field to the conductive electric-current density. It represents the collective plasma response without selecting a particular species, orbit class, direction, or transport mechanism.

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{plasma}} \cdot \mathbf{E}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductive electric-current-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the plasma electrical-conductivity tensor, and $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector. In components, $J_i = \sigma_{ij}E_j$, where $i$ identifies the current-density direction and $j$ identifies the electric-field direction. The tensor may be represented in the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, or in the magnetic-field-aligned basis $(\hat{b},\hat{e}_{\perp 1},\hat{e}_{\perp 2})$, where $\hat{b}$ is the local magnetic-field direction.

The full tensor retains all diagonal and off-diagonal couplings and is therefore broader than any single component coefficient. It excludes displacement current and contributions that are not the local conductive response of the plasma. The [radial conductivity](name:radial_conductivity), [toroidal conductivity](name:toroidal_conductivity), and [vertical conductivity](name:vertical_conductivity) are diagonal component instances in the cylindrical frame; [poloidal conductivity](name:poloidal_conductivity) and [parallel conductivity](name:parallel_conductivity) are corresponding projections in flux-surface-tangent and magnetic-field-aligned directions, respectively.
label_note: conductivity tensor J = sigma . E with resolving links to its component instances

description: Signed rotation of an elliptical beam cross-section’s principal axis relative to the local transverse basis attached to a beam-tracing propagation path.
documentation:
The tilt angle specifies the orientation of a selected principal axis of the elliptical cross-section associated with a beam-tracing beam, relative to the beam’s transverse basis. It describes ellipse orientation rather than the beam’s propagation direction, which is characterized separately by the [poloidal angle of the beam-tracing beam](name:poloidal_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam).

The principal-axis direction is defined by

$$
\hat{\mathbf a} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{\mathbf e}_1 + \sin\alpha\,\hat{\mathbf e}_2
$$

where $\alpha$ is the tilt angle, $\hat{\mathbf a}$ is the selected principal-axis unit vector, and $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel)$ is the local right-handed beam frame, with $\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel$ aligned with propagation. Because an ellipse is unchanged when a principal axis is reversed, the angle is defined modulo $\pi$; selecting the other principal axis changes the reference by $\pi/2$.

Sign convention: Positive when the selected principal axis rotates from $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ according to the right-handed orientation about $\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel$.

description: Full toroidal angular span of one limiter tile between its minimum and maximum φ coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The toroidal angular width of an individual limiter tile is the full angular span occupied by that tile around the machine symmetry axis. It is a non-negative geometric extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The width is defined from the extrema of the tile's toroidal-angle extent:

$$
\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the tile's toroidal angular width, and $\phi_{\max}$ and $\phi_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum toroidal-angle coordinates of the tile, evaluated on a continuous angular branch when the extent crosses the angular periodic boundary.

This quantity applies to one individual limiter tile and represents its complete toroidal span; it is not summed over tiles, limiter units, or periodic repetitions. It is distinct from a toroidal-angle coordinate, a tile-center angle, and the angular width of an entire limiter assembly.

The toroidal extent complements the boundary geometry described by the [vertical outline of the limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), while the analogous camera field-of-view quantity [toroidal angular width of a camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera) applies to an optical viewing extent rather than a structural tile.

In each of these zones, the unit outline remains the same. Leave this node empty for an axisymmetric unit. The first dimension gives the center and full width toroidal angle values for the unit. The second dimension represents the toroidal occurrences of the unit countour (i.e. the number of toroidal zones).

description: Effective radial velocity coefficient for advective, non-diffusive transport of total plasma momentum in the edge plasma, distinct from the plasma bulk flow velocity.
documentation:
This quantity is the effective coefficient describing the radial advective, non-diffusive transport of total plasma momentum in the edge plasma. It is a transport closure quantity, not an actual plasma bulk flow velocity.

For the selected total-momentum component, the radial convective flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{P_\mathrm{tot},r,\mathrm{conv}} = V_{\mathrm{tot},r,\mathrm{conv}} P_\mathrm{tot}
$$

where $\Gamma_{P_\mathrm{tot},r,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convective flux of total plasma momentum, $V_{\mathrm{tot},r,\mathrm{conv}}$ is this radial total-momentum convection velocity, and $P_\mathrm{tot}$ is the corresponding total plasma momentum density. The relation applies componentwise when the transported momentum component is resolved.

The scope is total plasma momentum in the edge plasma, aggregated according to the total-momentum transport equation and evaluated for radial transport. It excludes species-resolved, charge-state-resolved, neutral-only, and separately attributed momentum-convection contributions, and it must not be interpreted as the plasma bulk flow velocity. As a radial specialization of the [total momentum convection velocity](name:total_momentum_convection_velocity), it fixes the transport direction to the outward radial direction; it differs from the [radial neutral particle convection velocity](name:radial_neutral_particle_convection_velocity), which describes neutral-particle transport rather than total plasma momentum transport.

Sign convention: Positive when the associated convective total-momentum flux is directed toward increasing major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame for positive transported total-momentum density.

description: Characteristic outward distance over which a decaying plasma quantity decreases by one e-folding in the scrape-off layer.
documentation:
This quantity is the e-folding distance for a plasma quantity that decreases outward from the confined plasma into the open-field-line scrape-off layer. The operand may be a particle density, temperature, or heat-flux magnitude.

$$
L_f = \left|\frac{d\ln f}{dx}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $L_f$ is the e-folding length, $f$ is the positive scalar quantity or magnitude being characterized, and $x$ is outward distance from the confined plasma in the direction normal to magnetic flux surfaces. The scale is defined locally where the logarithmic gradient is nonzero.

The general quantity includes the electron number-density specialization [electron decay length](name:electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer), the ion number-density specialization [ion decay length], and the heat-flux specialization [heat decay length](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer). It does not select a species, transport channel, or particular decaying quantity.
label_note: unresolved [ion decay length]

description: Arclength of an individually traced magnetic field line during plasma initiation, resolving the field-line length distribution rather than reporting an average connection length.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric arclength of one magnetic field line traced during plasma initiation. It characterizes the distribution of individual field-line lengths associated with the evolving magnetic topology.

For a field-line trajectory parameterized by $(s)$, its length is

$$
L = \int_{s_0}^{s_1} \left\lVert \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} \right\rVert ds
$$

where $L$ is the field-line length, $(s)$ is the position vector along the traced magnetic field line, $s$ is a tracing parameter, and $s_0$ and $s_1$ delimit the traced segment.

The quantity applies separately to each traced magnetic field line during the plasma-initiation phase; it is not an average, sum, or charge-state aggregation. It does not impose the open-field-line averaging and closed-line replacement convention of [connection length](name:connection_length), and it is distinct from [field-line fraction], which describes the fraction of lines that are open.

The set of individual lengths provides a geometric characterization of magnetic topology, while the open-line fraction identifies the prevalence of open field lines within the same traced population.

description: Paraxial focal length of the collector optics associated with a charge-exchange spectroscopy line of sight, setting the distance from the principal plane to the focal point.
documentation:
The focal length is the paraxial distance from the principal plane of the collector optical system to the focal point for collimated incident rays. It characterizes the focusing geometry associated with a selected charge-exchange spectroscopy line of sight.

This quantity applies to the collector optics of that line of sight and is not the diameter of the focused image spot or the optical throughput. The [diameter of the line of sight] describes the focused spot size, while the [etendue of the line of sight](name:etendue_of_line_of_sight) describes its accepted optical phase space; both are related to, but distinct from, focal length.

description: Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the time-averaged amplitude of a magnetic-field perturbation projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field and normalized by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It does not include flux-surface averaging unless a more specific name states that aggregation.
documentation:
Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the time-averaged scalar amplitude of the component of a magnetic-field perturbation parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field, normalized by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It characterizes the parallel perturbation amplitude after the sign of the parallel projection has been removed.

The quantity is defined by averaging the normalized magnitude of the parallel perturbation over the time interval defining the quantity:

$$
\overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}} = \left\langle \frac{\left|\delta \mathbf{B}\cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}_0\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}} \right\rangle_t
$$

where $\overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}}$ is the time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude, $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic field, $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for normalization, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the time interval defining the quantity.

The scope is the time-averaged scalar amplitude before any spatial aggregation is added by a more specific qualifier. It applies wherever the magnetic-field perturbation, local equilibrium-field direction, and normalization reference are defined; this parent by itself does not prescribe a flux-surface, volume, line, or ensemble average.

This is not the instantaneous normalized perturbation, the signed normalized parallel component, the perpendicular perturbation, or the total magnetic-perturbation magnitude. The absolute value distinguishes it from signed parallel-field perturbations by discarding the sign of the parallel projection.

The [flux-surface-averaged time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying an additional magnetic-flux-surface average to this already time-averaged quantity; the additional qualifier changes the spatial aggregation, not the presence of time averaging.

description: Instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate of helium-4 delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection, with each helium-4 atom contributing two equivalent-electron counts.
documentation:
The helium-4 source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral helium-4 is admitted to the plasma vessel by gas-injection hardware, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. Each helium-4 atom contributes two counts because helium has atomic number 2.

The defining relation is:

$$
\dot{S}_{\mathrm{He4}} = Z_{\mathrm{He}}\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}} = 2\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}}
$$

where $\dot{S}_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the helium-4 atom delivery rate in atoms per second, and $Z_{\mathrm{He}}=2$ is helium's atomic number. This is the helium-4 component of the [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection); integrating it over time gives the [accumulated helium-4 count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection). The [helium-3 source rate due to gas injection](name:helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) uses the same atomic-number weighting but represents a separate isotope inventory.

Sign convention: Positive when helium-4 gas is delivered into the vessel, increasing the equivalent-electron particle inventory.

description: Total geometric area of the material surface forming the plasma-facing first wall, including installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where applicable.
documentation:
The first-wall area is the geometric measure of the material surface exposed toward the plasma and forming the innermost plasma-facing boundary. It includes installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where no armor is present, but excludes backing structures and surfaces that are not plasma-facing.

$$
A_{\mathrm{FW}} = \int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}} \mathrm{d}A
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the total first-wall area, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the plasma-facing first-wall surface, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is an elemental surface area. This surface measure is distinct from the enclosed [volume of the first wall](name:volume_of_first_wall) and provides the geometric basis for integrating areal loads such as [energy flux at the wall].
