description: Characteristic timescale for resistive diffusion of the plasma current distribution, determined by the minor radius and neoclassical resistivity.
documentation:
The resistive diffusion time is the characteristic timescale over which finite electrical resistivity allows the plasma current distribution to diffuse and evolve. It characterizes the slow resistive dynamics of the confined plasma.

The resistive diffusion time is defined by

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{R}} = \frac{\mu_0 \rho^2}{1.22\,\eta_{\mathrm{neo}}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{R}}$ is the resistive diffusion time, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $\rho$ is the plasma minor radius, $\eta_{\mathrm{neo}}$ is the neoclassical resistivity, and $1.22$ is the dimensionless coefficient in this characteristic-time definition.

This is a global characteristic time based on the plasma minor radius and applies to resistive current diffusion and resistive magnetohydrodynamic evolution. It is not a local diffusion time, a mode growth time, or an instantaneous current value.

The timescale increases with the square of the minor radius and decreases as neoclassical resistivity increases; it therefore reflects the plasma electrical conductivity and the evolution rate of the current distribution.

description: Rate of recurrent edge-localized mode events during an ELMing H-mode phase, expressing the cadence of pedestal-relaxation bursts rather than their amplitude or exhaust.
documentation:
The edge-localized mode frequency is the event rate of recurrent pedestal-relaxation bursts during an ELMing H-mode phase. It characterizes the cadence of ELM events, not their amplitude, duration, expelled particle content, or transient energy.

$$
f_{\mathrm{ELM}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{ELM}}}{\Delta t}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{ELM}}$ is the ELM event frequency, $N_{\mathrm{ELM}}$ is the number of identified ELM events, and $\Delta t$ is the elapsed interval over which those events are counted. The interval must represent the ELMing phase being characterized; isolated events outside that phase are excluded.

description: Geometric area of the designated diagnostic aperture surface that admits or collects radiation or particles.
documentation:
Diagnostic aperture area is the geometric extent of the designated limiting surface through which radiation or particles are admitted or collected. It may describe a clear aperture opening or a collecting face when that face defines the aperture.

The area is defined by the surface integral

$$
A = \int_S dS
$$

where $A$ is the diagnostic aperture area, $S$ is the designated aperture surface, and $dS$ is the differential area element on that surface.

This quantity applies to the specified aperture surface of the diagnostic and is not an automatically aggregated area for unrelated apertures. It is a geometric area, excluding surrounding housing, supports, and other structures unless they form the designated aperture surface; it is not an effective area weighted by transmission, sensitivity, or angular response.

The area is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the [width of a diagnostic aperture], which describe linear dimensions. For a circular aperture of radius $r$, where $r$ is the geometric distance from the aperture center to its boundary, the area satisfies $A = \pi r^2$, with $\pi$ denoting the circle constant.

description: Non-negative major-radius coordinate of a point on a ferritic element outline in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on a ferritic element outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the distance of that point from the toroidal symmetry axis. It specializes the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to ferritic-element outline points and is paired with the [vertical outline coordinate] for the same outline point.

The major radius is equivalently the norm of the horizontal Cartesian position vector:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinate components in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ parallel to the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$.

This coordinate denotes an outline-point location and is not a signed radial displacement, aggregate radial size, centroid position, or maximum radial boundary coordinate. The aggregate radial size is represented by [width of ferritic element](name:width_of_ferritic_element), the centroid position by [radial coordinate of ferritic element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), and the maximum radial boundary coordinate by [outer radius of ferritic element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element).

description: Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine k_phi/|k| of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point. It is the projection of the local unit wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $k_\phi=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude.

This is a launch-point quantity, not an integral or average over a beam path. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes the same toroidal direction cosine evaluated along a traced beam rather than specifically at launch. For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$ it satisfies $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$; together with the [radial normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:radial_wave_vector_normalized_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam], the cylindrical direction cosines obey $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2=1$. The [poloidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam] is instead a related projection in the meridional plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{k}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ is along the local $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Mode reference phase is the signed angular offset that sets the complex phase origin of an oscillatory mode relative to its zero-phase reference. It shifts the represented mode in phase without changing its amplitude, frequency, or mode identifiers.
documentation:
Mode reference phase is the scalar phase offset applied to the complex representation of an oscillatory mode to define its phase origin. It is a representation parameter for the mode as a whole, not a local value of the oscillating physical field.

A modal perturbation can be represented with the reference phase added to the modal phase argument:

$$
\delta f(\xi) = \Re\left\{\hat{f}(\xi)\exp\left[i\left(\Theta(\xi,t)+\varphi_\mathrm{ref}\right)\right]\right\}
$$

where $\delta f$ is the physical perturbation, $\hat{f}$ is its complex mode amplitude, $\Theta$ is the modal phase argument excluding the reference offset, and $\varphi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the mode reference phase.

This quantity fixes the arbitrary complex phase gage of a mode representation; it does not define the mode frequency, mode number, amplitude, or spatial eigenfunction. The [MHD mode reference phase](name:mhd_mode_reference_phase) is the magnetohydrodynamic specialization of this generic mode-level quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the offset increases the modal phase argument in the complex exponential representation.

description: Poloidal ion velocity at measurement position is the signed poloidal component of the ion flow velocity evaluated at the physical location of a measurement channel.
documentation:
Poloidal ion velocity at measurement position is the signed poloidal component of the ion flow velocity evaluated at the physical location of a measurement channel. It is the local projection of the ion population flow onto the poloidal tangent direction in the poloidal cross-section.

The local projection is defined by

$$
v_{\mathrm{pol},i}(\mathbf{x}_m) = \mathbf{v}_i(\mathbf{x}_m) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{pol,cw}}(\mathbf{x}_m)
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion flow velocity, $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the measurement position, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{pol,cw}}$ is the unit tangent in the poloidal direction in a fixed-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, oriented clockwise when the cross-section is drawn with increasing $R$ to the right and increasing $Z$ upward.

This quantity is local to the measurement position and is not a flux-surface average or a radial, toroidal, or velocity-magnitude quantity. For an ion species with unresolved charge states, the velocity denotes the density-weighted mean over all charge states of that species.

description: Signed toroidal angular displacement between a measurement position and its corresponding static reference position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed toroidal angular component of the incremental displacement associated with a measurement position. It represents a change from the corresponding static position, not an absolute angle such as the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angular offset is defined by

$$
\Delta\phi = \phi_{\mathrm{actual}} - \phi_{\mathrm{static}}
$$

where $\Delta\phi$ is the toroidal angular offset, $\phi_{\mathrm{actual}}$ is the toroidal angle of the displaced measurement position, and $\phi_{\mathrm{static}}$ is the toroidal angle of its corresponding static position. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases with toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The actual toroidal position is obtained by adding this increment to the static toroidal position; it must not be interpreted as the absolute [toroidal coordinate of a line of sight](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_line_of_sight).

Sign convention: Positive when the measurement position lies at a larger toroidal angle than the static reference position, in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

description: Reciprocal major-radius coordinate for a geometric point or specified location, serving as a positive geometric factor in toroidal equilibrium relations.
documentation:
Reciprocal major radius is the inverse of the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is a geometric quantity used to represent the radial dependence of toroidal equilibrium relations.

$$
R^{-1} = \frac{1}{R}
$$

where $R$ is the [major radius], namely the radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At the parent level, the quantity is evaluated pointwise or at a specified geometric location and has no averaging or integration implied. It is positive wherever the major radius is positive, and it is distinct from the major radius itself because it reverses the radial dependence rather than specifying the distance from the symmetry axis.

A flux-surface-averaged instance applies the flux-surface averaging operation to this reciprocal quantity; [flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius) is the corresponding geometric coefficient obtained by averaging over a magnetic flux surface.

description: Net parallel plasma current generated by fusion reactions, associated with fast alpha particles produced by deuterium–tritium reactions and distinct from other non-inductive current-drive mechanisms.
documentation:
This quantity is the net plasma current attributable to fusion reactions within the plasma, associated with fast alpha particles produced by deuterium–tritium reactions. It represents the parallel current contribution rather than the total plasma current.

The defining relation is

$$
I_{\mathrm{fus}} = \int_S \mathbf{j}_{\alpha} \cdot \mathbf{b}\, dS
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{fus}}$ is the fusion-reaction-driven current, $\mathbf{j}_{\alpha}$ is the current-density vector carried by the fusion-born fast-alpha population, $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector in the local magnetic-field direction, and $S$ is the cross-sectional surface through which the parallel current is evaluated; $dS$ is an element of that surface.

The quantity is a net signed aggregation over the fusion-born alpha population and the relevant plasma cross section. It includes only the current attributable to fusion reactions and is not a local current density, a current magnitude, or an all-population current.

It excludes current contributions driven by other mechanisms and must not be interpreted as the total plasma current or the total non-inductive current. It is an additive contribution to the non-inductive current balance.

Sign convention: Positive when the fusion-reaction-driven conventional current is parallel to the local magnetic-field direction.

description: Toroidal component of the total current density from the full kinetic distribution, including fast-particle current and electron and thermal-ion back-current.
documentation:
The toroidal driven current density is the signed toroidal component of the net conventional electric current carried by the complete driven kinetic distribution. It includes the current of nonthermal particles together with compensating electron and thermal-ion back-current, also called drag current.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$, the local quantity is defined by

$$
J_\phi(R,\phi,Z) = \sum_s q_s \int v_\phi f_s(R,\phi,Z,\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $J_\phi$ is the toroidal current-density component, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $s$ labels each particle species or combined distribution contribution, $q_s$ is its particle charge, $f_s$ is its driven velocity-distribution function, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal component of particle velocity, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The quantity is total over all represented distribution-function contributions, including superposed fast-particle distributions and the electron and thermal-ion populations responsible for back-current. A flux-surface-averaged value is the average of this same toroidal current density over a magnetic flux surface; it is not a separate current-drive mechanism. It is therefore distinct from [toroidal_current_density_due_to_fast_ion](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_fast_ion), which excludes the compensating back-current.

As the toroidal projection of [current_density_due_to_distribution_function_driven](name:current_density_due_to_distribution_function_driven), this quantity retains the parent vector's complete distribution-function scope while selecting only its $\hat{\phi}$ component.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Transverse semi-axis of the elliptical cross-section of a propagating electromagnetic wave beam, measured from the central ray to the beam-spot boundary.
documentation:
The width of a wave beam is a transverse semi-axis of its elliptical cross-section, measured from the central ray to the corresponding peripheral boundary ray.

For an elliptical beam cross-section, the boundary is defined by

$$
\frac{x^2}{w_1^2}+\frac{y^2}{w_2^2}=1
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are orthogonal transverse distances from the central ray, and $w_1$ and $w_2$ are the corresponding non-negative semi-axis widths. This quantity denotes one of these semi-axis widths, not the full diameter, a full-width-at-half-maximum measure, or the total cross-sectional area. The orientation of the elliptical axes is described separately by the [tilt angle of the beam-tracing beam](name:tilt_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam).

description: Poloidal component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, represented as a linear MHD eigenfunction and distinct from its radial and toroidal components.
documentation:
The poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential is the poloidal component of the first-order departure of the plasma magnetic vector potential from its reference state. In linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenfunction descriptions, it carries the poloidal part of the magnetic-vector-potential perturbation without selecting a real or imaginary phase component.

The perturbed magnetic field associated with the full vector potential perturbation satisfies

$$
\delta \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed plasma magnetic field, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, and $\delta \mathbf{A}$ is the full perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential. The poloidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.

This quantity is restricted to the poloidal component and is not the complete vector potential, its radial component, its toroidal component, or the perturbed magnetic field itself. It is also distinct from the real-valued specialization [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential real part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part), which selects one phase component of the corresponding eigenfunction.

The component is a specialization of the full [perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential); its curl contributes to the associated perturbed magnetic field. A gage transformation can change the vector-potential representation without changing this curl, so the vector-potential component is not uniquely identical to a magnetic-field component. The radial component provides an adjacent component specialization of the same perturbed-vector-potential family.

description: Toroidal angular coordinate of a beamlet-group center around the machine symmetry axis, using the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the toroidal angular coordinate of the representative center position of a beamlet group about the machine symmetry axis. It locates the group in the toroidal direction and is distinct from the position of any individual beamlet.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the group-center position is represented by

$$
\mathbf{r}_c = R_c\hat{\mathbf{R}}(\phi_c) + Z_c\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the beamlet-group center position, $R_c$ is its major-radius coordinate, $Z_c$ is its vertical coordinate, $\phi_c$ is its toroidal angle, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}(\phi_c)$ is the radial unit vector at that angle, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The basis is $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

The scope is the defined center position of the beamlet group as a whole. No aggregation over the toroidal angles of individual beamlets is implied; the quantity does not represent an individual beamlet's location, direction, trajectory, radial coordinate, or vertical coordinate. Together with the center's radial and vertical coordinates, it specifies the group's cylindrical position. Its angular convention is the same as that used for the [toroidal angle of an antenna strap](name:toroidal_angle_of_antenna_strap), while the owning object is different.

Sign convention: Positive when the center's angular displacement is in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

description: Signed x projection of the unit vector along an elliptic shatter cone’s minor geometric axis in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed projection of the unit vector directed along the minor geometric axis of an elliptic shatter cone onto the Cartesian x direction. It specifies one orientation coordinate of that hardware axis.

Let $u_x$ denote this x component, $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{minor}}$ the unit vector along the shatter cone’s minor axis, and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ the unit vector toward increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. The defining projection is

$$
u_x = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{minor}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{x}}
$$

The component is bounded between −1 and 1 because $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{minor}}$ is normalized.

This quantity applies only to the minor axis of the shatter cone and represents one Cartesian component; it is neither the complete direction vector, its magnitude, nor an aggregation over axes or hardware objects. It is distinct from the corresponding [x component of the major-axis unit vector](name:x_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone).

Together with the other Cartesian components of the same minor-axis unit vector, including the [z component of the minor-axis unit vector](name:z_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), this component specifies the minor-axis orientation.

description: Total neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the complete neutral population, combining thermal and fast particles across all internal states.
documentation:
Total neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the complete neutral-particle population. It combines thermal and fast neutral populations and includes all unresolved internal quantum states, rather than selecting one population or state.

For the total neutral distribution function $f_n(mathbf{x},mathbf{v})$, the pressure tensor and scalar pressure are defined by:

$$
\mathbf{P}_n = m_n \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n)(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n) f_n(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v,\qquad p_n = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}_n
$$

where $m_n$ is neutral particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $n_n=\int f_n\,d^3v$ is total neutral number density, and $\mathbf{u}_n=n_n^{-1}\int\mathbf{v}f_n\,d^3v$ is the total mean neutral flow velocity. Thus, the central moment includes both random motion and relative streaming between included populations. It is the aggregate counterpart of [neutral pressure], whereas [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure) excludes the fast population and [neutral internal state pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure) selects a specified internal state.

dd_sources.documentation: Pressure (thermal+non-thermal) (sum over charge states when multiple charge states are considered)
Pressure (thermal+non-thermal) (sum over charge states when multiple charge states are considered)

description: Maximum neutron energy flux escaping through the rear surface of a breeding blanket module toward vessel structures.
documentation:
This quantity is the greatest local neutron energy flux crossing outward through the rear surface of one breeding blanket module. It measures the escaping neutron load relevant to attenuation toward vessel structures.

The maximum is defined from the local back-surface neutron energy flux as

$$
q_{n,\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S_{\mathrm{back}}} q_n(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and $S_{\mathrm{back}}$ is the rear surface of the module.

The quantity applies to fusion neutrons from all included neutron energies, fusion reaction channels, and reacting populations, aggregated into a single local energy-flux value before taking the maximum over the rear surface of one module. It represents neutrons escaping outward from the module and excludes a surface-integrated module power and neutron flux incident on the module's front surface.

It is the maximum-over-surface transformation of [back-surface neutron flux](name:back_surface_neutron_flux), which describes the local value without selecting its maximum. It is distinct from [incident neutron power of a breeder blanket module](name:incident_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which is the total neutron power arriving at the module, and from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which describes energy deposited by neutron interactions within the module.

description: Instantaneous injection rate of silane (SiH4) gas into the plasma vessel, expressed as an electron-equivalent particle rate with 18 equivalent electrons for each SiH4 molecule.
documentation:
Instantaneous injection rate of silane ($\mathrm{SiH}_4$) gas into the plasma vessel is the silane gas source rate expressed on an electron-equivalent particle-counting basis. Each $\mathrm{SiH}_4$ molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons, equal to the total electron count of a neutral molecule.

The conversion from a molecular silane injection rate to this electron-equivalent source rate is

$$
S_{\mathrm{SiH}_4}=18\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH}_4}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{SiH}_4}$ is the silane source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH}_4}$ is the molecular injection rate of neutral silane into the plasma vessel, and 18 is the electron-equivalent count of one neutral $\mathrm{SiH}_4$ molecule.

This quantity applies only to silane gas introduced into the plasma vessel and is aggregated over all silane introduced into that vessel on the same electron-equivalent basis. It excludes source rates for other gasses, total gas-source rates, silicon-only or hydrogen-only atomic source rates, mass flow, neutral-gas inventory, and pressure.

The [silane source count] is the time integral of $S_{\mathrm{SiH}_4}$ using the same factor of 18 between molecular count and electron-equivalent count. This quantity is the silane analog of the [ethylene source rate](name:ethylene_source_rate) and [ethane source rate](name:ethane_source_rate); the molecular identity fixes the conversion factor in each case.

Sign convention: Positive when silane is added to the plasma vessel.

description: Electrical resistivity of material forming an individual limiter unit, governing the local relation between electric field and current density during electromagnetic response.
documentation:
Electrical resistivity of a limiter unit is the material property that determines how strongly its conducting material opposes electric current and converts electromagnetic energy into ohmic dissipation.

The local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric-current-density vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one limiter unit and represents a local material property rather than a sum over limiter units or a lumped electrical resistance of an entire structure. It excludes geometric path effects, contact contributions, and circuit-level inductive effects. The limiter-unit property is the component-specific counterpart of [resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component](name:resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component) and is distinct from the effective material property assigned to a broader wall through [resistivity_of_wall_material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material).

description: Ion momentum source rate is a scalar rate coefficient for proportional source, sink, or transfer terms in an ion momentum balance. Its population scope is ions, while child names may add qualifiers such as an implicit treatment; the parent does not choose a component, projection, isotope, or charge state.
documentation:
Ion momentum source rate is a scalar coefficient that parameterizes a source, sink, or transfer term proportional to an ion momentum quantity in an ion momentum-balance equation. Its population scope is ions, not electrons, neutrals, or a species-free momentum balance.

For a proportional contribution to an ion momentum source term, the defining relation is

$$
S_{M_i}^{(\gamma)} = \gamma_i M_i
$$

where $\gamma_i$ is the ion momentum source rate, $M_i$ is the associated ion momentum quantity for the ion population under consideration, and $S_{M_i}^{(\gamma)}$ is the corresponding proportional contribution to the ion momentum source term.

This quantity is the rate coefficient itself, not the ion momentum, the full source term, a force density, or a torque. The parent name does not select a spatial component, coordinate direction, flux-surface projection, explicit or implicit numerical treatment, isotope, or charge state; those distinctions require more specific names.

The [implicit ion momentum source rate](name:implicit_ion_momentum_source_rate) is an implicit-treatment specialization of this ion parent, used when the proportional source or sink contribution is represented implicitly. Source contributions that are not proportional to the associated ion momentum quantity are outside this rate-coefficient definition.

Sign convention: Positive when the proportional source term has the same sign as, or acts in the same direction as, the associated ion momentum quantity.
label_note: names the rate gamma_i and gives S to the source term, where the registry source-rate symbol is S

description: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its inner conducting boundary. It is nonnegative.
documentation:
Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,phi,Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to its inner conducting boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The inner boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected inner-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R_i - R_c)^2 + (Z_i - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annular cross-section center and $(R_i,Z_i)$ is the inner-boundary position in the same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This quantity specializes [radius_of_passive_loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) to the inner conducting boundary and complements [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). For a circular annulus, the conductor thickness is the outer radius minus this inner radius, and [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is determined by the difference of the squared outer and inner radii. It is a cross-sectional size, not the loop center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

dd_sources.documentation: Inner radius

description: Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to a selected mass-to-charge channel. It denotes a channel-resolved neutral contribution and does not require correspondence to a unique neutral species.
documentation:
Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to one mass-discriminated channel of a mass spectrometer. The channel denotes a response in mass-to-charge space after ionization, so the quantity is a pressure equivalent for neutrals that can contribute to that channel, not a pressure of the detected ions.

This quantity is neutral in scope: it excludes charged-particle plasma pressure, electron pressure, and any pressure contribution not represented as neutral gas before ionization. It is the neutral-specific counterpart of [pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel].

A channel value need not be the thermodynamic partial pressure of a single species, because fragmentation, isotopologues, charge states of produced ions, and isobaric species can overlap in the same mass-to-charge channel. Summing channel values represents [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) only when the calibrated channels are non-overlapping, span the neutral mixture being represented, and treat cross-sensitivities consistently.

description: Global volume-integrated rate of fusion events or reaction-product generation attributable to fusion between two nonthermal fuel-ion populations supplied by neutral beams.
documentation:
This quantity is the global rate of beam-beam fusion events or of production of a specified reaction product caused by collisions between two nonthermal fuel-ion populations originating from beam injection. It is a reaction-source quantity, not a local source density or directional flux.

The global rate is the volume integral of the local beam-beam fusion source rate:

$$
\dot{N}_X = \int_V S_X^{\mathrm{BB}}(\mathbf{r})\,d^3\mathbf{r}
$$

where $\dot{N}_X$ is the global rate for counted entity $X$, $X$ denotes either a fusion event or a specified reaction product, $V$ is the plasma volume over which beam-beam reactions occur, $S_X^{\mathrm{BB}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the corresponding local source rate density, and $\mathbf{r}$ is position.

The quantity aggregates the volume-integrated contribution from all represented beam-beam fuel-ion reaction channels and, when a product is specified, applies the corresponding product yield. Both reacting fuel-ion populations are nonthermal beam-origin populations; the generic quantity does not select a particular isotope pair, charge state, reaction product, or product channel. It excludes beam-thermal and thermal-thermal fusion contributions, as well as local source densities and surface or directional fluxes.

The [neutron rate due to beam-beam fusion](name:neutron_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) is a product-specific specialization that counts neutrons while retaining the same global volume integration and beam-beam channel aggregation. The [source rate due to beam-beam fusion](name:source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) represents the corresponding product-resolved source-rate family, whereas [rate due to beam-thermal fusion](name:rate_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion) uses one beam-origin and one thermal reacting population and is therefore a distinct fusion mechanism.
label_note: volume integral of the beam-beam source density; opening fits '{modifiers} rate {locus}'; dot-N as the registry gives; links resolve

description: Rate characterizing the addition, removal, or transfer of momentum to a plasma population, expressed relative to its associated momentum content.
documentation:
This quantity is a scalar rate for momentum supplied to, removed from, or transferred within a plasma population. It describes the temporal strength of a momentum source without selecting a particular particle species, direction, mechanism, or spatial region.

When the source is expressed relative to the associated momentum density, its defining relation is

$$
\nu_{p,\mathrm{src}} = \frac{S_p}{P}
$$

where $\nu_{p,\mathrm{src}}$ is the momentum source rate, $S_p$ is the momentum source density, and $P$ is the corresponding momentum density. The parent covers concrete specializations such as the [ion momentum source rate](name:ion_momentum_source_rate), while excluding the momentum density itself and any directional component not specified by the specialization.
label_note: first line never reaches 'source rate', against '{modifiers} source rate {locus}'; nu_p,src where the registry symbol is S

description: Plasma-volume-averaged volumetric production rate of runaway electrons, summed over Dreicer, avalanche, hot-tail, Compton, and tritium-decay generation mechanisms.
documentation:
Plasma-volume-averaged volumetric production rate of runaway electrons is the spatial average, over the plasma volume, of the local total rate at which electrons enter the runaway population. The total rate includes generation by Dreicer, avalanche, hot-tail, Compton, and tritium-decay mechanisms.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V = \frac{1}{|\Omega_p|}\int_{\Omega_p} S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged total runaway electron source rate, $S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [total runaway electron source rate] at position $\mathbf{x}$, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma-volume domain, $|\Omega_p|$ is the volume measure of that domain, and $dV$ is the volume element.

This quantity applies to the runaway-electron population within the plasma volume and uses an unweighted volume average of the total local volumetric production rate. The mechanism sum is part of the quantity definition; the total includes component production rates such as the [Dreicer runaway electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and the [hot-tail runaway electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), but is not restricted to either component.

It is the plasma-volume-averaged counterpart of the [total runaway electron source rate]. It is a production-rate density averaged over volume, not the absolute number of runaway electrons and not a current-density measure; in particular it is distinct from the [volume-averaged parallel runaway electron current density](name:volume_averaged_parallel_runaway_electron_current_density), which describes charge transport by the runaway population.

description: Radial coordinate of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of the oblique reference point anchoring one current-carrying filament element's rectangular cross-section.
documentation:
Radial coordinate of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate of the oblique reference point that anchors one current-carrying plasma filament element's rectangular cross-section. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to a single plasma filament element represented by oblique rectangular cross-sectional geometry. It is the coordinate of the reference point used by that representation, not the filament width, height, centroid position, magnetic-axis position, or a flux-surface radial coordinate; no averaging or summation over filament elements is implied.

Together with the [vertical coordinate of the plasma filament], it locates the oblique reference point in the poloidal plane. The [alpha angle of the plasma filament](name:alpha_angle_of_plasma_filament) and [beta angle of the plasma filament] are defined relative to this same reference point, and the [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) is a rectangular cross-section extent anchored by it.

description: The vertical coordinate of each point on a plasma-facing component boundary outline is the signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height $Z$ of each boundary-contour point belonging to a plasma-facing component. It describes the component boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For outline point $i$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is that point's position vector relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction. The quantity applies pointwise to one component boundary outline and is not an average, extremum, centroid coordinate, or integrated geometric measure. A closed outline does not repeat its first point as a closing point.

This coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the corresponding outline coordinate for a limiter tile or divertor tile, such as [vertical outline of limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and [vertical outline of divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but its locus is the plasma-facing component boundary in general.

Sign convention: Positive when $Z_i$ increases in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

description: Second local tangential (X2) back-surface radius of curvature of an optical element is the signed directional radius of the element back surface along its second object-local tangential direction, rather than along a machine-fixed axis.
documentation:
Second local tangential (X2) back-surface radius of curvature of an optical element is the signed directional radius of curvature of the element's back surface in the surface-normal section whose tangent is the second object-local tangential direction. It characterizes the local surface figure of that back face when the back surface is curved.

The directional radius is the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature in the same surface direction:

$$
R_{2,\mathrm{back}} = \frac{1}{\kappa_{2,\mathrm{back}}}
$$

where $R_{2,\mathrm{back}}$ is the second local tangential back-surface radius of curvature of the optical element and $\kappa_{2,\mathrm{back}}$ is the signed normal curvature of the optical-element back surface in the same second object-local tangential direction.

The quantity applies to one optical element and to its back surface only. It is defined only for curved back-surface types for which a second local tangential radius is specified; it is not a planar-surface parameter, not an average over surfaces, optical elements, or tangential directions, and not a radius along any machine-fixed axis.

The [first local tangential back-surface radius of an optical element](name:first_local_tangential_back_surface_radius_of_optical_element) is the corresponding radius on the same back surface along the orthogonal first object-local tangential direction. The [second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element](name:second_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element) is the opposite-surface counterpart along the same second object-local tangential direction. In optical-element surface names that use vertical for this surface direction, such as [vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) and [vertical front-surface radius of an optical element](name:vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element), vertical denotes the same object-local second tangential direction, not a machine-fixed direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the center of curvature of the back-surface normal section in the second local tangential direction lies in the direction of the oriented local normal of the back surface.

description: Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It equals 1 for a plasma containing only singly charged hydrogen-isotope ions and increases with impurity charge content.
documentation:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It is the on-axis value of [effective charge](name:effective_charge). It equals unity for a plasma containing only singly charged hydrogen-isotope ions, and higher-charge impurity ions contribute disproportionately because the charge number is squared.

For a local ion mixture, the on-axis effective charge is defined by:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}) Z_s^2}{n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species or ionization states present at the magnetic-axis location, $n_s$ is the corresponding ion number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the positive ion charge number, $n_e$ is the electron number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ denotes the magnetic-axis location.

The sum includes charged ions and excludes neutral atoms, neutral molecules, and electrons. For a locally quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$, so the same quantity may be interpreted as the ion-density-weighted ratio $\langle Z^2 \rangle / \langle Z \rangle$. This locus-specific value is distinct from [effective charge at the plasma boundary](name:effective_charge_at_separatrix).

description: Vacuum spatial period of a probing electromagnetic wave propagating as a diagnostic beam, defining its spectral wavelength.
documentation:
Vacuum wavelength of a wave beam is the spatial period of its electromagnetic phase in vacuum, assigned to the beam’s carrier radiation. It characterizes the beam itself rather than a spectral transition or an instrument-response feature.

The vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ is related to the beam’s temporal frequency $f$ by:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{c}{f}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $f$ is the temporal oscillation frequency of the electromagnetic wave.

This quantity applies to a probing electromagnetic wave beam and describes its vacuum propagation property, independent of plasma-induced changes in phase velocity. It is assigned to the beam as a whole and is not a sum, average, or integral over beams, paths, channels, or spectral components. It excludes the in-medium wavelength and wavelengths associated with filters, detector pixels, or spectral transitions.

This beam-specific specialization of [vacuum electromagnetic wavelength] supplies the wavelength used to characterize the beam’s propagation and its interaction with plasma. For a vacuum plane wave, the magnitude of its [wave vector] satisfies the equivalent relation $|\mathbf{k}| = 2\pi/\lambda_0$, where $\mathbf{k}$ is the vacuum wave vector.

Wavelength used for polarimetry

description: Dimensionless toroidal-flux label locating the top of the H-mode edge pedestal on a nested magnetic surface relative to the magnetic axis and last closed flux surface.
documentation:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at the pedestal top is the dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the top of the H-mode edge pedestal. It locates that position within the nested closed-flux-surface family, rather than representing a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

For a nested equilibrium, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ped}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{LCFS}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped})$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a magnetic surface, $\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top position, $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes the magnetic axis, and $\mathrm{LCFS}$ denotes the last closed flux surface.

The value applies specifically at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, the inner shoulder of the edge transport barrier. Its position is defined by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). This is a single coordinate evaluation: no species, charge-state, or population aggregation applies, and no surface averaging is implied. It is distinct from a cylindrical radial distance and from the unnormalized [toroidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top).

This entry is the pedestal-top specialization of the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), with the same axis-to-boundary normalization. It should not be interpreted as the corresponding [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which labels surfaces using poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic flux.

The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)

description: Effective kinematic coefficient governing down-gradient transport of a selected component or projection of aggregate edge-plasma momentum.
documentation:
This quantity is the effective kinematic momentum diffusivity associated with a selected component or projection of edge-plasma momentum. Edge-plasma momentum is the aggregate plasma momentum carried in the edge region; the field-aligned specialization is [parallel edge-plasma momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity).

For a scalar down-gradient closure for selected qualifier $a$, the diffusive flux of edge-plasma momentum is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{a} = -\rho D_{a} \nabla u_{a}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{a}$ is the diffusive flux vector of edge-plasma momentum associated with qualifier $a$, $\rho$ is the mass density of the transported aggregate, $D_{a}$ is this diffusivity, $u_{a}$ is the corresponding edge-plasma velocity component or projection, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient. The minus sign specifies down-gradient transport.

The qualifier $a$ identifies the resolved momentum component, projection, or transport direction; it is not necessarily the direction in which the flux crosses a surface. The transported aggregate is ion-fluid momentum density summed over ion species and charge states, excluding electron inertial momentum, so this quantity is distinct from species-resolved momentum diffusivities and from non-edge plasma momentum diffusivity.

description: Volumetric production rate of runaway electrons generated when the high-energy tail survives rapid thermal-quench cooling.
documentation:
This quantity is the local production rate of electrons entering the runaway-electron population through the hot-tail mechanism. It represents runaway generation from the high-energy tail that remains populated as the bulk electron population cools rapidly.

The hot-tail contribution to runaway-electron density evolution is defined by

$$
S_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{hot}} = \left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{hot}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot-tail runaway-electron source rate, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron number density, $t$ is time, and the subscript `hot` denotes the hot-tail contribution to the density change.

The quantity applies specifically to runaway electrons identified by the adopted runaway criterion and is evaluated locally, without spatial averaging. It includes only production caused by the hot-tail mechanism; it excludes runaway generation from mechanisms such as Dreicer acceleration and Compton scattering, as well as hot-tail production that does not satisfy the runaway criterion.

The threshold separating the runaway population from the non-runaway tail is related to the [runaway-electron critical momentum due to hot-tail generation](name:runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_hot_tail). This source is a mechanism-resolved contribution to the [volume-averaged total runaway-electron source rate](name:volume_averaged_total_runaway_electron_source_rate), which aggregates source contributions over the plasma volume and across the relevant generation mechanisms; the [runaway-electron source rate due to Dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and [runaway-electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) are distinct mechanism-resolved contributions.

description: Imaginary quadrature component of the complex wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed imaginary quadrature component of the parallel electromagnetic wave electric-field phasor. It retains phase information and is not the field amplitude or magnitude.

$$
\tilde E_\parallel = \tilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b} = E_{\parallel,R}+iE_{\parallel,I},\qquad E_{\parallel,I}=\operatorname{Im}(\tilde E_\parallel)
$$

Here $\tilde{\mathbf E}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $E_{\parallel,R}$ and $E_{\parallel,I}$ are its real and imaginary quadrature components. The imaginary component, together with the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), specifies the complex parallel field; its algebraic sign follows the selected temporal phasor convention. It is distinct from the [parallel wave electric field amplitude].

Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary quadrature electric-field component points along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.

description: Cumulative net count of neutral particles deposited into the wall through plasma–wall exchange, referenced to zero at the start of accumulation.
documentation:
This quantity is the retained neutral-particle inventory accumulated through net exchange between the plasma and the wall. It is not the instantaneous number of neutral particles present at the wall.

The inventory is defined by the time-integrated net particle flux across the wall surface:

$$
N_{\mathrm{wall}}(t)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}}\left[\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x},t')-\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x},t')\right] \,\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the accumulated neutral inventory, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the wall surface, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the inward and outward neutral-particle flux densities. The inward contribution is related to the [neutral particle flux at wall], while recombination provides one process-resolved contribution to outward flux through [neutral particle flux at wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The accumulation is for the selected neutral species and represents net exchange rather than a global gas-injection inventory.

description: Number density of free electrons per physical volume averaged along a complete plasma propagation chord, equal to the path integral divided by chord length.
documentation:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume averaged along a complete propagation chord is the path-normalized continuum count density of the unqualified free-electron population along that chord.

For local [electron density](name:electron_density) $n_e(l)$, the defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_e = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_e(l)\,dl
$$

where $\bar{n}_e$ is the line-averaged electron density, $n_e(l)$ is the local free-electron density at path coordinate $l$, $l$ is distance along the complete propagation chord, and $L$ is the full chord length.

This quantity applies to the complete unqualified free-electron population along the chord, aggregating all contributing free-electron populations rather than selecting thermal or fast electrons. It is a path average over the chord and is not a pointwise [electron density](name:electron_density) or a line-integrated column density.

The numerator in the defining relation is the [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density); dividing it by the chord length produces this path-normalized quantity. The same line-averaging construction applies to species-specific quantities such as [line-averaged hydrogen density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density), while this quantity remains specific to free electrons.

description: X-axis component of a camera's unit viewing-direction vector in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed projection of a camera’s line-of-sight direction unit vector onto the Cartesian x axis. It specifies one component of the camera viewing orientation.

If $\hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam}$ is the camera’s line-of-sight direction unit vector and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector, the component is defined by:

$$
d_x = \hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam} \cdot \hat{\mathbf x}
$$

Here $d_x$ is this quantity, $\hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam}$ is the camera direction vector, and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the unit vector along increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame. The corresponding y- and z-axis components are given by [y-direction unit vector of camera](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [z-direction unit vector of camera](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera); these components together specify the viewing direction and satisfy unit-vector normalization.

description: Multiplicative radiometric coefficient that converts a corrected visible-camera detector signal into absolute photon radiance integrated over the admitted spectral band.
documentation:
A visible-camera radiometric factor converts a consistently corrected detector signal into band-integrated photon radiance. It represents the combined response of the optical throughput, detector sensitivity, pixel etendue, and exposure treatment rather than the radiance itself.

The defining conversion is

$$
L_{\mathrm{vis}} = C_{\mathrm{vis}} S_{\mathrm{corr}}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is the [visible-camera brightness](name:brightness_of_visible_camera), $C_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is this visible-camera factor, and $S_{\mathrm{corr}}$ is the corrected detector signal. The spectral dependence is integrated over the relevant visible passband. Unlike the resulting brightness, the factor is a calibration coefficient and must be applied to the corrected signal; it is the camera-specific component of the parent [factor of visible camera].

description: Cumulative post-breakdown propane inventory delivered by gas injection, expressed as 26 equivalent electrons for each neutral molecule.
documentation:
This quantity is the cumulative inventory of neutral propane ($\mathrm{C_3H_8}$) molecules delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown. It represents delivered propane inventory, not the number of free electrons in the plasma or the ionization state of the propane.

For evaluation time $t$ after breakdown, the equivalent-electron count is defined by:

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = 26N_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t) = \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} 26\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t)$ is the cumulative number of propane molecules delivered by time $t$, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t')$ is the instantaneous propane molecular delivery rate at integration time $t'$, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $t'$ is the integration variable. The factor 26 is the total number of electrons in one neutral propane molecule: three carbon atoms contribute six each and eight hydrogen atoms contribute one each.

The scope is restricted to propane introduced by gas injection after breakdown and includes all such molecules delivered up to the evaluation time. It excludes prefill propane and does not represent inventory from other gas species, free plasma-electron content, or an ionization-state-resolved amount.

Unlike the [propane prefill count](name:propane_prefill_count), which covers propane introduced before breakdown, this quantity covers the post-breakdown interval. Unlike the [propane source rate](name:propane_source_rate), it is cumulative rather than instantaneous.

description: Toroidal angular coordinate of the reciprocating probe’s average measurement position during a plunge, referenced to the facility’s toroidal-angle origin.
documentation:
The toroidal coordinate $\bar{\phi}_{\rm probe}$ identifies the azimuthal location of the reciprocating probe’s average position formed from its measurement locations. It is an angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame.

For an averaged position represented in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ basis, with $z$ aligned with $Z$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe} = \\operatorname{atan2}(\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}, \\bar{x}_{\\rm probe})
$$

where $\\bar{x}_{\\rm probe}$ and $\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the averaged position. This identifies the probe location analogously to the toroidal coordinate at a [beam tracing point](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point), but the locus here is the reciprocating probe’s average position.

Sign convention: Positive when $\\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe}$ increases in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\\phi$.

description: Global rate of particle-number removal from the plasma by pumping through the wall, aggregated over carrier species and charge states rather than resolved as an areal flux.
documentation:
The particle pumping rate is the global throughput of particles removed from the plasma at the wall by pumping. It represents particle number, not energy or momentum, and is not an areal flux density.

The rate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{p,pump}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{p,removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{p,pump}}$ is the particle-number removal rate due to pumping, $N_{\mathrm{p,removed}}$ is the cumulative number of particles removed through the wall by pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies globally over the wall and aggregates the removed particle population without selecting a species or charge state. It is not resolved by wall area or position and does not represent a neutral-only rate or an electron-equivalent rate.

The explicit particle channel identifies the removed particle-number throughput within the broader pumping-rate family. It has the same global wall and pumping scope as [rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping](name:rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping), while distinguishing particle-number removal from any other transport channel.

description: Limiting signed field-line winding number on the innermost closed flux surface, giving toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the magnetic axis.
documentation:
The safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting signed field-line winding number as nested closed magnetic flux surfaces contract toward the magnetic axis. It gives the toroidal transits per complete poloidal circuit in that limit.

The axis value is defined by

$$
q_{\rm axis} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_{\rm axis}} q(\psi)
$$

where $q_{\rm axis}$ is the safety factor at the magnetic axis, $q(\psi)$ is the safety factor on the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\psi_{\rm axis}$ is the value of that flux-surface label at the magnetic axis.

This quantity applies only to the magnetic-axis limit of nested closed flux surfaces in an equilibrium. It is a single equilibrium winding value with no species, population, or charge-state aggregation, and it is distinct from safety factor values on finite-radius surfaces such as the [safety factor at the plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary).

It is the magnetic-axis specialization of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor): the parent quantity describes field-line winding as a function of flux-surface label, while this quantity selects its limiting value at $\psi_{\rm axis}$. The parent relation is the signed flux-increment ratio $q = d\Phi_{\rm tor}/(d\Phi_{\rm pol}/2\pi)$, where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-flux increment $d\Phi_{\rm tor}$ and poloidal magnetic-flux increment $d\Phi_{\rm pol}$ have the same sign for the positively oriented field-line circuit, with $\phi$ increasing in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

description: Full aperture extent of one rectangular filter window along its object-local second tangential axis, distinct from the window’s orthogonal width and curvature radius.
documentation:
The second local tangential width is the full distance between the two opposite boundaries of a single rectangular filter window along its object-local second tangential axis. It defines one linear dimension of the filter aperture.

$$
W_2 = \left|x_{2,+} - x_{2,-}\right|
$$

where $W_2$ is the second local tangential width, and $x_{2,+}$ and $x_{2,-}$ are the coordinates of the opposing aperture boundaries along that local axis.

This quantity applies only to rectangular filter-window geometry and refers to one filter window, not an aggregate over multiple windows or channels. It is a full boundary-to-boundary extent rather than a half-width, position, or signed coordinate.

The width describes the linear aperture dimension, whereas the [second local tangential radius of the filter window](name:second_local_tangential_radius_of_filter_window) describes curvature along the same local direction; the two quantities are not interchangeable.

description: Power-deposition-weighted flux-surface amplitude of the right-hand circularly polarized E-minus wave-electric-field phasor for each toroidal mode number.
documentation:
This quantity is the nonnegative amplitude of the right-hand circularly polarized (E-minus, or R-wave) component of a coherent wave electric-field phasor. It represents the mode-resolved field strength after power-deposition-weighted averaging over a magnetic flux surface.

For toroidal mode number $n$, the amplitude is defined by

$$
\mathcal{E}_{-,n}^{\mathrm{amp}} = \left|\frac{\langle p_{\mathrm{dep}}\,\widetilde{E}_{-,n}\rangle_{\psi}}{\langle p_{\mathrm{dep}}\rangle_{\psi}}\right|
$$

where $\mathcal{E}_{-,n}^{\mathrm{amp}}$ is the amplitude of the E-minus wave-electric-field component, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, $\widetilde{E}_{-,n}$ is its complex phasor, $p_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the power-deposition density, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes a flux-surface average, and $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface. The definition applies where the power-deposition-weighted denominator is nonzero.

The quantity is restricted to the right-hand circular polarization and to one toroidal mode at a time. It excludes the left-hand circularly polarized component, the total electric-field amplitude obtained by combining polarizations, and an unweighted average or an average of pointwise amplitudes; the modulus is taken after the weighted complex averaging.

It is the toroidal-mode-resolved amplitude specialization of the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field amplitude](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude). The corresponding complex E-minus phasor is described by the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), while this quantity retains only its amplitude.

description: Radius of the circular collimating aperture forming a neutron detector’s sensitive opening, measured from its center to the circumferential boundary.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric radius of the circular collimating aperture or sensitive opening associated with an individual neutron detector. It defines the transverse boundary of the opening and its geometric acceptance, not the detector efficiency or energy response.

For a circular aperture, the radius is related to the full aperture diameter by

$$
r = \frac{D}{2}
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius and $D$ is the full diameter of the [diagnostic aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The quantity applies only to circular aperture geometry and represents one detector aperture; no plasma-population, charge-state, or detector-array aggregation is included. It excludes rectangular aperture dimensions, such as the [first local tangential width of the neutron detector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_neutron_detector) and [second local tangential width of the neutron detector], as well as detector efficiency and energy-response parameters.

The aperture radius contributes to the geometric acceptance represented by the [neutron-detector solid angle](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector), but it is a physical aperture dimension rather than a solid angle or an efficiency.

description: Maximum gas flow is the largest pressure-volume throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the upper bound of its controllable range.
documentation:
Maximum gas flow is the upper reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It represents the aggregate gas stream rather than a particular molecular species, charge state, mass flow, or particle-number rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput at the upper delivery limit is

$$
Q_g^{\max} = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g^{\max}$ is the maximum gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is the gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to gas delivered through a gas injection valve for fueling, impurity seeding, or disruption mitigation. The maximum qualifier denotes a reliable upper delivery limit for the aggregate gas stream, not a species-resolved flow, mass-flow rate, or particle-number rate.

The quantity is the upper-bound member of the [gas flow] family: gas flow denotes the same pressure-volume throughput without an upper-limit restriction, while [minimum gas flow](name:minimum_gas_flow) denotes its lower reliable operating limit.

description: Root-mean-square wavelength spread of a spectrometer channel’s response about its reference vacuum wavelength, representing instrumental broadening for monochromatic input.
documentation:
The root-mean-square spectral width is the wavelength spread of a spectrometer channel’s instrumental response about its reference vacuum wavelength. It characterizes broadening produced by the channel rather than the intrinsic width of the incident spectral line.

For a monochromatic input, the width is the second-moment spread of the channel response:

$$
w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}} = \left[\frac{\int (\lambda-\lambda_0)^2 R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\int R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}}$ is the root-mean-square spectral width, $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength, $\lambda_0$ is the channel reference vacuum wavelength, and $R(\lambda)$ is the channel spectral response.

This quantity applies to one spectrometer channel and aggregates the complete spectral response over wavelength through its second moment. It excludes physical broadening of the incident spectral line and is not an interval obtained by integrating the response.

The RMS width is the statistical form of [spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:root_mean_square_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel); for a Gaussian response, it is the Gaussian standard deviation used by that parent quantity. It is distinct from the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which is a response-equivalent wavelength interval rather than an RMS spread.

description: Dimensionless ratio of a species’ particle mass to a positive reference mass, preserving relative inertial scales in normalized kinetic equations.
documentation:
This quantity expresses the inertial mass of one particle of a specified species relative to a strictly positive reference mass. It is the normalized counterpart of [particle mass], rather than an independent mass or mass density.

The normalized particle mass is defined by

$$
\bar{m}_s = \frac{m_s}{m_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$ and $m_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference mass used by the normalization. The result preserves the relative inertial ordering of species while removing the mass scale from normalized equations of motion.

The reference mass must be kept fixed when comparing normalized masses; changing it rescales all such ratios by the same factor. This quantity excludes mass associated with a population or volume and does not represent a mass density.

description: Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one correction-coil cross-section, taken perpendicular to the local conductor path and treated as constant along the coil length.
documentation:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one correction-coil cross-section is the cross-sectional measure of the electrical conductor on a plane normal to the local conductor path. It is a property of one correction-coil conductor element, not a sum over separate turns or parallel conductor elements.

The area includes the conducting material in that cross-section and excludes voids, insulation, coolant channels, nonconducting supports, and any winding-pack or coil-footprint area outside the conductor material. For hollow or compound conductors, only regions that are part of the electrical conductor are included.

It is distinct from radius_of_correction_coil, [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil), and [width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil), which specify particular dimensions of a cross-section; different cross-sectional shapes can have the same area.

description: Full toroidal width of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Full toroidal width of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the edge-to-edge extent between the two toroidally separated sides of the strap conductor.

For a strap represented at a characteristic major radius, the toroidal width is related to the angular separation of the two toroidal edges by:

$$
w_\phi = R_\mathrm{strap}\,\Delta\phi
$$

where $w_\phi$ is the toroidal width, $R_\mathrm{strap}$ is the representative major radius of the strap, and $\Delta\phi$ is the smaller non-wrapping angular separation between the two toroidal edges.

This is a full width, not a half-width or a signed coordinate difference. It is distinct from the poloidal extent [height_of_antenna_strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap) and from the local-normal extent [thickness_of_antenna_strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the same strap conductor.

description: Net conduction current circulating around the vacuum vessel, induced by time-varying magnetic flux linked with the vessel.
documentation:
This quantity is the net conduction current carried by the vacuum-vessel material in the toroidal direction. It represents an induced eddy current driven by changing magnetic flux linked with the conducting vessel, excluding currents in the plasma, external coils, and other conductors.

The net current is the signed cross-sectional integral of the toroidal conduction-current density:

$$
I_{\mathrm{vessel}} = \int_S j_\phi\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the conduction-current density, $S$ is a cross section of the vessel material normal to the toroidal direction, and $\mathrm{d}S$ is its area element. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Faraday induction drives the current through the changing linked magnetic flux; its response is determined by the vessel's electromagnetic impedance. This is a vessel-specific instance of [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure) and is distinct from [toroidal current of cryostat](name:toroidal_current_of_cryostat).

Sign convention: Positive when the net conduction current points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

description: Local effective ionic charge of the plasma mixture at the separatrix, reflecting charge-squared weighting across all contributing ion species and charge states.
documentation:
The effective ionic charge at the separatrix is a dimensionless measure of the charge composition of the local plasma ion mixture. It weights each ionic population by the square of its charge and relates the resulting charge-weighted ion density to the local electron density.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective ionic charge, $i$ indexes each included ion species and charge-state population, $n_i$ is the number density of that population, $Z_i$ is its ionic charge number, and $n_e$ is the local electron number density.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region. The numerator is summed over the contributing ion species and charge states; the quantity is not a single-species or single-charge-state charge number, and it is not averaged over the separatrix surface.

The corresponding [flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary] averages the local effective-charge field over the boundary surface, and is therefore distinct from this local separatrix value.

description: Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one sensing turn of the closed winding. It is a geometric area factor; with winding turn density it determines the ideal current-sensing sensitivity.
documentation:
Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one sensing turn of a closed Rogowski winding. It is a scalar geometry factor of the winding, not the signed current threaded by the coil or the measured coil voltage.

In the ideal uniformly wound limit, the area appears as the non-negative sensitivity factor in the linear constitutive relation between coil voltage and enclosed-current time derivative:

$$
V_R(t) = \sigma \mu_0 n A \frac{d I_\mathrm{enc}}{dt}
$$

where $A$ is the Rogowski-coil area, $n$ is the winding turn density along the closed winding path, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_\mathrm{enc}$ is the signed [Rogowski-coil current](name:current_of_rogowski_coil) threaded by the coil, $V_R$ is the [Rogowski-coil voltage], and $\sigma$ is the sign set by winding orientation and terminal polarity.

The effective area may represent a calibrated equivalent for a real winding with finite pitch or nonuniform cross-section, but it remains a per-turn area factor. It is in the same geometric-coil-area family as [area of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [area of a toroidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); multiplying by turn density, turn number, or path length gives related sensitivity factors, not this quantity.
