description: Signed vertical Z coordinate of a contour point defining the geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height of a point on the geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor, represented in a poloidal cross-section. It describes the sensor boundary geometry, not the sensed current or the optical path.

$$
Z = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the point position relative to the coordinate origin and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The quantity is geometrically analogous to the contour coordinate used for [vertical outline of wall material](name:vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component), but applies to the fiber-optic current sensor boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the outline point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

description: Vertical plasma vorticity divided by the local major radius, retaining the signed rotation rate about the vertical axis with inverse-length scaling.
documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius-scaled form of [vertical vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity), measuring local bulk-plasma rotation about the vertical direction per unit major radius. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\omega_Z^*(R,\phi,Z)=\frac{\omega_Z(R,\phi,Z)}{R},\qquad \omega_Z=(\nabla\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $\mathbf{v}$ is the plasma bulk-velocity vector, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The scaling applies to the vertical-vorticity component itself and does not represent the full [vorticity](name:vorticity) vector.

Sign convention: Positive when the bulk-flow rotation is in the $+Z$ sense, namely counterclockwise in the $(R,\phi)$ plane when viewed from $+Z$.

description: Local electromagnetic radiation power emitted by the electron population per unit volume, without specifying a particular radiation mechanism.
documentation:
Electron emissivity is the local electromagnetic radiation power emitted by the electron population per unit volume. It represents an emission source attributable to electrons, not the net energy change of the electron population.

At position $\mathbf{x}$, the emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_e(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_e^{\mathrm{rad}}}{dV}
$$

where $\varepsilon_e$ is electron emissivity, $P_e^{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiation power emitted by electrons, $V$ is volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position.

A particular radiation mechanism may be selected by the surrounding physical context, but no mechanism is implied by this name. The quantity excludes absorbed power and differs from [power density due to radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), which is not electron-specific, and from [electron power density], which denotes net energy transfer in the electron energy balance.

description: Change in ion-state mean ionization potential is the signed difference between the concentration-weighted mean cumulative ionization potential of an ion charge-state bundle after and before a specified state change.
documentation:
Change in ion-state mean ionization potential is the signed difference in the [ion-state mean ionization potential] of an ion charge-state bundle across a specified state change. The base quantity is the concentration-weighted mean of the cumulative successive ionization energies required to reach, from the neutral ground state, the charge states represented in the bundle.

The change is defined as the value after the change minus the value before the change:

$$
\Delta \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s} = \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{after}} - \bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{before}}
$$

where $\bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{after}}$ and $\bar{E}_{\mathrm{ion},s}^{\mathrm{before}}$ are the [ion-state mean ionization potentials] of the same ion-state bundle after and before the change.

This quantity accounts only for the change in the mean cumulative ionization energy associated with the represented charge-state composition. It excludes thermal internal energy, excitation energy, radiation losses, and kinetic energy exchanged during ionization or recombination.

Defined as sum (x_z* (sum of Epot from z'=0 to z-1)), where Epot is the ionization potential of ion Xz’+, and x_z is the relative concentration of a given charge state in the bundle, i.e. sum(x_z) = 1 over the bundle.

description: Instantaneous equivalent-electron tritium source rate delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection, with each injected tritium atom contributing one equivalent-electron count.
documentation:
The tritium source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral tritium with atomic number $Z_{\mathrm{T}} = 1$ is admitted to the plasma vessel by gas injection hardware, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. It is the tritium-specific component of the [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection).

The defining relation is:

$$
\dot{S}_{\mathrm{T}} = Z_{\mathrm{T}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{T}} = \dot{N}_{\mathrm{T}}
$$

where $\dot{S}_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the raw tritium atom delivery rate in atoms per second, and $Z_{\mathrm{T}}$ is tritium's atomic number. The rate is the instantaneous derivative of the accumulated inventory [accumulated tritium count due to gas injection], and it counts delivered atoms rather than plasma electron content or ionization state.

Sign convention: Positive when tritium gas is being delivered into the vessel, increasing the equivalent-electron inventory.

description: Full-width frequency interval passed by the intermediate-frequency bandpass filter of an electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel, setting the emission frequencies contributing to its radiation-temperature signal.
documentation:
The bandwidth is the total frequency span passed by the intermediate-frequency bandpass filter associated with one electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel. It characterizes the channel's accepted spectral interval rather than an emission intensity or a plasma frequency.

The full width is defined by

$$
\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}} = f_{\mathrm{high}} - f_{\mathrm{low}}
$$

where $\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}}$ is the intermediate-frequency bandwidth, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ is the upper bandpass edge frequency, and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ is the lower bandpass edge frequency.

This quantity applies to one ECE channel and uses the full-width convention; it is not the center frequency, a reference carrier frequency, or a wavelength-domain response width such as the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). The accepted interval determines which electron-cyclotron-emission frequencies contribute to the [radiative temperature at an ECE channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel) and can therefore affect the channel's effective radial localization.

description: Normalized toroidal magnetic-flux surface label assigned to each pellet location, identifying the nested magnetic surface reached along the pellet’s in-plasma ablation trajectory.
documentation:
This quantity identifies the nested magnetic surface containing the pellet at a specified location along its in-plasma ablation trajectory. It is a magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

At pellet position $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$, the normalized toroidal flux coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$ is the pellet position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux labeling the magnetic surface through that position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary. The position is interpreted in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is the pellet’s in-plasma ablation trajectory, with the coordinate evaluated pointwise at each pellet location. It does not represent distance traveled along the path, a path integral, an average over the trajectory, or an aggregate over multiple pellets.

This is the locus-specific realization of the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). The axis and boundary references set the coordinate endpoints, so the value increases outward across nested magnetic surfaces while remaining distinct from a cylindrical radial coordinate.

description: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of neutral atomic and molecular gas introduced during prefill before plasma breakdown, weighted by bound-electron count.
documentation:
This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of neutral gas introduced during the plasma prefill phase before breakdown. It provides a common counting convention for atomic and molecular species.

The equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_s Z_s N_s
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron inventory, $N_s$ is the number of injected neutral atoms or molecules of species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the total number of bound electrons per neutral atom or molecule of that species.

The quantity is cumulative over the prefill interval and excludes instantaneous injection rate, actual plasma-electron content, ionization-state effects, and post-breakdown inventory. Species-specific instances include [deuterium prefill count](name:deuterium_prefill_count), [ammonia prefill count](name:ammonia_prefill_count), and [argon prefill count](name:argon_prefill_count).

description: Local production rate of hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung photons per plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over a specified photon-energy band.
documentation:
Hard-X-ray emissivity is the local bremsstrahlung photon production rate per plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over the selected hard-X-ray photon-energy band. It represents emission from suprathermal electrons at a physical location and in a specified emission direction.

The band-integrated emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E_1,E_2)=\int_{E_1}^{E_2}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}(\mathbf{r},\Omega,E)\,\mathrm{d}E
$$

where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}$ is the band-integrated hard-X-ray photon emissivity, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}$ is the differential photon emissivity with respect to photon energy, $\mathbf{r}$ is the emission location, $\Omega$ is the emission direction labeled by solid angle, $E$ is photon energy, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper limits of the selected energy band.

This quantity is local and directional: it is not integrated along a line of sight, over a plasma volume, or over emission directions. It applies to hard-X-ray photons produced by suprathermal-electron bremsstrahlung and excludes the total bremsstrahlung electromagnetic power and detector-received radiation.

In an optically thin plasma, [hard X-ray brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) is obtained from the corresponding local emissivity by propagation and integration along a viewing path; brightness is therefore a received radiance, whereas this quantity is the local photon source density.

description: Charge-state-summed local number density of argon ions at the H-mode edge pedestal top, excluding neutral argon.
documentation:
The local argon-ion number density at the H-mode edge pedestal top is the physical count of argon ions per plasma volume at that locus, aggregated across ionization states. It excludes neutral argon and is neither chord-averaged nor volume-averaged.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{z=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the total local argon-ion number density, $z$ is the positive integer argon charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{z+}}$ is the local number density of argon ions in charge state $z$. The sum includes Ar+ through Ar18+.

The quantity is evaluated at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, whose location is defined by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). It is a locus-specific form of [argon density](name:argon_density), whereas [line-averaged argon density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) represents averaging along a plasma path rather than a local value.

description: Displacement of a passive structure is the signed linear displacement of a selected point or defined surface target on a passive component relative to a reference configuration, projected along a defined positive direction.
documentation:
Displacement of a passive structure is the signed scalar component of the motion of a selected material point, attachment point, or defined reference point on a passive structural component relative to a reference configuration. It is the passive-structure instance of mechanical displacement, not an absolute position, velocity, acceleration, or strain.

The signed projected displacement is defined by

$$
u(t) = \left[\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_u
$$

where $u(t)$ is the scalar displacement, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is the current position vector of the selected point, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the position vector of the same point in the reference configuration, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$ is the unit vector defining the positive direction of the displacement component. All vectors and the unit direction are expressed in the same right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, with $\hat{z}$ vertical.

The selected point, reference configuration, and positive direction are part of the semantic definition of any instance. An undeformed, surveyed, calibrated, initial, or previous-time configuration may serve as $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ only if that choice is fixed; changing it changes the displacement, and using a previous-time reference defines an incremental displacement over the interval. A single value describes one projected local displacement; deformation or strain requires spatial variation of displacement or a separate deformation measure.

Sign convention: Positive when the selected point is displaced from $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$.

description: Signed logarithmic derivative of a selected particle-species density with respect to normalized minor radius, expressing the relative change of that density as the normalized minor-radius coordinate increases. For charge-state-aggregated ion species, the density is summed over all charge states.
documentation:
Signed logarithmic derivative of a selected particle-species density with respect to normalized minor radius is the local derivative of that species density's natural logarithm along the normalized minor-radius coordinate. It represents the relative change of the selected species density with respect to that coordinate.

The derivative is defined by

$$
G_{n_s} = \frac{\partial \ln n_s}{\partial \rho} = \frac{1}{n_s}\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial \rho}
$$

where $G_{n_s}$ is this logarithmic derivative, $n_s$ is the density of the selected particle species $s$, and $\rho$ is the [normalized minor radius], the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

The scope is one selected particle species at the position where the derivative is evaluated. When the selected species represents a charge-state-aggregated ion population, $n_s$ is the charge-state-summed density over all charge states; it is not a density-weighted charge-state mean and not a total over unrelated species.

This quantity is the derivative of the logarithmic density with respect to $\rho$, not the density itself, not the logarithm alone, and not a coordinate-specialized value of a logarithm-of-density quantity. Logarithmic-gradient conventions that add an extra minus sign or differentiate with respect to an unnormalized minor-radius coordinate denote different quantities.

Sign convention: Positive when $\ln n_s$ increases with increasing normalized minor-radius coordinate $\rho$.

description: Toroidal azimuthal coordinate of the center of the surface on which a grating image is focused, locating that image-field center around the machine symmetry axis.
documentation:
This quantity is the toroidal angular position of the center of a grating image field. The center denotes the focused image-surface center, or the corresponding point when the image surface is planar, rather than an arbitrary point or a generic mechanical center of the grating.

$$
\phi_c = \operatorname{atan2}(Y_c, X_c)
$$

where $\phi_c$ is the toroidal angle, and $X_c$ and $Y_c$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the image-field center in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$. The angle is equivalently the azimuthal coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to one geometric image-field center associated with one grating. It is a point coordinate, not an average over the image surface, a coordinate of the grating body as a whole, or a position varying along a beam path.

Like the [toroidal coordinate of a Bragg crystal](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), it locates a diagnostic component geometrically around the machine symmetry axis; its locus is instead the grating image-field center. It is distinct from the [toroidal coordinate](name:toroidal_coordinate) of a wave-beam position along a propagation path.

Sign convention: Positive when the angular displacement from the $\phi=0$ reference is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

description: Signed inclination of the first side of a plasma-filament oblique cross-section, measured counterclockwise from the outward radial direction in the poloidal plane.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed inclination of the first side of the oblique parallelogram representing an individual plasma-filament cross section. It specifies the orientation of that side in the poloidal plane relative to the outward radial direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\left(\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_Z,\,\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_R\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the first-side inclination, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the directed vector along the first parallelogram side, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_R$ is the outward radial unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_Z$ is the positive vertical unit vector, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the radial projection toward the vertical projection.

The quantity applies separately to each discrete plasma-carrying filament and is not an aggregate orientation averaged over the plasma. It describes only the first side of the oblique cross section; it is not the inclination of the second side or either side length.

The companion [tilt angle of a plasma filament](name:tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament) specifies the inclination of the other parallelogram side, while the [major length of a plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament) and [minor length of a plasma filament](name:minor_length_of_plasma_filament) specify cross-sectional dimensions. Together these geometric quantities define the filament cross-section orientation and shape.

Sign convention: Positive when the directed first side is rotated counterclockwise from the outward radial direction toward the positive vertical direction in the poloidal plane.

dd_sources.documentation: Inclination of first angle measured counter-clockwise from horizontal outwardly directed radial vector (grad R).

description: Signed y coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z aligned to vertical Z.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian y position of the geometric centroid of one ferritic element. The coordinate is defined in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with coordinate values $(x,y,z)$ and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$.

$$
y_c = \frac{1}{V_e}\int_{V_e} y\,dV
$$

where $y_c$ and $y$ are Cartesian y coordinates measured in m, $V_e$ is the ferritic-element volume measured in m$^3$, and $dV$ is a differential volume element. The integration covers the entire element, so this is a volume centroid rather than a surface centroid or a selected-point coordinate. The corresponding orthogonal centroid coordinates are [x coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [z coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid).

Sign convention: Positive when the centroid displacement from the coordinate origin has a positive projection onto $\hat{y}$.

description: Exponential e-folding time for the electron-temperature decrease at the magnetic axis during a disruption.
documentation:
This quantity is the characteristic e-folding time of the electron temperature at the magnetic axis during a disruption. It describes exponential temperature loss and is distinct from the [linear electron decay time at the magnetic axis](name:linear_electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption), which uses a 20–80% definition.

For an exponential decay beginning at reference time $t_0$, the temperature is represented by:

$$
T_e(t)=T_{e,0}\exp\left[-\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right]
$$

where $T_e(t)$ is the electron temperature at time $t$, $T_{e,0}$ is its value at the reference time $t_0$, and $\tau$ is the decay time constant. The quantity applies specifically to the magnetic-axis temperature and the disruption-related decay; it is not a volume-averaged or runaway-electron decay time.

description: Perturbed electrostatic potential amplitude is the phase-independent magnitude of a fluctuating electrostatic-potential perturbation represented as a complex quantity. It is the modulus of the perturbation and excludes the arbitrary complex phase.
documentation:
Perturbed electrostatic potential amplitude is the phase-independent magnitude associated with an electrostatic-potential fluctuation. It represents the strength of the scalar perturbation after removal of the arbitrary complex phase of a complex perturbation representation.

The amplitude is defined by the complex modulus of the perturbation:

$$
A_{\tilde{\Phi}} = \left|\tilde{\Phi}\right|
$$

where $A_{\tilde{\Phi}}$ is the perturbed electrostatic potential amplitude, $\tilde{\Phi}$ is the complex electrostatic-potential perturbation, and $|\cdot|$ denotes the complex modulus.

This quantity applies to electrostatic-potential fluctuations in turbulence for the perturbation variable being represented. No aggregation over species, modes, times, or spatial regions is implied by the name.

It is distinct from the complex perturbation itself, from the complex phase of that perturbation, and from amplitudes of other fluctuating fields. It does not denote a vector component, vector magnitude, or vector projection; electrostatic potential is a scalar field.

The [normalized perturbed electrostatic potential amplitude](name:normalized_perturbed_electrostatic_potential_amplitude) is a reference-scaled instance of this parent quantity: the same modulus operation is applied to a normalized electrostatic-potential perturbation.

description: Signed coefficient multiplying total ion particle density to form the implicit contribution to the total ion particle source term.
documentation:
This quantity is the coefficient of total ion particle density in the implicit part of the total ion particle source term. It represents the stiff, primary-quantity-dependent contribution separated from the source term's explicit part.

The implicit source contribution is defined by

$$
S_{i,\mathrm{imp}} = \alpha_{i,\mathrm{imp}} n_i
$$

where $S_{i,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit contribution to the total ion particle source, $\alpha_{i,\mathrm{imp}}$ is this source-rate coefficient, and $n_i$ is the total ion particle density.

The quantity applies to the aggregate ion population, with the total ion density and corresponding source contribution summed over the included ion species and charge states. It is a scalar coefficient for the particle channel, not the complete particle source and not the explicit, primary-quantity-independent contribution.

Its role is analogous to the coefficient in [implicit electron particle source rate](name:implicit_electron_particle_source_rate), while [implicit ion energy source rate](name:implicit_ion_energy_source_rate) applies the same implicit decomposition to the ion energy channel. The full source contribution combines the implicit term $\alpha_{i,\mathrm{imp}} n_i$ with the separately represented explicit term.

Sign convention: Positive when the implicit contribution is a net gain of total ion particles; negative when it is a net loss.

description: Radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of a circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. In the hollow-disk geometry it denotes either the inner or outer boundary radius.
documentation:
Radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of a circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. The cross-section is a hollow disk bounded by concentric inner and outer circular boundaries, so this generic quantity denotes either boundary radius when the boundary is not otherwise specified.

For a circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the radius $a$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
a = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section.

An annular plasma filament has an [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) and an [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), with $0 \le a_\mathrm{inner} \le a_\mathrm{outer}$; the current-carrying cross-section occupies the region between those two circular boundaries. This quantity excludes the curvature radius of a noncircular contour segment and the major radius of a filament centerline about the toroidal symmetry axis.

description: Signed Z-direction cosine of a camera’s viewing-direction unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The camera direction component along the Cartesian Z axis is the signed directional cosine of the camera’s viewing-direction unit vector. It specifies how strongly the viewing direction points along the positive or negative Z direction.

The component is defined by

$$
d_z = \mathbf{d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $d_z$ is the Z component, $\mathbf{d}$ is the camera’s direction unit vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the positive-Z basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the viewing direction of an individual camera, with no spatial, population, or charge-state aggregation. It is a directional component rather than the camera position, the image-up orientation, or the magnitude of the direction vector.

Together with the corresponding [x direction unit vector of the camera](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [y direction unit vector of the camera](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera), it specifies the complete viewing-direction vector; the three components satisfy $d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1$, where $d_x$ and $d_y$ are the X and Y components of that same unit vector.

description: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory introduced as carbon gas during plasma prefill, with six count units assigned to each injected carbon atom.
documentation:
This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of carbon introduced by gas injection during the plasma prefill phase, before plasma breakdown. It represents injected carbon atoms rather than an instantaneous injection rate.

The defining relation is

$$
N_{\mathrm{C,eq}} = Z_{\mathrm{C}}N_{\mathrm{C}} = 6N_{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{C,eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the cumulative number of injected carbon atoms, and $Z_{\mathrm{C}}=6$ is the carbon atomic number. Both counts are dimensionless.

The prefill interval ends at plasma breakdown, so post-breakdown carbon delivery is represented separately by [accumulated carbon count due to gas injection]. The aggregation convention parallels [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count), with the atomic number providing the equivalent-electron weighting.

description: Instantaneous electron-equivalent source rate supplied by surface emission of material from plasma-facing surfaces, weighted by the electron contribution of each emitted species after ionization.
documentation:
Instantaneous electron-equivalent source rate supplied by surface emission is the rate at which ionization of material released from plasma-facing surfaces adds electrons to the plasma particle balance. It aggregates all emitted fuel, molecular, and impurity species over all plasma-facing surfaces, with each emitted particle weighted by the number of bound electrons it can contribute after full ionization.

The global rate is defined by integrating the emitted particle flux density over the plasma-facing surface area:

$$
S_e^{\mathrm{surf}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{pf}}} \sum_s \nu_{e,s}\,\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA
$$

where $S_e^{\mathrm{surf}}$ is the electron-equivalent surface-emission source rate, $A_{\mathrm{pf}}$ is the total plasma-facing surface area, $s$ indexes emitted species, $\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the emitted particle flux density of species $s$ at surface position $\mathbf{x}$ directed toward the plasma, $dA$ is a surface element, and $\nu_{e,s}$ is the electron yield of one emitted particle on full ionization. For an emitted atom, $\nu_{e,s}=Z_s$ with $Z_s$ the nuclear charge number; for an emitted molecule or compound particle, $\nu_{e,s}$ is the sum of the nuclear charge numbers of its constituent atoms.

Surface emission includes recycling, delayed outgassing, and physical or chemical sputtering only insofar as the released material returns toward the plasma and is ionized. This quantity is the electron-specific counterpart of source_rate_due_to_surface_emission, is distinct from externally supplied material represented by [electron_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection), excludes electron loss by incidence on surfaces, and contributes to [total_electron_source_rate](name:total_electron_source_rate).

Sign convention: Positive when ionization of material emitted from plasma-facing surfaces supplies electron-equivalent particles to the plasma.

description: Fraction of the launched power of an electron-cyclotron beam carried by the ordinary polarization mode, ranging from pure X-mode to pure O-mode.
documentation:
The ordinary-mode power fraction quantifies the share of one launched electron-cyclotron beam carried by the ordinary (O) polarization mode rather than the extraordinary (X) mode.

It is defined by the ratio

$$
f_O = \frac{P_O}{P_{\mathrm{EC}}}
$$

where $f_O$ is the ordinary-mode power fraction, $P_O$ is the launched power in the ordinary mode, and $P_{\mathrm{EC}}$ is the total launched power of the electron-cyclotron beam.

The quantity applies to a single electron-cyclotron beam and uses launched beam power aggregated over the beam's ordinary-mode content. It excludes power from other beams and does not represent the total launched power itself. Values of $f_O=1$ and $f_O=0$ denote pure ordinary-mode and pure extraordinary-mode launch, respectively.

This power partition is distinct from [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam), which describes the shape and handedness of a polarization ellipse rather than the O-mode fraction of an electron-cyclotron beam.

dd_sources.documentation: Fraction of EC beam power launched in ordinary (O) mode. If all power is launched in ordinary mode (O-mode), o_mode_fraction = 1.0. If all  power is launched in extraordinary mode (X-mode), o_mode_fraction = 0.0

description: Total equivalent-electron rate of neutral and ion particles re-emitted from all divertor surfaces into the plasma by recycling.
documentation:
This quantity is the aggregate particle source produced when neutral and ion particles are re-emitted from divertor surfaces into the plasma by recycling.

The defining rate is

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{eq}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the total recycled particle source rate, $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the cumulative equivalent-electron count of re-emitted particles, and $t$ is time.

The quantity covers all divertor surfaces and combines the neutral and ion contributions using equivalent-electron counting. It is a total source rate rather than a local surface flux density, and it excludes particle sources produced by processes other than recycling or originating outside the divertor.

This is a gross re-emission rate and does not by itself represent the net particle balance after incident-particle losses. Unlike [power of the divertor due to recombination](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), it counts recycled particles without weighting them by deposited energy.

description: Electrical drive potential applied to a gas-injection valve to actuate its opening and control the resulting neutral-gas throughput.
documentation:
This quantity is the electrical drive potential applied to an individual gas-injection valve. It is the actuator input for opening the valve, not the resulting gas flow, particle source rate, or plasma electrostatic potential.

The valve response relates the applied voltage to the gas flow through

$$
G = F(V)
$$

where $V$ is the applied valve voltage, $G$ is the gas flow rate through the valve, and $F$ is the valve-specific response function. The quantity represents one valve's applied potential difference and is not an average or sum over multiple valves.

The resulting gas flow contributes to the [total neutral source rate due to gas injection](name:total_neutral_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), but this voltage remains distinct from that source rate and from any response-curve parameter.

description: Signed ratio of the aggregate plasma center-of-mass velocity along the local magnetic-field direction to the magnitude of the total magnetic field.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed local ratio of the plasma bulk center-of-mass velocity parallel to the magnetic field to the magnitude of the local total magnetic-induction vector. It represents parallel plasma motion weighted by the inverse field strength.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{v_{\parallel,\mathrm{plasma}}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
= \frac{\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{plasma}} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the plasma bulk velocity component parallel to the magnetic field, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the aggregate plasma center-of-mass velocity vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic-induction vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude.

The velocity is aggregated as the center-of-mass velocity of the plasma species and is evaluated locally. It is not a species-resolved velocity or a neutral-particle velocity, and the denominator is the total field magnitude rather than a signed toroidal or poloidal field component.

The numerator is the [parallel plasma velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity), while the denominator is the [magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude); consequently, this quantity retains the numerator's flow direction while scaling it by the inverse local field strength. It is distinct from the [parallel Mach number](name:parallel_mach_number), whose denominator is the local plasma sound speed.

Sign convention: Positive when the aggregate plasma bulk velocity points along the local magnetic-field vector.

description: Dimensionless fraction of all converter atoms that are nuclei of the target species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
documentation:
This quantity is the normalized composition factor for target nuclei in the converter material of a neutron detector. It identifies the share of converter atoms belonging to the nuclear species that produces the intended neutron-induced detection reaction.

The target atomic fraction is defined by

$$
f_{\mathrm{target}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{target}}}{N_{\mathrm{all}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the number of target-species nuclei and $N_{\mathrm{all}}$ is the total number of atoms in the converter material. It is the nuclear-target realization of [target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter], rather than a fraction based on converter volume, mass, or detector efficiency. The fraction is bounded between zero and one.

description: Cumulative power transferred from electromagnetic waves to electrons, ions, and fast populations within a selected magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
Cumulative absorbed electromagnetic-wave power deposited in the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface. It includes absorption by electron, ion, and fast populations and represents an enclosed quantity rather than a local power density.

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} p_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs}}(\psi)$ is the cumulative absorbed wave power, $\psi$ is the label of the selected magnetic flux surface, $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by that surface, $p_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total absorbed wave power density at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$ summed over electrons, ions, and fast populations, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

This quantity is cumulative over the enclosed volume and is not a local deposition density or a population-resolved contribution. Population-specific quantities such as [thermal electron power at an inside flux surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) and [thermal ion power at an inside flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) resolve components of this aggregate. When the selected surface encloses the full absorbing plasma volume, it equals [total absorbed wave power](name:total_absorbed_wave_power).

description: Radial coordinate of a rectangle center is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of a rectangular cross-section, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Radial coordinate of a rectangle center is the major-radius coordinate \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) of the geometric center of a rectangular cross-section. It is measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, whose basis \((\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})\) satisfies \(\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}\); \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height.

The relation between this coordinate and Cartesian coordinates of the same center point is

$$
R_{\mathrm{rect,c}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{rect,c}}^{2} + y_{\mathrm{rect,c}}^{2}}
$$

where \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) is the radial coordinate of the rectangle center, and \(x_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\) are the first and second Cartesian coordinates of that center in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})\) frame whose \(\hat{z}\) direction is vertical and whose origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity applies to the center point of the rectangle as a whole; for an axisymmetric rectangular element, that point is the center of the generating rectangle in a surface of constant \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame. It is not the rectangle's inner radius, outer radius, radial width, corner coordinate, boundary coordinate, or a centroid of a non-rectangular object, and no area or volume averaging is implied.

The companion [height of the rectangle center] gives \(Z_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\), the vertical coordinate of the same center; the pair \((R_{\mathrm{rect,c}},Z_{\mathrm{rect,c}})\) locates the center in a surface of constant \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame. As a major-radius coordinate, \(R_{\mathrm{rect,c}}\ge 0\) and is not a signed radial offset from another reference point.

description: Particle number density of tungsten ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all tungsten ion charge states and excluding neutral tungsten.
documentation:
Particle number density of tungsten ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the tungsten-ion population at that flux-surface location.

The number density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{W}} = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_{\mathrm{W}}}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the tungsten-ion number density, $N_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the number of counted tungsten ions, and $V$ is volume.

This quantity is the tungsten-specific member of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The count is summed over all tungsten ionic charge states and excludes neutral tungsten. It is evaluated at the internal transport barrier rather than at a divertor target, as distinguished by [tungsten density at the divertor target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target).

description: Commanded detector-bias potential difference applied by the high-voltage supply associated with one spectrometer channel.
documentation:
This quantity is the requested electrical potential difference that establishes the detector-bias setpoint for one spectrometer channel.

The setpoint is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{set}} = V_{\mathrm{bias}} - V_{\mathrm{return}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{set}}$ is the requested channel bias voltage, $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ is the electrical potential of the high-voltage bias terminal, and $V_{\mathrm{return}}$ is the electrical potential of the associated supply return.

The quantity applies to one spectrometer channel and represents a commanded setpoint rather than an aggregated value across channels. It specifies the intended bias potential of the channel's high-voltage supply; it does not represent the channel's actual electrical output signal, which is described by [voltage of a spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel).

As a requested control quantity, it is distinct from the realized or measured channel voltage and is analogous in semantic role to the bias setpoint represented by [requested voltage of a neutron detector](name:requested_voltage_of_neutron_detector).

description: Volume-integrated kinetic energy of bulk thermal electrons contained within the plasma pedestal, excluding suprathermal electrons and non-electron populations.
documentation:
Pedestal thermal electron energy is the total kinetic energy carried by bulk thermal electrons within the plasma pedestal region. It is an extensive stored-energy content, not a power or energy-transfer rate.

$$
W_{\mathrm{ped},e} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{ped}}} u_e(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{ped},e}$ is the pedestal thermal electron energy, $V_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the volume occupied by the pedestal region, $u_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local thermal electron kinetic-energy density at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $dV$ is a differential volume element.

The integral includes only the thermal electron population and sums its energy throughout the pedestal volume. It excludes fast suprathermal electrons, ions, and other non-electron populations. This quantity is the pedestal-region contribution to the broader [thermal electron energy](name:thermal_electron_energy); it is distinct from [pedestal thermal ion energy](name:pedestal_thermal_ion_energy), which represents ion thermal energy in the same region.

dd_sources.documentation: Value

label_note: electron thermal energy integrated over the pedestal region, as the source; W_ped,e as the registry W and e give; links resolve

description: Optical depth measuring cumulative attenuation of electromagnetic radiation along a specified propagation path through a medium. It uses the wavelength, frequency, spectral band, or broadband weighting assigned to the attenuation coefficient.
documentation:
Opacity is the optical depth accumulated by electromagnetic radiation along a specified propagation path through a medium that removes radiation from that path. It represents cumulative extinction by absorption and, when the attenuation coefficient includes it, scattering out of the propagation path.

The opacity for a spectral selection $\chi$ along a path $\Gamma$ is defined by integrating the matching local attenuation coefficient:

$$
\tau_\chi(\Gamma) = \int_\Gamma \alpha_\chi(s)\,ds
$$

where $\tau_\chi(\Gamma)$ is the opacity for path $\Gamma$ and spectral selection $\chi$, $\alpha_\chi(s)$ is the local attenuation coefficient for the same selection at path position $s$, and $ds$ is the differential path element along $\Gamma$.

The spectral selection $\chi$ may be a wavelength, a frequency, a finite spectral band, or a broadband weighting; $\tau_\chi$ and $\alpha_\chi$ must use the same selection. This name denotes the accumulated path quantity for the radiation component under consideration and does not by itself choose one of those spectral conventions.

Opacity is not the local attenuation coefficient, a material-specific mass attenuation coefficient, emitted radiance, or the [spectral absorptivity of a filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter); it is the line-integrated optical depth that governs attenuation along the path. For pure attenuation with no emission into the path and no scattering into the path, incident intensity $I_\chi^\mathrm{in}$ and transmitted intensity $I_\chi^\mathrm{out}$ for the same spectral selection satisfy $I_\chi^\mathrm{out}/I_\chi^\mathrm{in} = \exp[-\tau_\chi(\Gamma)]$, so opacities of consecutive path segments add.
label_note: tau = int alpha ds with matched spectral selection; opens 'Opacity is'; tau as the registry gives; link resolves

description: Logarithm of a selected plasma density, representing the natural-log transform of that density relative to a specified reference for the same density quantity. It is the base logarithmic density quantity from which coordinate derivatives may be formed.
documentation:
Logarithm of density is the natural logarithm of a selected plasma density after normalization by a reference value for the same density quantity. It represents the logarithmic density variable itself, not a spatial derivative or gradient.

The defining logarithmic transform is

$$
L_n = \ln\!\left(\frac{n}{n_\mathrm{ref}}\right)
$$

where $L_n$ is the logarithm of density, $n$ is the selected plasma density, and $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference value used for the same selected density.

The scope covers the logarithmic transform for any explicitly selected density population or component; a more specific standard name supplies the particular population, coordinate dependence, or reference convention. It excludes the density $n$ itself, a density ratio before applying the logarithm, and any coordinate derivative or gradient of $L_n$.

A derivative specialization such as [logarithmic-density derivative with respect to normalized minor radius](name:derivative_of_logarithm_of_density_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius) denotes a derivative of $L_n$, not $L_n$ itself. For any coordinate $x$, the corresponding logarithmic derivative is $dL_n/dx = (1/n)\,dn/dx$ when $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is independent of $x$, where $x$ is the coordinate of differentiation.
label_note: L_n = ln(n/n_ref) for a selected density; n is the registry n_s without a species subscript; link resolves

description: Non-negative span of a divertor target’s plasma-facing surface along the major-radius direction, measured between its minimum and maximum R coordinates.
documentation:
The radial span of a divertor target is the extent of its plasma-facing surface along the major-radius direction. It is a geometric extent, not the distance along the target surface or a power-deposition width. The direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$.

For the plasma-facing surface $S$, the span is defined by

$$
L_R = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S} R(\mathbf{x}) - \min_{\mathbf{x}\in S} R(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on $S$ and $R(\mathbf{x})$ is its major-radius coordinate. The quantity includes the full specified target surface and is non-negative. It complements the [vertical length of the divertor target](name:vertical_length_of_divertor_target), which uses the extrema of $Z$, while the [x coordinate of the divertor target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) identifies a Cartesian center rather than a surface span.

dd_sources.documentation: Target length projected on the major radius axis

description: Radial wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the local wave-vector component projected along increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is a signed local phase-propagation component along the ray or beam path.
documentation:
Radial wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed projection of the local wave vector carried by a beam-tracing ray or beam onto the major-radius direction. The radial direction is the $\hat{R}$ basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by projecting the local wave vector:

$$
k_R = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{R}
$$

where $k_R$ is the radial wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local [wave vector of the beam-tracing beam], and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the beam-tracing beam itself at a specified point along its path; no average, integral, or summation over the path or beam cross-section is implied. It is the cylindrical radial component only, not the radial position coordinate, not a direction unit-vector component, and not a flux-surface-normal or magnetic-field-perpendicular projection.

It is one component of the cylindrical decomposition $\mathbf{k}=k_R\hat{R}+k_\phi\hat{\phi}+k_Z\hat{Z}$, where $k_\phi$ is the [toroidal wave-vector component](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave-vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\hat{\phi}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the toroidal and vertical basis directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Its normalized counterpart is the [radial refractive-index component], $N_R = c k_R/\omega$, where $N_R$ is the radial refractive-index component, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the wave.

Sign convention: Positive when the local wave vector has a component in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Wave vector component in the major radius direction

description: Net torque transferred to a plasma particle population through collisional interactions with other particles, expressed as the corresponding rate of angular-momentum change.
documentation:
This quantity is the net angular-momentum transfer to a specified plasma particle population caused by collisions with other particles. It applies to electron, fast-particle, and ion populations, including the concrete [ion collisional torque](name:ion_torque_due_to_collisions) and [fast collisional torque](name:fast_torque_due_to_collisions) forms.

The scalar torque is defined by

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{coll}} = \frac{dL_{\mathrm{pop}}}{dt}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional torque, $L_{\mathrm{pop}}$ is the relevant angular-momentum component of the population, and $t$ is time.

The quantity represents the net exchange integrated over the plasma volume and over the collisional partners included in the population definition. It is distinct from the local [electron collisional torque density](name:electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions), which gives torque per unit volume.
label_note: dL/dt of the population's angular momentum, volume-integrated; no registry entry applies; links resolve

description: Detected photon count rate at a single pixel of an X-ray crystal spectrometer detector, giving the number of Bragg-diffracted X-ray photons registered at that pixel per unit time.
documentation:
The photon count rate at a detector pixel quantifies how many X-ray photons diffracted by the crystal arrive at one pixel element per second during a spectrometer acquisition frame. Each pixel samples a narrow photon-energy interval determined by the Bragg diffraction geometry; the characteristic photon energy assigned to a pixel is given by [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), with spectral bounds defined by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

The mapping from pixel position to photon wavelength follows the Bragg condition

$$
2d\sin\theta = \lambda
$$

where $d$ is the crystal plane spacing, $\theta$ is the local diffraction angle at the pixel, and $\lambda$ is the corresponding photon wavelength.

The count rate is recorded by solid-state detector arrays (CCDs, strip detectors, or pixel arrays) and constitutes the primary observable for X-ray crystal spectroscopy of highly charged impurity emission lines. The physical size of each pixel, relevant for geometric efficiency corrections, is described by extent_of_detector_pixel. The count rate may be normalized to a reference value to form normalized_count_at_detector_pixel, and its temporal evolution is tracked by time_derivative_of_count_at_detector_pixel.
label_note: narrows the generic pixel count to an X-ray crystal spectrometer and Bragg diffraction

description: Lumped ohmic resistance of the selected shunt resistor, relating its terminal voltage to the current flowing through that shunt.
documentation:
The shunt resistance is the lumped electrical opposition between the terminals of the selected shunt resistor. It characterizes one shunt member used to relate its terminal voltage to the current flowing through it.

For nonzero shunt current, the resistance is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{sh}} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{sh}}}{I_{\mathrm{sh}}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the selected shunt resistance, $V_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the terminal voltage represented by [voltage of shunt](name:voltage_of_shunt), and $I_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the current through the selected shunt.

The quantity applies to the individual selected shunt and is a lumped circuit property; it is not a material resistivity, the resistance of the entire divertor or vessel structure, or the shunt terminal voltage itself. The associated current can be inferred from the terminal voltage as $I_{\mathrm{sh}} = V_{\mathrm{sh}} / R_{\mathrm{sh}}$, so the resistance and [voltage of shunt](name:voltage_of_shunt) jointly define this current-inference relationship.

dd_sources.documentation: Shunt resistance

label_note: R_sh = V_sh/I_sh as a lumped circuit property; no registry entry applies; links resolve

description: Full physical extent of a rectangular Motional Stark Effect detector aperture along its first local tangential axis.
documentation:
This quantity is the full boundary-to-boundary extent of a Motional Stark Effect detector aperture measured along the detector's first local tangential direction. It describes one transverse dimension of the detector aperture and applies only to rectangular aperture geometry.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first local tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and $x_{1,\min}$ are the coordinates of the two opposite aperture boundaries along the first local tangential axis.

The quantity applies to the complete detector aperture rather than to an individual outline vertex or a partial opening. It is a non-negative geometric extent and is distinct from the aperture dimension along the second local tangential direction, represented by [second local tangential width of detector](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_detector). The boundary coordinates used to establish this extent are represented by quantities such as [first local tangential coordinate of detector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_detector).

dd_sources.documentation: Full width of the aperture in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3

label_note: narrows the generic detector width to a Motional Stark Effect detector aperture; also never reaches 'width' in the first line, against the width templates

description: Geometric acceptance of a neutron detector aperture as viewed from a neutron emission point, independent of detector efficiency and material response.
documentation:
The solid angle is the geometric measure of the aperture’s apparent extent from a neutron emission point. It is nonnegative and depends only on the aperture geometry, its orientation, and the source-point location; detector efficiency and converter response are excluded.

For a point source, the solid angle is defined by

$$
\Omega = \int_A \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\,dA
$$

where $A$ is the aperture surface, $r$ is the distance from the source point to an aperture element, and $\theta$ is the angle between the aperture normal and the line from the source point to that element. For a finite source region, the quantity denotes the specified volume average of this point-source solid angle; it does not imply weighting by the neutron emission profile. The geometric aperture dimensions described by [area of neutron detector] and [radius of neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) can determine the acceptance but do not include detector efficiency, which is a separate quantity described by [efficiency of neutron detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_neutron_detector).

dd_sources.documentation: Average solid angle that the detector covers within the voxel

description: Non-negative radius-like toroidal-flux label identifying the magnetic flux surface at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier.
documentation:
This quantity is the non-negative, radius-like toroidal-flux label of the magnetic flux surface at the H-mode [pedestal top](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal), the core-side shoulder of the edge transport barrier. It locates that surface on the physical toroidal-flux scale rather than specifying a geometric distance.

The coordinate is defined from enclosed toroidal magnetic flux by:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\rm tor}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux, $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal-field magnitude that sets the coordinate scale, and $\pi$ is the circular constant.

The value applies to the single nested magnetic flux surface passing through the pedestal top. It is a local flux-surface label, not a flux-surface or volume average, and it has no particle-population or charge-state aggregation.

This is the pedestal-top specialization of the parent [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), obtained by evaluating that coordinate on the pedestal-top surface. Unlike the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top), it retains the radius-like physical scale of the toroidal flux coordinate.

dd_sources.documentation: Toroidal flux coordinate. rho_tor = sqrt(b_flux_tor/(pi*b0)) ~ sqrt(pi*r^2*b0/(pi*b0)) ~ r [m]. The toroidal field used in its definition is indicated under global_quantities/b0

description: Normalized perturbed pressure Bessel-1 is the dimensionless total pressure response of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, formed from parallel and perpendicular pressure moments weighted by the first-order Bessel function evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument and normalized to the equilibrium species pressure.
documentation:
Normalized perturbed pressure Bessel-1 is the dimensionless total pressure response of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, formed from parallel and perpendicular pressure moments weighted by the first-order Bessel function evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument and normalized to the equilibrium species pressure. It is a species-resolved complex amplitude representing the finite-Larmor-radius part of the gyrocenter pressure response.

For species $s$, it is defined by the sum of the first-order Bessel-weighted parallel and perpendicular pressure moments divided by the equilibrium species pressure:

$$
\widehat{P}^{(J_1)}_s = \frac{P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} + P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}}{p_s}, \qquad P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s v_\parallel^2 J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}, \qquad P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s \frac{v_\perp^2}{2} J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}
$$

where $P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)}$ and $P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}$ are pressure-moment amplitudes with pressure units, $p_s=n_sT_s$ is the equilibrium species pressure when $T_s$ is expressed as energy per particle, $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are velocities parallel and perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the perturbation amplitude of the gyrocenter distribution. The first-order Bessel function $J_1$ is evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument $\lambda_s=k_\perp v_\perp/\Omega_s$, with $k_\perp$ the magnitude of the wave vector perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field and $\Omega_s=|q_s|B/m_s$ the positive cyclotron-frequency magnitude.

The total moment is the sum of parallel_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1 and [perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1](name:perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1). It is a gyrocenter-distribution moment with explicit $J_1(\lambda_s)$ weighting; it is distinct from normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure, which lacks this Bessel-1 weighting, and from particle-distribution pressure perturbations such as normalized_perturbed_pressure and normalized_total_particle_perturbed_pressure_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode. Because $J_1(0)=0$, this member vanishes at zero gyroaveraging argument.

In a linear eigenmode, $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the complex coefficient multiplying the chosen harmonic phase factor. This moment inherits the same arbitrary global amplitude and phase normalization as the eigenmode; changing the reference phase multiplies all perturbation amplitudes by the same complex factor, so its sign and phase are defined only relative to that reference.

dd_sources.documentation: Normalised pressure, defined as the sum of pressure_parallel and pressure_perpendicular

label_note: (P_par + P_perp)/p_s with J_1 weighting of the gyrocenter distribution, as the source sum; p_s as the registry gives; link resolves

description: Instantaneous equivalent-electron lithium source rate delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection systems, with each injected lithium atom contributing three equivalent-electron counts.
documentation:
The lithium source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral lithium with atomic number $Z_{\mathrm{Li}}=3$ is admitted to the plasma vessel by gas injection hardware, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. It is the lithium-specific component of the [source rate due to gas injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), rather than the raw lithium-atom delivery rate.

For lithium, the defining relation is:

$$
\dot{S}_{\mathrm{Li}} = Z_{\mathrm{Li}}\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Li}} = 3\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Li}}
$$

where $\dot{S}_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the lithium equivalent-electron source rate, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the raw lithium atom delivery rate in atoms per second, and $Z_{\mathrm{Li}}=3$ is lithium's dimensionless atomic number.

The equivalent-electron convention assigns three source counts to each injected lithium atom and excludes other gas species. This rate is the time derivative of the corresponding [accumulated lithium count]; its atomic-number weighting distinguishes it from the [helium-3 source rate due to gas injection](name:helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection).

Sign convention: Positive when lithium is delivered into the vessel, increasing the equivalent-electron particle inventory.

dd_sources.documentation: Value

label_note: dot-S where the registry symbol is S; unresolved [accumulated lithium count]

description: Signed coordinate of each vertex on a diagnostic-aperture boundary along the aperture’s object-local second tangential axis, defining one dimension of its geometric outline.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed position of a diagnostic-aperture boundary vertex along the aperture’s second local tangential direction. It is an intrinsic object-local coordinate used with the first local tangential direction to define the aperture outline, rather than a coordinate in the machine cylindrical frame.

For a vertex at position $\mathbf{r}_v$, relative to the local-frame origin $\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

Here $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the more-horizontal local tangent oriented toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ is the plasma-facing normal, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the resulting second local tangent. The toroidal angle is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This coordinate is distinct from the aggregate [area of the diagnostic aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture) and follows the same local-axis convention as the [second local tangential coordinate of a neutron detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector).

Sign convention: Positive when the vertex displacement projects in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$.

Positions along x2 axis

description: Dimensionless vector ratio of plasma flow velocity to the local sound speed, retaining directional components of the flow.
documentation:
The Mach-number vector is the plasma flow velocity normalized by the local sound speed. Its magnitude expresses flow speed relative to sound speed, while its directional components retain the signed flow projection. The family includes directional quantities such as the [parallel Mach number](name:parallel_mach_number).

$$
\mathbf{M} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{c_s}
$$

where $\mathbf{M}$ is the Mach-number vector, $\mathbf{v}$ is the plasma flow-velocity vector, and $c_s$ is the local sound speed. For a specified direction $a$, the corresponding component is $M_a = v_a/c_s$, where $v_a$ is the flow-velocity projection along that direction.

The quantity is dimensionless and is distinct from the unnormalized flow velocity; the sound-speed definition and the selected projection determine the specific physical interpretation of each component.
label_note: M = v/c_s with directional components; no registry entry applies; link resolves

description: Geometric distance from the center of a circular Bragg-crystal aperture to the edge of its active diffracting surface.
documentation:
The Bragg-crystal aperture radius is the transverse geometric extent of the circular active diffracting surface, measured from its center to its circumferential edge. It describes aperture size rather than the curvature of the crystal substrate.

For a boundary point of the aperture, the radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{ap}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}} \right\rVert
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ is the aperture radius, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}$ are position vectors in the aperture plane, with $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ expressed in meters.

For an ideal circular aperture, this distance is the same for every boundary point. It is analogous to the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), but must not be confused with the [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal] or its [vertical curvature](name:vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal).

dd_sources.documentation: Radius of the circle, used only if geometry_type/index = 2

label_note: writes r_ap where the registry radius symbol is R; unresolved [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal]

description: Radius of the circular ion-source surface from which neutral beams are extracted, defining the radial extent of its extraction aperture.
documentation:
This quantity is the radius of the circular ion-source surface from which a neutral-beam injector extracts its beam. It defines the radial extent of the extraction aperture.

For a circular boundary, the radius is the distance from the surface center to any point on its circumference:

$$
r_s = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_c \right\rVert
$$

where $r_s$ is the ion-source-surface radius, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position of a point on the circular boundary, $\mathbf{x}_c$ is the position of the circle center, and the norm denotes Euclidean distance.

The quantity applies to one neutral-beam injector unit and only to its circular ion-source geometry. It is not an aggregate over injector units and does not represent the radius of a beamlet-group tangency surface or another injector-associated aperture. For a rectangular ion-source aperture, the corresponding transverse dimensions are given by the [first local tangential width of the neutral-beam injector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_neutral_beam_injector) and [second local tangential width of the neutral-beam injector](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_neutral_beam_injector), rather than by this radius.

dd_sources.documentation: Radius of the circle, used only if geometry_type = 2

description: Wall-integrated neutral-particle number rate emitted into the plasma by surface-emission processes, with cold, thermal, and fast energy categories represented separately.
documentation:
This quantity is the total number rate of neutral particles emitted from plasma-facing wall surfaces into the adjacent plasma-facing region by surface-emission processes. It represents the contribution from the selected neutral population and energy category rather than a local surface flux.

The surface-integrated rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} \Gamma_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}$ is the emitted neutral-particle number rate, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutral-particle flux density due to surface emission at wall position $\mathbf{x}$, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the emitting wall surface, $\mathrm{d}A$ is its differential area element, and $c$ identifies the cold, thermal, or fast neutral energy category.

The aggregation is over the contributing wall surface; “total” does not imply summation over the cold, thermal, and fast categories, which remain distinct contributions. The quantity describes particles leaving the wall and excludes neutral particles incident on the wall, net incoming-minus-outgoing flux, and volumetric plasma sources.

It is the area integral of [neutral particle flux density due to surface emission](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission), whereas [incident neutral particle flux at the wall](name:incident_neutral_particle_flux_at_wall) describes particles arriving at the wall and is not included in this outgoing rate. It is also distinct from the per-area recombination contribution represented by [neutral particle flux at the wall due to recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

dd_sources.documentation: Particle flux from the wall corresponding to the conversion into various neutral types (first dimension: 1: cold; 2: thermal; 3: fast)

description: Vertical coordinate of a polarizer is the signed Z position of the polarizer geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Vertical coordinate of a polarizer is the $Z$ coordinate of the polarizer geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is the vertical component of the position of that center:

$$
z_{\mathrm{pol}} = Z(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{pol}})
$$

where $z_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the polarizer and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the position vector of the polarizer geometric center.

This quantity applies to the polarizer element itself and only to its geometric center. It is not a vertical extent, surface normal component, orientation angle, or local tangential coordinate of the polarizer.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a polarizer](name:radial_coordinate_of_polarizer) and [toroidal coordinate of a polarizer](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_polarizer), it specifies the polarizer center position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarizer geometric center lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the vertical origin.
