description: Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar diffusion coefficient governing runaway-electron spreading perpendicular to the magnetic field and across magnetic flux surfaces.
documentation:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar coefficient for Fickian diffusion of runaway electrons perpendicular to the magnetic field. In flux-surface transport descriptions, it represents the cross-surface diffusive transport component along the flux-surface normal, positive toward increasing flux label.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial \ell_\perp}
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive part of the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux), $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway-electron density](name:runaway_electron_density), and $\ell_\perp$ is distance along the local flux-surface-normal direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. The minus sign states that a positive diffusivity gives diffusive flux from larger toward smaller runaway-electron density.

This quantity applies only to the runaway-electron population and only to its perpendicular diffusive particle transport. It is not a parallel transport coefficient, not a convective velocity, and not the full [runaway-electron diffusivity](name:runaway_electron_diffusivity) when that broader quantity includes additional directional components.

The [perpendicular runaway-electron convection velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) gives the advective contribution to the same perpendicular particle balance, whereas $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ multiplies the density gradient. The sum of diffusive and convective contributions forms the modeled [perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

dd_sources.documentation: Effective diffusivity

description: Local plasma electrostatic potential at a Langmuir-probe position, representing the electrical state of the surrounding edge or boundary plasma rather than the probe’s floating potential.
documentation:
The local plasma electrostatic potential is the electric potential of the plasma evaluated at the spatial position of a Langmuir probe. It represents the surrounding plasma potential, not the electrical bias at which the probe draws zero net current.

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{U}{q}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the local plasma electrostatic potential, $U$ is the electrostatic potential energy of a positive test charge relative to the chosen electrical reference, and $q$ is that test charge.

This quantity applies locally at a Langmuir-probe position in the plasma edge, scrape-off layer, or boundary region. It is not a spatially averaged or globally representative potential, and it excludes the distinct floating potential defined by the zero-net-current condition on the probe.

It is a position-specific specialization of the broader [electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential); the parent quantity has the same physical meaning without requiring evaluation at a Langmuir-probe locus.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric potential energy of a positive test charge is greater than at the chosen electrical reference.

dd_sources.documentation: Plasma potential
Plasma potential

label_note: local plasma potential, distinct from the floating potential, as v_plasma; no registry entry applies; link resolves

description: Toroidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium ratio of volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure to the magnetic pressure of a reference toroidal field.
documentation:
Toroidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale of a reference toroidal field. It characterizes pressure relative to the toroidal magnetic field rather than the plasma-current-generated poloidal field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{2\mu_0}{V B_0^2}\int_V p_\perp\,dV
$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal beta, $p_\perp$ is the total perpendicular plasma pressure, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic-field strength, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability.

The volume integral aggregates the perpendicular pressure of all included plasma populations over the entire confined plasma volume, so this quantity is global rather than local or species-resolved. It is distinct from the current- and major-radius-based normalization of [poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta), and it does not include the additional engineering normalization applied by [normalized_toroidal_beta](name:normalized_toroidal_beta).

As the toroidal member of the [beta](name:beta) family, toroidal beta uses the reference toroidal magnetic pressure $B_0^2/(2\mu_0)$ as its denominator. The [beta](name:beta) parent represents this same toroidal pressure ratio at the family level, while the explicitly named toroidal form identifies the magnetic-field normalization.

description: Spectrometer-channel factor is the inverse effective spatial-and-angular acceptance of a single spectrometer channel. It normalizes a contribution aggregated over the channel's sampled volume and accepted viewing directions to a density per solid angle.
documentation:
Spectrometer-channel factor is the scalar inverse effective acceptance associated with one spectrometer channel. It represents the normalization from a quantity aggregated over the channel's sampled spatial region and accepted viewing directions to the corresponding density per solid angle.

The factor is defined from the effective spatial-and-angular acceptance of the channel:

$$
F_c = \left[\int_{\mathcal{V}_c}\int_{\Delta\Omega_c} W_c(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}})\, d\Omega\, dV\right]^{-1}
$$

where $F_c$ is the spectrometer-channel factor for channel $c$, $\mathcal{V}_c$ is the sampled volume, $\Delta\Omega_c$ is the accepted [solid angle], $W_c(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}})$ is the relative channel acceptance weighting at position $\mathbf{x}$ and viewing direction $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$, $dV$ is an infinitesimal volume element, and $d\Omega$ is an infinitesimal solid-angle element.

The scope is a single spectrometer channel and the aggregation is over the full spatial region and full accepted range of viewing directions represented by that channel. The population normalized by this factor is the set of signal contributors accepted by that same channel; the factor itself does not specify a particle species, charge state, wavelength interval, or spectral line.

This quantity is not the viewed volume, the solid angle, the étendue, detector gain, spectral response, detector efficiency, or a measured spectrum. For uniform acceptance it reduces to the reciprocal of the product of the sampled volume and accepted solid angle, and for nonuniform acceptance the integral gives the corresponding effective acceptance.

description: Geometric distance from the center of a reflector’s circular aperture to its circumferential boundary in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.
documentation:
The reflector aperture radius is the geometric distance from the center of the circular opening to its circumferential boundary. It defines the circular cross-section of the optical reflector through which light is directed toward the crystal.

For a circular aperture, its area is related to the radius by

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $A$ is the aperture area, $r$ is the reflector aperture radius, and $\pi$ is the mathematical constant relating a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

This quantity applies only to a reflector with circular aperture geometry. It describes the aperture radius, not a curvature radius of the reflector surface or the radius of a different optical element. The same geometric concept is used for the circular Bragg-crystal opening represented by [radius of Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal), while [radius of aperture](name:radius_of_aperture) describes a channel-level collimating aperture rather than the reflector aperture.

description: Signed component along the y axis of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror’s translation direction or rotation axis at its home position, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The quantity is the signed y projection of the unit vector defining an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror’s translation direction or rotation axis at its home position.

Let $d_y$ denote this component, $chat{\mathbf d}$ the defining unit direction vector, and $chat{\mathbf y}$ the unit vector along the positive y axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis:

$$
d_y = \hat{\mathbf d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf y}
$$

The corresponding [x-axis component](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [z-axis component](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) complete the Cartesian components of the same unit vector. This quantity describes direction, not the mirror’s position or displacement.

description: Dimensionless tritium-production contribution from one breeder-blanket module, normalized by the common incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.
documentation:
This quantity is the contribution of one breeder-blanket module to the blanket-level [tritium breeding ratio](name:tritium_breeding_ratio). It counts tritium atoms produced within that module's breeding regions and uses the common incident fusion-neutron normalization for the complete blanket.

$$
TBR_{\mathrm{module}} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{module}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{module}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in the module's breeding regions and $N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}$ is the incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.

For modules that partition the blanket breeding regions and share this denominator, the module contributions add to the blanket tritium breeding ratio. The quantity excludes tritium production outside the specified module and is not a separate normalization of the module's incident neutron count.

description: Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative geometric separation through the upper cap, measured normal to its exterior boundary and main-body interface.
documentation:
Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the cap that closes the module at its upper end. The reference surfaces are the upper exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the upper cap joins the main module body. It is the top-cap poloidal thickness in a poloidal $(R,Z)$ section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is distinct from the overall [thickness of a breeder blanket module] and the corresponding [lower thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The upper-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between the reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{upper}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are corresponding points on the upper exterior boundary and cap-to-body interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the upper cap in the poloidal section, and $t_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper-cap thickness. The quantity applies to one breeder blanket module and is not summed or averaged over modules. It is a non-negative geometric magnitude; it is not a signed coordinate, vertical height, or displacement and excludes the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or shielding layers.

dd_sources.documentation: Top cap poloidal thickness

label_note: opens 'Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is' against 'Thickness {locus}'; t_upper where the registry thickness symbol is d

description: Coolant mass throughput across a fluid-flow boundary, representing the rate at which coolant mass passes through a port or cooling loop.
documentation:
Coolant mass flow rate is the rate of coolant mass crossing a reference section of a fluid-flow path. It represents fluid throughput for cooling loops and plant-component ports without selecting one particular physical location.

The defining mass flow rate is

$$
\dot{m} = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m$ is the coolant mass crossing the reference section, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate coolant stream and is not a volumetric flow rate, coolant temperature, transit time, or thermal power. The enthalpy transport associated with the flow is $\dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the specific enthalpies of the coolant at the outlet and inlet; the [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) helps characterize the outlet state. The [coolant transit time of a plant component port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) is a related elapsed-time quantity, not part of the mass flow rate itself.

Sign convention: Positive when coolant crosses the reference section in the designated positive flow direction from inlet toward outlet.

Mass flow of the coolant going through the loop

description: Normalized phase-independent magnitude of an electrostatic-potential fluctuation relative to its reference field. It describes amplitude only, not the signed potential perturbation or its phase.
documentation:
Electrostatic potential amplitude is the phase-independent magnitude of a normalized electrostatic-potential fluctuation about a specified reference field. It represents the size of the fluctuation in the scalar electrostatic potential while discarding its sign or complex phase.

The amplitude is defined from the normalized fluctuation as:

$$
A_\Phi = \left|\frac{\Phi_\mathrm{fluc}}{\Phi_\mathrm{norm}}\right|
$$

where $A_\Phi$ is the electrostatic-potential amplitude, $\Phi_\mathrm{fluc}$ is the electrostatic-potential fluctuation relative to the chosen reference field, and $\Phi_\mathrm{norm}$ is the potential normalizing quantity specified for that fluctuation. The vertical bars denote the modulus; for a real representation they denote absolute value.

This quantity excludes the signed fluctuation, the reference potential itself, and the complex phase of a fluctuation representation. Electric-field perturbations require the signed or complex potential fluctuation; amplitude alone is insufficient to recover sign, phase, or gradient direction. The [perturbed electrostatic-potential amplitude](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_amplitude) is the perturbation-specific specialization of this amplitude concept.

description: Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region.
documentation:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member of [radius of a plasma filament], paired with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two radii. For the same annular geometry, the [area of a plasma filament] $A$ satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).

description: Minor length of an iron-core segment is the non-negative Euclidean length of the beta-side of the segment's oblique poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. The beta-side is inclined with respect to the height axis Z and defines the segment's extent along that side.
documentation:
Minor length of an iron-core segment is the non-negative Euclidean length of the $\beta$-side of the segment's oblique poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The $\beta$-side is the side whose direction in that poloidal cross-section is inclined by the angle $\beta$ with respect to the height axis $Z$.

This quantity applies to the geometric cross-section of one iron-core segment. Its aggregation convention is none: it is a single side length for the specified segment. It is not the toroidal extent, material volume, or any magnetic property of the iron core.

It is the $\beta$-side counterpart of the [major length of an iron-core segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment), which refers to the other oblique side length. Together with the corresponding inclination angles, these side lengths define the size of the segment's oblique poloidal cross-section.

description: Dimensionless factor controlling the relative contribution of an interferometer beam’s line-integrated electron-density residual to an equilibrium objective function.
documentation:
The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$, $y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density, either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the [calibration coefficient of an interferometer beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the [equilibrium weight of a flux loop] and the [equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe]; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint to which they apply.

description: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-tritium fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of D-T neutron emission per unit volume at each point in the plasma.
documentation:
The deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DT}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-T fusion reactions. Each D-T fusion reaction produces exactly one neutron, so this quantity is equal to the local D-T fusion reaction-rate density.

For reacting deuterium and tritium ion populations, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity, the velocity-averaged fusion cross-section evaluated over the relative-velocity distribution of the reacting ion populations; for thermal reactants it is the thermally averaged reactivity at the local ion temperature. No symmetry factor appears because the reactants are distinct species.

This quantity counts neutron production, not fusion energy deposition or neutron power. It is the D-T channel of the parent emissivity_due_to_fusion and the counterpart of [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which covers the neutron-emitting D-D branch. Its energy-weighted counterpart is [deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion), and integrating the emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the per-reaction neutron energy connects to the total_neutron_power.

description: Thermal radiation emitted by all divertor target surfaces, with each surface contribution weighted by its emissivity and summed over the divertor.
documentation:
This quantity is the total thermal radiative power emitted by the surfaces of all divertor targets. It represents surface emission governed by the local surface temperature and emissivity.

$$
P_{\mathrm{bb}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}} \int_{A_i} \epsilon_i\,\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}\,T_i^4\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the emitted thermal radiative power, $\mathcal{D}$ is the set of divertor target surfaces, $A_i$ is the surface area of target $i$, $\epsilon_i$ is its local thermal emissivity, $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, $T_i$ is its local absolute surface temperature, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element.

The quantity is aggregated over every divertor target surface and includes emissivity effects. It describes radiation emitted by the targets, not plasma power incident on them or radiation retained after reflection.

It is distinct from [absorbed radiated power of the divertor](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_divertor), which is the net radiative power deposited on the targets after accounting for incident and reflected radiation, and from [total incident power of the divertor](name:total_incident_power_of_divertor), which describes incoming plasma power rather than surface emission.

description: Time interval between successive sawtooth crash events, representing the duration of one complete sawtooth oscillation cycle in a tokamak plasma.
documentation:
The sawtooth period is the elapsed time from one sawtooth crash to the next consecutive crash, including the intervening growth and relaxation phases.

For successive crash times $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$, the period is defined by

$$
T_{\mathrm{st}} = t_{k+1} - t_k
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the sawtooth period and $t_k$ is the time of the $k$th crash. The quantity refers to the temporal spacing of consecutive crash events, not the duration of the crash itself or the duration of the preceding growth phase alone.

description: Characteristic outward distance over which a decaying heat-flux magnitude decreases by one e-folding in the scrape-off layer, without selecting an electron or ion channel.
documentation:
This quantity is the e-folding distance for a heat-flux magnitude that decreases outward from the confined plasma into the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It represents the common decay-length concept for both electron and ion heat fluxes without selecting either channel.

$$
L_q = \left|\frac{d\ln q}{dx}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $L_q$ is the e-folding length, $q$ is the positive heat-flux magnitude, and $x$ is outward distance normal to magnetic flux surfaces. The scale is defined locally where the logarithmic gradient is nonzero. The quantity is the heat-flux specialization of [decay length over scrape-off layer](name:decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer); its species-resolved instances include [electron heat decay length](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) and [ion heat decay length](name:ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

description: Poloidal beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative to the magnetic-pressure scale of the plasma-current-generated poloidal field.
documentation:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale generated by the plasma current. It characterizes pressure relative to the poloidal magnetic field rather than the toroidal magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{R_0\,\mu_0\,I_p^2}
$$

where $\beta_p$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current.

The pressure integral extends over the entire confined plasma volume and aggregates the pressure of all included plasma populations, so this quantity is global rather than local or species-resolved. It excludes any separate normalization based on minor radius or reference toroidal magnetic-field strength.

As the poloidal-field member of the [beta](name:beta) family, poloidal beta uses a current- and major-radius-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. It is distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which normalizes pressure to a toroidal magnetic-field scale, and from normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta, which applies an additional engineering normalization.

description: Counter-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the counter-passing orbit class. Counter-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction.
documentation:
Counter-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the counter-passing orbit class. Counter-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction.

The source contribution to the evolution of the counter-passing thermal particle number density is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)=\left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{source}}
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is this source rate, $n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged number density of counter-passing thermal particles, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $t$ is time, and the source subscript denotes the explicit particle-source contribution. Positive values represent net particle addition, while negative values represent net particle removal.

This quantity applies only to the thermal population in the counter-passing orbit class and is averaged over magnetic flux surfaces. It is not summed over co-passing or trapped orbit classes and excludes nonthermal particle populations. The corresponding [co-passing thermal particle source rate](name:co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) applies the same source definition to the co-passing orbit class.

The broader [thermal particle source rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate) aggregates the orbit-population contributions, including this counter-passing component; this quantity therefore represents only the counter-passing contribution rather than the total thermal source.

description: Coulomb logarithm is the dimensionless logarithm of the ratio between the largest Debye-shielded Coulomb impact parameter and the minimum effective impact parameter. It parameterizes the weak logarithmic sensitivity of binary Coulomb collisions to long- and short-range cutoffs.
documentation:
Coulomb logarithm is the dimensionless logarithm of the ratio between the largest Debye-shielded Coulomb impact parameter and the minimum effective impact parameter. It represents the cutoff factor for binary Coulomb collisions in a weakly coupled plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
\ln\Lambda = \ln\!\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $\Lambda$ is the Coulomb impact-parameter ratio, $b_{\max}$ is the maximum effective impact parameter set by Debye shielding, and $b_{\min}$ is the minimum effective impact parameter set by the short-range cutoff of the Coulomb interaction.

The unqualified quantity is the general Coulomb logarithm for a plasma population, without encoding a specific locus, species, or charge state. It has no intrinsic summation, volume-integration, or averaging convention; a localized or averaged Coulomb logarithm is a different qualified quantity. It is not itself a density, temperature, collision frequency, resistivity, Coulomb coupling parameter, Debye screening length, or impact parameter.

A locus-qualified member such as the [Coulomb logarithm at pedestal top](name:coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top) is the same physical quantity evaluated at that locus. Classical Coulomb-collision rates and collisional transport coefficients contain $\ln\Lambda$ as a multiplicative logarithmic factor; those coefficients include other plasma parameters and are distinct quantities.

description: Elevation angle of the central beamlet in a neutral-beam injector, measured between its axis and the horizontal plane at the center of the injection-unit surface.
documentation:
This quantity is the vertical elevation angle of the central beamlet in a neutral-beam injector, describing the beam's inclination relative to the horizontal plane at the center of the injection-unit surface.

For a signed elevation angle, the defining relation is:

$$
\alpha_v = \arcsin\left(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}\right)
$$

where $\alpha_v$ is the vertical inclination angle, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the central beamlet axis, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to the central beamlet of one neutral-beam injector unit and its associated beamlets group. It is a geometric direction parameter; no aggregation over the other beamlets in the group is included.

This angle describes vertical elevation only and does not specify horizontal or toroidal pointing, beamlet-group extent, or injector power. The related [vertical width of the beamlet group](name:vertical_width_of_beamlet_group) describes transverse beamlet-group extent rather than beam direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the central beamlet axis has a component toward increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

description: Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional torque vector transferred to thermal ions in a selected charge state.
documentation:
Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional torque vector transferred to thermal ions in a selected charge state is the net vector angular-momentum transfer received by that thermal-ion population through Coulomb collisions. It retains all spatial components of the collisional torque rather than only a single projection.

It is defined as the volume integral of the local Coulomb-collisional torque density transferred to the selected charge-state population:

$$
\boldsymbol{T}^{\mathrm{coll}}_{i,\chi} = \int_V \boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{coll}}_{i,\chi}(\boldsymbol{x})\, dV
$$

where $\boldsymbol{T}^{\mathrm{coll}}_{i,\chi}$ is this torque vector, $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{coll}}_{i,\chi}$ is the local Coulomb-collisional torque density transferred to thermal ions in charge state $\chi$ of ion species $i$, $\boldsymbol{x}$ is position, $V$ is the integrated plasma volume, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The scope is one thermal-ion species in one selected charge state within the integrated plasma volume; as an extensive vector quantity, it is volume-integrated and not averaged. It is charge-state-resolved, not summed over charge states, and excludes electrons, neutrals, fast ions, external momentum input, noncollisional electromagnetic torques, charge-exchange or other atomic-process torques, transport-flux divergences, and wall or boundary torques.

When resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, [`toroidal_thermal_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions`](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions) is the $\phi$ projection of this vector. Only that toroidal projection enters [`total_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions`](name:total_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions); the radial and vertical components of this vector are not included in that scalar total. The charge-state-summed vector [`thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions`](name:thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions) is obtained by summing this vector over all charge states of the same thermal-ion species.

Sign convention: Positive when a component resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame points along $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$, respectively; the toroidal projection is positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

description: Net radiative power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces, equal to incident plasma radiation minus the portion reflected back toward the plasma.
documentation:
Net absorbed radiative power is the total photon power retained by plasma-facing wall surfaces after reflection losses. It represents the wall's radiative power load and excludes nonradiative particle, conductive, and other thermal-power contributions.

The net retained power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs,wall}} = P_{\mathrm{inc,wall}} - P_{\mathrm{ref,wall}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs,wall}}$ is the absorbed radiative power at the wall, $P_{\mathrm{inc,wall}}$ is the total plasma-radiation power incident on the wall, and $P_{\mathrm{ref,wall}}$ is the portion of that incident radiation reflected away from the wall. The quantity is integrated over the wall rather than expressed as a local power per unit area.

This wall-wide quantity includes the aggregate radiative load over all applicable plasma-facing wall surfaces. It is broader than [absorbed radiated power of divertor](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_divertor) and [absorbed radiated power of breeder blanket module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which apply the same incident-minus-reflected principle to specified wall components, and it is distinct from [total incident neutral energy flux at wall](name:total_incident_neutral_energy_flux_at_wall), which describes neutral-particle energy transport rather than absorbed photon power.

description: Ratio of ambient water-vapor partial pressure to its saturation vapor pressure at the detector, describing local moisture conditions that can affect detector performance.
documentation:
Relative humidity at the detector is the ambient water-vapor content expressed relative to the maximum water-vapor content supported at the local air temperature.

It is defined by

$$
RH = \frac{p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}{p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)}
$$

where $RH$ is relative humidity, $p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ is the partial pressure of water vapor surrounding the detector, $p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)$ is the saturation vapor pressure of water, and $T$ is the local air temperature. The reported fraction is bounded from 0 to 1.

This quantity describes the environmental moisture condition at the detector and is not absolute humidity, air temperature, or a detector-response property. It is distinct from an intrinsic detection metric such as [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which describes photon-registration probability rather than the surrounding environment.

description: Parallel refractive index is the signed component of the refractive-index vector projected onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction, equal to the parallel wave-vector component normalized by the vacuum wavenumber.
documentation:
The parallel refractive index $N_\parallel$ is the signed component of the refractive-index vector projected onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It is the field-aligned part of the electromagnetic phase-gradient direction normalized to the vacuum reference and retains whether phase propagation is along or against the magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
N_\parallel = \mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}}{k_0}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $N_\parallel$ is the parallel refractive index, $\mathbf{n}$ is the [refractive-index vector](name:refractive_index), $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the local equilibrium magnetic field.

This quantity applies locally to the electromagnetic wave under consideration at the point where the wave vector and magnetic field are evaluated. It is a signed scalar projection, not the full [refractive-index vector](name:refractive_index), not a coordinate component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and not an aggregate over multiple waves, ray branches, or launch-spectrum components unless a separate quantity explicitly defines such an aggregate.

The complementary field-normal representation is the [perpendicular refractive index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index), which is the magnitude of the projection onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field. With that convention, the refractive-index magnitude satisfies $|\mathbf{n}|^2 = N_\parallel^2 + N_\perp^2$, where $N_\perp$ is the perpendicular refractive index.

Sign convention: Positive when the wave-vector component parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field points in the direction of that magnetic field.

description: Green-function coefficient giving expected neutron-detector counts from one neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and energy bin.
documentation:
The neutron-detector response function is the expected registered count contribution from a neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and neutron-energy bin. It characterizes the detector-specific mapping from neutron emission to detected events.

The response enters the forward relation

$$
N_d = \sum_v \sum_k G_d(v,E_k)\,S(v,E_k)
$$

where $N_d$ is the total expected count for detector $d$, $G_d(v,E_k)$ is this response function, $v$ labels a plasma voxel, $E_k$ labels the $k$th neutron-energy bin, and $S(v,E_k)$ is the neutron yield from voxel $v$ in that bin.

The quantity applies to one neutron detector and to the contribution of a specified source voxel and energy bin; its count response is aggregated over the detector events attributable to that source contribution. It is not the neutron emissivity, the geometric acceptance alone, or an energy-dependent efficiency alone. The geometric distinction is given by [solid angle of a neutron detector](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector) illustrates an efficiency quantity that does not represent this neutron-specific source-to-count response.

description: Energy-dependent probability that an incident neutron within a specified energy band is recorded as an accepted count by the neutron detector.
documentation:
Neutron spectral efficiency is the conditional probability that an incident neutron in the detector's assigned energy interval produces an accepted detector count.

For incident neutron energy $E$, the efficiency is defined by

$$
\epsilon(E) = \frac{N_{\mathrm{recorded}}(E)}{N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)}
$$

where $\epsilon(E)$ is the detection probability, $N_{\mathrm{recorded}}(E)$ is the number of accepted counts produced by neutrons in a narrow interval around energy $E$, and $N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)$ is the number of neutrons impacting the detector in that interval.

This quantity applies only to the neutron detector and its specified incident-energy band. It is a conditional probability for individual incident neutrons, not a sum over neutron populations or energy bands, and it excludes the incident neutron flux itself and detector signals rejected by the counting criterion.

The energy domain is bounded by the detector-band limits, including the [maximum neutron energy of the neutron detector](name:neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector). It is the neutron counterpart of [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which describes the analogous counting probability for photons rather than neutrons.

description: Rate at which particles represented as equivalent electrons are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping, giving global electron-equivalent exhaust throughput.
documentation:
The rate at which particles of the electron-equivalent population are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping is the global scalar representation of the wall particle-removal flux. It describes pumped particle exhaust using equivalent-electron counting rather than a local wall flux density.

The global removal rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}}$ is the pumped particle-removal rate expressed in equivalent electrons, $N_{e,\mathrm{removed}}$ is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by wall pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is aggregated over the wall and represents the total pumping throughput for the electron-equivalent population. The electron-equivalent basis does not assert that all removed particles are physical electrons, and the quantity is not an areal flux density, an electrical current, or a rate for one specified neutral species.

It is the electron-specific specialization of the general [particle-removal flux at the wall due to pumping](name:particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping). In contrast, [neutral particle flux at the wall due to pumping](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping) uses a specified neutral species as its counting population rather than equivalent-electron counting.

description: Dimensionless orbit average of a specified function along a marker's final transit or trapping orbit.
documentation:
An orbit integral is the normalized accumulation of a dimensionless function along the trajectory of a single test-particle marker. The function may represent an orbit-dependent phase, drift contribution, equilibrium factor, or perturbation harmonic.

For a marker orbit ending at evaluation time $t$, the orbit integral is defined by

$$
I(t) = \frac{1}{\tau} \int_{t-\tau}^{t} f(t')\,dt'
$$

where $I(t)$ is the orbit-integral value, $\tau$ is the marker's transit or trapping time, $t$ is the evaluation time, $t'$ is the integration time, and $f(t')$ is the specified dimensionless function evaluated along the marker trajectory.

The quantity applies to one marker and to its last transit or trapping orbit; it is an orbit average rather than an unnormalized time integral. It does not itself denote a Fourier mode number, particle distribution, or orbit duration.

When $f$ contains Fourier harmonics, its arguments may include the [toroidal wave mode number](name:toroidal_wave_mode_number) or [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number). Those mode numbers parameterize the integrand, whereas the orbit integral is the resulting trajectory-averaged value.

dd_sources.documentation: Values of the orbit integrals

label_note: orbit average (1/tau) int f dt' over the marker's last transit or trapping orbit; no registry entry applies; links resolve

description: Net ion momentum source is the area-normalized vector rate of directional momentum transfer to all ion charge states, including all contributing physical processes.
documentation:
Net ion momentum source is the area-normalized vector rate of directional momentum transfer to the total ion population, summed over all ion charge states. It retains the direction of the net transfer rather than reducing it to a magnitude.

The charge-state and process aggregation is

$$
\mathbf{S}_{i} = \sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \mathbf{S}_{i,z,p}
$$

where $\mathbf{S}_{i}$ is the total-ion momentum source vector, $z$ indexes ion charge states in $\mathcal{Z}_{i}$, $p$ indexes contributing physical processes in $\mathcal{P}$, and $\mathbf{S}_{i,z,p}$ is the corresponding source for one charge state and process. The [ion momentum source](name:ion_momentum_source) defines the same directional momentum-transfer concept at the general species and projection level.

This quantity includes all ion charge states and excludes neutral species. Its directional projections are components of the same vector, including the [parallel net ion momentum source](name:parallel_net_ion_momentum_source).

Sign convention: Positive when a projected component points along its defined positive direction—$+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, or along the defined positive field-parallel direction.

description: Reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum-wavelength intercept of the channel's linear detector-pixel dispersion relation at pixel coordinate k = 0.
documentation:
Reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum wavelength assigned by a linear wavelength calibration to detector-pixel coordinate $k=0$. It is the intercept term of the affine relation between detector-pixel coordinate and vacuum wavelength for that channel.

The linear calibration relation is

$$
\lambda(k) = g k + \lambda_0
$$

where $\lambda(k)$ is the vacuum wavelength at detector-pixel coordinate $k$, $k$ is a dimensionless detector-pixel coordinate, $g$ is the signed dispersion coefficient in $\mathrm{m}$ per pixel-coordinate unit, and $\lambda_0$ is the reference calibration wavelength.

This quantity is the intercept $\lambda_0$, not the dispersion coefficient $g$ and not the wavelength evaluated at any nonzero detector-pixel coordinate. The sign of $g$ encodes whether vacuum wavelength increases or decreases with increasing $k$; the reference calibration wavelength itself is a wavelength value at the chosen coordinate origin.

description: Poloidal angle of a beam-tracing beam point is its angular position about the magnetic axis in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from the outward +R direction.
documentation:
Poloidal angle of a beam-tracing beam point is the angular coordinate of that point about the magnetic axis in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is measured from the outward $+R$ direction and uses the clockwise poloidal-angle sense in the $(R,Z)$ plane.

The clockwise branch of the angle is defined by the displacement of the beam point relative to the magnetic axis:

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[-(Z - Z_\mathrm{axis}),\, R - R_\mathrm{axis}\right]
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle of the beam-tracing beam point, $R$ and $Z$ are the beam point major radius and vertical height, and $R_\mathrm{axis}$ and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ are the major radius and vertical height of the magnetic axis. The function $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ is the quadrant-resolving arctangent; the negative first argument makes increasing $\theta$ clockwise when the cross-section is viewed with $R$ increasing to the right and $Z$ increasing upward.

The scope is the position of beam-tracing beam trajectory points in the wave-propagation geometry. The value is pointwise for each trajectory point; no averaging over beam cross-section, path segment, or multiple beams is implied.

This quantity is not the beam launch angle, propagation-direction angle, wave-vector pitch, toroidal angle $\phi$, or a flux-surface label. It is the beam-point locus counterpart of the [poloidal angle of a measurement position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position) and uses the same angular sense as the [poloidal angle of a flux surface](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface); the distinction is the locus, not the angular convention.

Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the magnetic axis to the beam point is clockwise from the outward $+R$ direction in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame viewed with $R$ increasing to the right and $Z$ increasing upward.

description: Full physical extent of the rectangular soft X-ray detector aperture measured between its two boundaries along the detector-local first tangential (X1) direction.
documentation:
This quantity is the full end-to-end width of a soft X-ray detector's rectangular aperture along its object-local first tangential axis, denoted X1. It defines one dimension of the detector acceptance geometry used in etendue calculations.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\mathrm{max}} - x_{1,\mathrm{min}}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first-local-tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\mathrm{max}}$ and $x_{1,\mathrm{min}}$ are the coordinates of the two opposing aperture boundaries along X1.

The quantity applies to one soft X-ray detector aperture with rectangular geometry and represents the complete boundary-to-boundary extent, not a half-width, an outline coordinate, the second local tangential width, or an aggregate over multiple detectors. The boundary coordinates used in the defining difference are provided by the [first local tangential coordinate of the soft X-ray detector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector). The same geometric convention is used for the corresponding [first local tangential width of a hard X-ray detector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_hard_xray_detector), while [extent of the soft X-ray detector](name:extent_of_soft_xray_detector) denotes a broader detector-size quantity rather than this specifically defined X1 aperture dimension.

description: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
Thermal electron power at an inside flux surface quantifies the total rate at which coherent wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume bounded by a given magnetic flux surface. It is the thermal-electron contribution to [electron power at an inside flux surface](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), distinct from the suprathermal contribution [fast electron power at an inside flux surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The quantity is obtained by integrating the flux-surface-averaged thermal-electron power density $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho') \frac{dV}{d\rho'} \, d\rho'
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho)$ is the cumulative absorbed power, $\rho$ labels the limiting magnetic flux surface, $\rho'$ is the integration variable, $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ is the local thermal-electron absorbed power density, and $dV/d\rho'$ is the differential enclosed volume per unit flux-surface label. Only absorption by bulk thermal electrons is included; fast-electron and ion absorption, launched power, and absorption outside the enclosed volume are excluded. At the outermost closed flux surface, it gives the total wave power absorbed by thermal electrons.

description: Deuterium prefill count is the total amount of neutral deuterium introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with one count unit per atom.
documentation:
Deuterium prefill count is the total amount of neutral deuterium (D) introduced during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each neutral deuterium atom contributes one equivalent electron.

The equivalent-electron count is obtained by accumulating injected deuterium atoms over the prefill interval and weighting them by the deuterium atomic number:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{D,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{D}} N_{\mathrm{D,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{D}} \int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\,dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{D,prefill}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{D,prefill}}$ is the accumulated neutral-deuterium atom count, $Z_{\mathrm{D}}=1$ is the deuterium atomic number, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the deuterium atom injection rate, $t_0$ is the prefill start time, and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time.

This quantity includes only deuterium introduced before breakdown and excludes wall recycling, neutral-beam or pellet fueling, later gas injection, and retained or ionized inventory. It is the deuterium-specific component of [prefill_count](name:prefill_count) and uses the same isotope-resolved convention as tritium_prefill_count.

description: Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies redistribution of reflected radiation between ideal specular and ideal diffuse behavior: 0 denotes ideal specular reflection and 1 denotes ideal diffuse reflection.
documentation:
Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies how the element partitions reflected radiation between a specular component and a diffuse component. The endpoint value zero denotes ideal specular reflection, and the endpoint value one denotes ideal diffuse reflection.

The parameter is defined from the reflected-power partition as

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{spec}} + P_{\mathrm{diff}}, \qquad r = \frac{P_{\mathrm{diff}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{spec}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}}, \qquad 0 \le r \le 1
$$

where $r$ is the roughness parameter, and $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{spec}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{diff}}$ are radiant powers in watts for the total reflected, ideal-specular, and diffuse reflected components under the same incident radiation and optical state.

This quantity is not a metrological surface-height roughness such as an rms height or correlation length. Intermediate values specify the diffuse fraction of reflected power in the stated partition; they do not by themselves prescribe the angular distribution of the diffuse component, require Lambertian scattering, or include transmitted or absorbed power.

description: Toroidal coordinate of a neutron detector is the angular location of the detector's geometric center about the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Toroidal coordinate of a neutron detector is the angular coordinate of the detector's geometric center about the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate.

For a detector center whose projection onto the plane perpendicular to $\hat{Z}$ has Cartesian coordinates $x_c$ and $y_c$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and $\phi=0$ along $+\hat{x}$, the toroidal coordinate is

$$
\phi_\mathrm{n} = \operatorname{atan2}(y_c, x_c)
$$

where $\phi_\mathrm{n}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the neutron detector, and $x_c$ and $y_c$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the detector geometric center projected onto the plane perpendicular to $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies specifically to a neutron detector and to the point representing its geometric center. The aggregation convention is none: it denotes one detector center, not an average, sum, or representative angle over several detectors; it is geometrically undefined for a center on the symmetry axis, where no toroidal direction is selected.

It is not a detector orientation, angular extent, line-of-sight direction, or the toroidal coordinate of an aperture or other component. It specializes the generic [toroidal coordinate of a detector](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_detector) to neutron detectors and is distinct from [toroidal coordinate of an aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture), which refers to an aperture's own geometric center.

Sign convention: Positive when the detector geometric center is displaced in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

description: Total electromagnetic power emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron radiation while their gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field.
documentation:
Power due to synchrotron radiation is the total electromagnetic power emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron radiation while their gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field. It is a mechanism-specific contribution to the plasma radiative power and refers to emitted radiation, not stored electromagnetic energy.

For an emitting plasma volume $V$, the quantity is defined by the volume integral of the local synchrotron volumetric emissivity:

$$
P_{\mathrm{syn}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{syn}}$ is the power due to synchrotron radiation, $p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local synchrotron volumetric emissivity formed from the relativistic electron phase-space distribution and the local magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $dV$ is a volume element.

This quantity includes only synchrotron emission and excludes [bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and [power due to line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation). It denotes gross electromagnetic power emitted by the radiating electrons and is distinct from net synchrotron power escaping a plasma-facing or material boundary after reabsorption or reflection.

description: Electron temperature averaged along an open magnetic field line between upstream and downstream locations in the scrape-off layer.
documentation:
This quantity is the mean bulk-electron thermal temperature along an open magnetic field line through the scrape-off layer, between specified upstream and downstream locations. It represents the connected-field-line average rather than the local electron temperature at a single position.

The field-line average is defined by

$$
\overline{T}_e = \frac{1}{L_{\parallel}} \int_{s_u}^{s_d} T_e(s)\,ds
$$

where $T_e(s)$ is the local electron temperature, $s$ is arc length along the magnetic field line, $s_u$ and $s_d$ are the upstream and downstream endpoints, and $L_{\parallel}=s_d-s_u$ is the connection length.

The quantity applies to the bulk electron population in the scrape-off layer and is aggregated by arc-length averaging along one open field line. It excludes local single-point temperature values and does not represent a flux-surface or volume average.

This is the electron-species specialization of the [field-line-averaged temperature over the scrape-off layer](name:field_line_average_temperature_over_scrape_off_layer). It is distinct from the corresponding [ion field-line-averaged temperature](name:ion_field_line_average_temperature_over_scrape_off_layer), which uses the ion temperature, and from [temperature over the scrape-off layer](name:temperature_over_scrape_off_layer), which averages over the region rather than along a connected field line.

description: Number density of the effective deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
Number density of the effective deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for that effective species evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local effective deuterium-tritium number density is the zeroth velocity moment of its distribution function at a boundary point:

$$
n_{DT}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \int f_{DT}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{DT}$ is the effective deuterium-tritium fuel-pseudo-species number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity of the effective pseudo-species, $f_{DT}$ is its phase-space distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies to the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture represented as one effective pseudo-species, rather than to separate deuterium and tritium populations. It is a local boundary value with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume, and no additional charge-state aggregation is implied by the effective-species representation.

It is the deuterium-tritium-specific instance of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). Unlike flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary, it denotes the local value at the plasma boundary rather than an average over that last closed magnetic flux surface.

description: Dimensionless ratio comparing a particle species’ kinetic temperature with the positive reference temperature on the same magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
The quantity expresses the kinetic temperature of a selected particle species relative to a single reference thermal scale on the same magnetic flux surface. It is the normalized counterpart of [particle temperature](name:particle_temperature), while retaining the species dependence of the numerator.

It is defined by

$$
T_p^{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{T_p}{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $T_p$ is the kinetic temperature of the selected particle species and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference temperature for the flux surface.

The ratio is dimensionless and is not an absolute temperature; its value depends on the specified reference temperature.

description: Dimensionless ratio quantifying how effectively a plant system converts input power or energy into a specified useful output, abstracting over thermal and net efficiency definitions.
documentation:
The efficiency of a plant system is a dimensionless performance metric expressing the fraction of input power or energy that the plant converts into a specified useful output. The exact physical scope depends on the efficiency type applied: [thermal efficiency](name:thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system) characterizes heat-to-work conversion across all thermodynamic conversion stages, while [net efficiency](name:net_efficiency_of_plant_system) accounts for the signed ratio of exported electrical power to total plant electrical consumption including recirculating power.

The general defining relation takes the form:

$$
\eta = \frac{W_\text{out}}{W_\text{in}}
$$

where $W_\text{out}$ is the useful output (work, exported electrical power, or heat converted to work) and $W_\text{in}$ is the total input power or energy over the same operating interval.

Efficiency is evaluated from calorimetric heat-flow surveys, electrical generation meters, and auxiliary power consumption measurements across all plant subsystems. For fusion facilities, thermal conversion efficiencies in steam-cycle plants lie in the range 30–45%, and net electrical efficiencies are further reduced by recirculating power fractions for heating, current drive, and cooling systems.
